Headline: WATCH FOR: Cargo and transport disruption in Catalonia due to Supreme Court ruling
Details: Risk Analysis: There is a significant likelihood of ongoing protests by pro-Catalan independence activists in Barcelona and the wider Catalonia region in response to Spain’s Supreme Court barring Catalonia’s regional president from holding office, as seen at Plaza Sant Jaume, Barcelona, on 29 September. Although concerns about the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) virus are likely to limit numbers of protesters to several hundreds in any single location, previous protests by activists, including those from the left-wing pro-independence Arran and CRD groups, have caused significant disruption in central Barcelona. The risk of street fighting and vandalism will escalate if anti-independence activists connected to the far-right Vox party mount counter-protests. Headline: Distribution of Tribune Publishing Newspapers Temporarily Disrupted by Malware Attack
Details:
On Friday, December 28, a malware attack disrupted production of multiple newspapers owned by Tribune Publishing. This includes the Los Angeles Times, the Chicago Tribune, the Baltimore Sun, and the San Diego Union-Tribune. The malware was initially detected on Friday night and affected the ability of the papers to distribute Saturday editions. Additionally, west coast editions of the Wall Street Journal and New York Times were also affected as they share a production platform with the Los Angeles Times. There have been no reports that personal data of subscribers, online users, or advertising clients was compromised. 
 
	Assessment: As of this writing, no group had claimed responsibility for the malware attack. Initial assessments deemed the malware originated outside the United States and may be a form of  Ryuk  ransomware. These types of attacks are generally used to deliberately target specific assets within the affected network. Cybersecurity experts have warned it is difficult to ascertain the identity of attackers because malware code is freely distributed online. It is possible that since this attack only affected distribution of papers and did not affect personal data, it was meant to be more disruptive rather than malicious. Normal distribution has resumed at all of the newspapers that were affected. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring developments involving malicious cyber threats and to maintain strong cybersecurity practices in order to mitigate the risk of a compromising attack.

Headline: Cocaine Seizures at Brazil Ports Rose by 50 Percent in 2019; Risk of Disruption for Affected Cargo
Details:
Brazil s Department of Federal Revenue (RFB) recently announced that the number of cocaine seizures at ports in Brazil has jumped 50 percent between January and October of this year, compared to the year prior. Authorities this year have seized 47.1 tons of cocaine at ports, compared to 35.1 tons last year. The majority of seizures have occurred in the ports of Santos, Paranagua, Natal, and Itajai. Authorities found that traffickers would bribe port workers to break open sealed containers and hide cocaine inside, while the companies shipping their legal goods would not necessarily be aware their shipments had been compromised. Brazilian authorities cited an increase in cocaine production in Andean countries as a factor in the rise of confiscations, while also remarking that training of RFB agents has increased and the majority of ports are now equipped with x-ray machines.

Assessment: The apparent increase in cocaine smuggling through Brazilian ports to destinations in Europe poses challenges to businesses that could face shipment disruptions as a result of increased screening at ports, or even delays or confiscations of legitimate shipments used by traffickers to conceal drug shipments. Chemicals and coffee have been among the cargoes targeted for smuggling. Although the Netherlands, France, and Belgium have been primary intended European ports of arrival for confiscated drug shipments through Brazilian ports, the RFB has recorded increased seizures of drugs heading to Portugal and Italy as traffickers attempt alternate routes with the aim of avoiding the scrutiny along more established routes for drug shipments. While no major disruptions to port operations had been indicated by authorities in conjunction with the increase in cocaine seizures this year, it is advised to be aware of the potential for delay or disruption from any major anti-drug operations as well as overall efforts to improve screening at ports with high recorded drug trafficking attempts.

Headline: Explosion Targets Oil Tanker at Port of Jeddah, Highlighting Vulnerability to Commercial Shipping
Details:
No injuries were reported following an explosion that targeted an oil tanker at the Saudi Arabian Port of Jeddah early on Monday, December 14. According to Saudi sources, the British-owned, Singapore-flagged tanker, BW Rhine, was reportedly targeted by a bomb-laden boat at approximately 12:40 AM local time, causing an explosion and a fire. Although the ship’s crew and firefighters reportedly extinguished the fire, the attack caused damage to the tanker’s body, though there are no concerns as of this writing of an oil spill. Reports also indicated that the attack shut down Jeddah port, though as of now, it remains unclear if operations have resumed. The BW Rhine had docked at Jeddah on December 12, carrying over 65,000 tons of gasoline from an Aramco refinery at Yanbu for consumption in the Kingdom. Following the attack, the United Kingdom Marine Trade Operations issued an advisory, stating that an investigation has been opened, and urging all ships in the area to exercise caution. The attack has not yet been claimed by any group. 



Assessment: The incident underscores the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure, and highlights risks posed to commercial shipping in the Red Sea. The explosion also marks the fourth such assault targeting Saudi energy infrastructure in a month. Most recently, a mine exploded off the coast of Shuqaiq and damaged a Maltese-flagged oil tanker on November 25, in an attack claimed by Houthi rebels. Although Saudi officials have not blamed anyone for the most recent attack on December 14, bomb-laden boats and limpet mines have been used periodically by Houthi rebels in the past, suggesting the Shia militia was likely responsible. Saudis typically claim to intercept and destroy unmanned, bomb-laden boats; however, any damage to commercial vessels in this region has the potential to damage production facilities, possibly affecting supply chains and oil prices, as the Red Sea is a vital shipping lane for international energy supplies and other cargo. If attacks successfully damage oil production or result in casualties, this would further increase the risk of conflict in the area. Heightened security is likely at all commercial ports in the Bab al Mandeb Strat in the Red Sea, as well as the Persian Gulf, in the coming days.

Headline: Criminal Investigation Ongoing Following Fire and Explosion Involving Butane at LA Warehouse
Details:
On Saturday, May 16, over 200 firefighters responded to multiple explosions and large fire at a warehouse, near Boyd St and S San Pedro St, in Los Angeles, CA. The warehouse was owned by Smoke Tokes, a supplier of butane honey oil. Butane is highly flammable and is believed to be the reason for the explosions Saturday. At least 12 firefighters were injured, including two critically. A large explosion occurred around 6:30 PM PDT while a number of firefighters were already inside the building, which led to the majority of the injuries. There were no reports of widespread evacuations in relation to the fire and explosions. On Monday, authorities announced that a criminal investigation had been opened into the explosion. 



Assessment: No further disruptions from the fire are being reported and there are no reports the fire was started intentionally. The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) is working in conjunction with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) on the criminal investigation related to the explosion. City officials stated that Smoke Tokes is considered a “ghost business” as they do not appear in local regulatory records. The butane honey oil the company produces is used in smoking and vaping products; however, because of the volatility of butane there are strict restrictions on where facilities using it are allowed to operate. Such businesses are normally limited to specific industrial areas and are not legal within the city of Los Angeles. Media sources also reported that a fire at a different business called Smoke Tokes occurred at a nearby address in 2016. That fire also involved over 160 firefighters and multiple pressurized gas cylinders; however, there were no reports of injuries in the 2016 fire. As of this writing, it remains unclear if the two businesses are connected or the same business.

Headline: Security Increased across the Country for Eid al-Adha on 8/22; No Specific Threats Reported
Details:
On Tuesday, Inspector General of Police Mohammad Javed Patwary said that security had been increased across the country for Eid al-Adha on Wednesday, August 22. Special attention has been given to prayer grounds in Dhaka, Chittagong, Sylhet, Barisal, Khulna, Rajshahi, and Rangpur. Additional security has also been deployed to Bangladesh s largest prayer ground at Sholakia in Kishoreganj, Dhaka Division, where three people died in an attack in 2016 that was carried out by the Jamaat-ul-Mujahideen Bangladesh (JMB) Islamist militant group during Eid al-Fitr. Police are also monitoring transportation hubs like bus terminals, railway stations, and ports. 
 
	 
		Assessment: While police have not reported any specific threats associated with Eid al-Adha, there is still a significant threat in the country from JMB. Police continue to arrest JMB militants across the country, including last week in Dhaka where four JMB militants were detained and found with sharp weapons and bomb-making materials. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue and exercise caution, especially around religious sites that have been targeted in the past. Delays associated with an increased security presence should also be expected.

Headline: MQM Worker Killed in Overnight Shooting
Details:
Pakistani media sources report that a worker from the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) was killed in a gun attack in Karachi late Monday. Another MQM worker was injured in the incident, which involved six gunmen on motorcycles who opened fire on the MQM-P union council (UC) office in the New Karachi area of the city. The assailants fled the scene and reportedly remain at large. 
 
	Assessment: No group immediately claimed credit for the attack, and the motivation behind it remains unclear. In the past, secular-minded parties such as MQM have been targeted by Islamist militant groups, including in Karachi. The MQM has also come under pressure from the Pakistani security establishment, which has waged a crackdown against the party in recent years. From a security standpoint, demonstrations and labor strikes are common in association with acts of political violence in Pakistan, most of which are accompanied by rioting and other forms of civil unrest. Although no specific details have been announced in this regard, Resilience360 customers in Karachi should monitor local media outlets for associated security developments.

Headline: Pirates Kidnap Three from Tanker in Gulf of Guinea; Highlighting High Threat from Piracy
Details:
Earlier this week, sources reported that pirates kidnapped three crewmembers from a tanker in the Gulf of Guinea. Details on the incident remain scarce and disputed; however, the Stelios K tanker reportedly went dark on November 16 either off the coast of Lagos, Nigeria or Lome, Togo. The vessel is believed to have been boarded by pirates who remained onboard until at least November 19. The vessel has since been located and three crewmembers have been reported missing. The Nigerian Navy is searching for the attackers, but no arrests have immediately been reported.



Assessment: The incident brings the total number of kidnappings in the Gulf of Guinea to at 23 so far this year, including 10 in November alone. It also brings the total number of crewmembers kidnapped to nearly 120. While kidnappings remain common in the Gulf of Guinea and are often carried out by piracy groups to secure ransom payments, there have been some suggestions that the latest incident may instead have been related to a business dispute. Regardless, the incident has highlighted the high threat from piracy across the Gulf of Guinea, particularly during the dry season, which generally runs from November to March. Due to the high threat from pirates, all nonessential travel in the Gulf of Guinea should be avoided. Those continuing to operate in the area are urged to exercise a high level of vigilance at all times and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to deter potential attackers.

Headline: Chinese and Hong Kong Business Sectors Targeted in String of Measures in Ongoing Tensions with US
Details:
A number of recent steps taken by the United States government have the potential to impact businesses with operational ties to China or Hong Kong as relations between China and the US continue to deteriorate. This week, the US commerce department further restricted Chinese technology company Huawei from using US technology by adding 38 additional companies linked to Huawei to the department’s Entity List. The move is designed to stop Huawei’s access to US computer chips and other technology, even generic products not expressly designed for use by Huawei, by requiring companies to receive authorization from the US before being able to sell technology to Huawei or linked companies. A full list of impacted companies is available here: https://www.commerce.gov/news/press-releases/2020/08/commerce-department-further-restricts-huawei-access-us-technology-and. 



As part of the US’s recent revocation of Hong Kong’s special status under which it was treated separately from mainland China, beginning on September 25, products manufactured in Hong Kong must be labeled as “made in China.” On Thursday, Hong Kong officials announced that they would challenge this change at the World Trade Organization (WTO). 



On Wednesday, the US suspended multiple treaties that had been in place with Hong Kong, including an agreement on reciprocal income tax exemptions for ships operating internationally, and an extradition agreement (with France and Germany being some of the other most recent countries to have ended extradition to Hong Kong). On Tuesday, the US state department wrote to American universities asking them to consider removing investments in Chinese companies from their endowments and warning of the potential for Chinese companies to be delisted from American stock exchanges. The request apparently relates to a recent recommendation from a US treasury department working group that Chinese companies be delisted from US exchanges if they fail to comply with transparency and accounting oversight regulations by January 2022. Finally, on Monday, US President Donald Trump stated his intention to formulate tax credits for US companies that remove manufacturing from China and warned that companies that keep operations in China may be blocked from receiving US government contracts.



Assessment: Taken together, the recent measures have the potential for strong impacts to business ties and could potentially draw Chinese retaliation, although China is probably more limited in its options to respond than the US. Huawei is one of the largest telecommunications and technology companies in the world. The previous US restrictions placed on the company’s technology access, which were expanded this week, had already done damage to Huawei’s operations, according to company executives. Huawei had already been forced to make certain changes in response, including by reworking supply chains. According to US officials, the additional restrictions are being enacted due to Huawei attempting to evade the earlier regulations. The Chinese government has condemned the more recent moves against Huawei but has so far not taken any direct retaliatory steps, probably fearing that taking moves against American companies operating in China would be more damaging to the Chinese economy. In the past, Beijing has threatened to create a list of foreign businesses that it says represent threats to Chinese security, and take corresponding measures against them, but has not yet officially done so. 



The “made in China” labeling that will be required on Hong Kong products beginning on September 25 is unlikely to have a drastic effect on exports from the city, although it will put such products under the same tariff regime that applies to items from mainland China. Hong Kong is more important as a reshipping point for logistics purposes, and only around one percent of products that are exported from the city are actually manufactured there. If the government does take the issue to the WTO, the initial call will be for consultations with the US there and will move to a dispute panel only if the issue is not resolved. It is advised to remain abreast of developments as US-Chinese relations remain soured, and to be aware of the potential for some form of Chinese economic retaliation, even if on a smaller scale, in response to the US moves.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - More shipping lines introduce additional surcharge due to congestion at Sydney port
Details: Updated sources indicated on September 10 that CMA CGM has also announced an Emergency Port Congestion Surcharge amid heavy congestion at the container terminals at Sydney Port. CMA CGM’s surcharge of USD 285 per TEU will be implemented from September 17 and affect all dry as well as reefer cargo to and from Sydney regardless of point of origin or next destination. The surcharge will go into effect for US ports from October 10. Previously, industry sources indicated on September 9 that the MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company will apply a Congestion Surcharge (CGS) of an additional USD 300 from September 14 and for cargo to/from the U.S. on October 8. The congestion follows industrial actions which have impacted Sydney's terminals' productivity. Those shipping at Sydney Port should anticipate delays and higher costs of shipping and should plan accordingly.

Headline: Likely collapse of Yemen's Hodeidah ceasefire and government offensive...
Details: (FIRST PUBLISHED 19 MARCH 2019)The Houthi movement announced at a news conference in Sanaa on 16 March that its forces would strike Riyadh and Abu Dhabi with ballistic missiles if the implementation of the United Nations (UN)-sponsored peace deal in the port city of Hodeidah was breached. The Houthis claimed to have intelligence that the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, is preparing to resume its offensive on the port city. The Hodeidah ceasefire came into force on 18 December 2018, but there has since been no progress on implementation of a joint withdrawal from the city. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are reportedly now insisting that they are no longer willing to wait.Significance: IHS Markit assesses that the fundamental disagreement between the Houthis and the government over who will provide the 'local forces' to provide security in Hodeidah after a withdrawal is unlikely to be resolved peacefully, and that the UN-sponsored ceasefire is very likely to collapse in the coming weeks. Should this be the case and a government offensive to recapture the city goes ahead, there would be a severe risk of indiscriminate property damage in the city and the adjacent port from Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and shelling, and protracted urban warfare. Faced with the loss of Hodeidah, the Houthi movement would most likely destroy port facilities and deploy sea mines, making the port unusable for at least several months, and resume missile and IED attacks against coalition shipping in the Red Sea. An indicator signalling an imminent government offensive would be an intensification in shelling of Hodeidah's southeastern neighbourhoods. An agreement by both sides to further face-to-face talks on a specific date would at least temporarily reduce the likelihood of a government offensive. In the event of a government offensive, Houthi retaliation would probably also involve the launch of 'Scud'-type missiles and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strikes at military and infrastructure targets against Saudi Arabia, although their impact would be mitigated by Saudi Patriot air defences. Houthi UAVs are unlikely to have the range to strike targets in the UAE, despite a claimed UAV attack.Risks: Civil war, TerrorismSectors or assets affected: Marine, Ground cargo                    Content provided by IHS Markit Foresight © 2019

Headline: Work-to-Rule Labor Action Called at St Petersburg Ford Sollers Factory Facing Shutdown
Details:
On Friday, a union leader from the Ford Sollers automobile plant in Vsevolzhsk, about ten miles northeast of St Petersburg, announced a work-to-rule strike from the morning of Monday, April 8. The call for labor action short of a full strike was made during a meeting with about 300 workers. Ford is restructuring its operations in Russia and plans to close the St Petersburg site. The work-to-rule plan is intended to apply pressure for renegotiating the terms of planned layoffs, seeking two years  salary for released workers, at least double what Ford is currently offering. A union official claimed production could be heavily slowed if even half of the approximately 900 factory workers strictly function based on the terms of their employment and factory regulations. Pickets and demonstrations are possible during the labor action, union leadership noted, though no specific mobilizations had been immediately announced. 
 
	Assessment: The Ford Sollers plant manufactures the Focus and Mondeo models, and it has experienced similar disruptive labor actions in the past. In 2003, the Ford Focus became the best-selling foreign car model in Russia and held the spot for about a decade before the country s economic crisis heavily dented car sales. Ford is planning to halt passenger vehicle sales in Russia by June of this year while continuing to produce Ford Transit commercial vehicles at a plant in Elabuga managed by Sollers through a joint venture. Though not officially confirmed, the work-to-rule labor action at the Vsevolzhsk facility could be expanded by some workers to a full strike depending on the progress of negotiations. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring developments and anticipate possible supply chain disruptions due to the planned labor action.

Details: Heavy rainfall and storms caused flooding across Cebu City and Mandaue in recent days. Three people were killed in flood-related incidents. In addition, a landslide in Sitio San Jose, Barangay Maguikay early Wednesday, October 14 destroyed ten homes and impacted 60 people. Flooding also temporarily blocked the Marcelo Fernan Bridge in Mandaue City, but the bridge has since reopened. The mayor of Cebu ordered that waterways in the city be cleared. Clean up operations and damage assessments have been initiated following the flooding. Residual flooding-related disruptions are possible. This event is closed.

Headline: Central & Southern Taiwan   Rains and floods subside as relief operations continue. Incident closed.
Details: Media sources report that heavy rainfall and flooding have subsided across central and southern Taiwan. Relief operations are ongoing to ease flooding, and updates indicate that flood-related disruptions have largely subsided in Kaohsiung and surrounding areas. Earlier, at least seven people were killed and 116 people were injured in flood and storm-related incidents. In addition, at least 14 people were missing after multiple ships ran aground due to strong waves off of Kaohsiung Harbor. The areas that were most affected by the flooding included Changhua County, Yunlin County, Wuhu District, Pingtung County, Chiayi County, Kaohsiung, and Tainan. In Tainan, the Anping Canal overflowed and 942 people were evacuated from flood-prone areas. Over 6,000 people were evacuated in total. At least 157 schools were damaged. Disruptions were reported to Taiwan Railway services throughout the region, however rail service has resumed. This incident is closed.

Headline: IT issues disrupt operations at Port of Hamburg
Details: On March 12, German media sources are reporting that IT issues disrupted operations at the port of Hamburg for several hours and resulted in long truck queues in the port area. The disruptions were reportedly caused by a computer failure at HHLA Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG and affected all of its three major container terminals Burchardkai, Altenwerder und Tollerort. The affected terminals handle around 19,000 TEU per day. The IT issues were fixed around 12pm and all systems are operational again according to a spokesperson of HHLA Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG. No further information on when operations will resume as normal are available, but further delays are expected for the rest of the day. Investigations into the cause of the computer failure are ongoing.

Headline: Oil Tanker Reported “Hijacked” in Strait of Hormuz, Reflecting Persistent Risk of Maritime Incidents
Details:
Reports from July 15 indicated that an oil tanker was hijacked on July 5 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates. It was not immediately clear what happened aboard the Dominica-flagged MT Gulf Sky, as the tanker’s tracker had been turned off around 4:30 AM local time on July 5, though satellite photos showed the vessel in Iranian waters on July 14, off the coast of Hormuz Island. The ship’s captain reported that two of the ship’s sailors are currently in Tehran, while the twenty-six other crew members returned to India. The tanker had previously been positioned near Khor Fakkan, a city on the eastern coast of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for months, after the US had accused the ship’s Iranian buyers of attempting to purchase the vessel in coordination with the US-sanctioned National Iranian Oil Company, National Iranian Tanker Company, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Quds Force. It remains unclear how the tanker was able to leave the shores of the UAE after being seized by local authorities. No government officials have yet commented on the incident. 



Assessment: The incident stands to aggravate tensions between the US and Iran in the Gulf region. Although Tehran has appeared to scale back incidents of harassment and other provocative activities around the Strait of Hormuz, following an uptick in such incidents last summer, low-level attacks on tankers using limpet mines and incidents of detaining oil vessels have routinely been blamed on Iran. Most recently, a Hong Kong-flagged oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was briefly seized on April 14, allegedly by Iran’s IRGC. Lingering tensions between Washington and Tehran leave open the possibility of further contentious encounters, especially considering that the latest seizure of the MT Gulf Sky represents a possible violation of US sanctions. Tankers in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Bab al Mandeb Strait continue to be targets as part of Tehran’s efforts to push back against the US, which could potentially result in the indiscriminate detentions of civilian vessels.

Headline: Renamo Calls on President Nyusi to Resign Amid Debt Scandal, Raising Risk of Protests and Unrest
Details:
On Friday, media sources reported that Mozambique s largest opposition party called on President Filipe Nyusi to step down amid allegations of possible corruption. Renamo spokesperson Jose Manteigas issued a statement during a news conference to  demand  that Nyusi resign with immediate effect. The statement was issued after a Lebanese businessman accused Nyusi of benefitting from a U.S $2 billion debt scandal stemming from the purchase of military and fishing vessels from Abu Dhabi-based company Prinivest. During testimony in New York on Wednesday, the businessman, Jean Boustani, stated that Nyusi coordinated fraud, including U.S. 200 million in loans that was spent on bribes and kickbacks and used some of the money on his 2014 election campaign. The allegations remain unsubstantiated.

Assessment: The allegations of corruption against Nyusi could further fuel anti-government sentiment and raise the risk of protests over the coming days and weeks. Renamo could also use the allegations as justification to reject the August 2019 peace agreement it signed with the government to end its insurgency, potentially raising the risk of ambushes and attacks in Renamo s strongholds in central Mozambique. Due to the heightened risk of protests and unrest, customers with interests in Mozambique are advised to monitor developments related to the debt scandal and are urged to exercise an elevated level of vigilance over the coming days and weeks. Customers are also reminded to avoid all protest-related activities, as well as areas where ambushes and unrest have recently been reported, due to the potential for violence.

Headline: COTP for Delaware Bay declares Port Condition WHISKEY
Details:
Industry sources and government announcements indicate the Captain of the Port (COPT) for the Delaware Bay region has declared Port Condition WHISKEY in anticipation of gale force winds, increased seas, surf, coastal flooding, tidal surge and extremely low tides. Such conditions will likely cause delays for all marine cargo and port activity in Delaware. The declaration applies to all Delaware and New Jersey coastlines and intracoastal waters. Port Condition WHISKEY is usually declared by COPTs in anticipation of such weather within 72 hours; ports remain open to traffic for the time being, but all vessels in the area must report their intentions to remain in port or depart within 12-hours of the arrival of gale-force winds.     

The COPT published the following additional requirements for vessels in the area: Vessels must have effective mooring and anchorage arrangements for anticipated high wind; vessel agents are asked to notify vessel masters of this requirement. Facilities must minimize debris that could become missile hazards. Lightering, bunkering, and cargo operations must cease when sustained winds exceed 40 mph.

Headline: Over 40,000 tons of cargo diverted from Barranquilla due to draft emergency
Details: Local media sources in Colombia reported on April 9, 2019 that over 43 tons of cargo have been diver from the Port of Barranquilla to other port such as Cartagena or Santa Maria due to the draft emergency that has affected that part of the country over the last month. The Magdalena River has 8.4 meters of depth, which is too low to cargo vessels with exceeding 200 meters in length (dimension of a ship from the bow to the stern). The local port authority Dimar has affirmed that for the entrance of boats with length of 180 to 200 meters it will be of 8.5 meters, with daylight restriction. As for vessels with lengths of up to 200 meters, the authorized draft will be 8.4 meters without restrictions. Finally, the authorized draft for boats smaller than 180 meters is 8.7 meters with daylight restriction.

Headline: UPDATE - Australia: Evacuation orders issued for areas in Queensland due to bushfires
Details: Evacuation orders have been issued for areas of Queensland due to the ongoing bushfires. Residents at Tarome in the Scenic Rim, Noosa Banks, west of the Gold Coast, Laidley Thornton in the Lockyer Valley, and Jimna inland of the Sunshine Coast have all been issued with 'leave now' orders due to fires. Headline: Railway Operators Agree to Suspend Train Services Ahead of Severe Storms
Details:
On Wednesday, representatives from 22 different railway operators gathered for a closed-door meeting hosted by the Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism Ministry. The representatives included six individuals from separate Japan Railways (JR) lines and 16 individuals from private railway lines in Tokyo, Osaka, and other major cities. The attendees broadly agreed to suspend train operations ahead of severe storms. A summary of the meeting is expected to be released in the coming days. 
 
	 
		Assessment: Railway companies in Japan have become more proactive in suspending train services when major storms are forecast to hit. Dozens of railway lines suspended operations ahead of Typhoon Trami and Typhoon Jebi, both of which hit the country in the past two months. The proactive suspensions have been credited with reducing the number of casualties, although the result has been longer disruptions to train services. Resilience360 customers are advised to closely monitor major storms that are forecast to hit Japan and expect train services to be disrupted around the dates where high winds or heavy rains are expected.

Headline: Government instability: If confirmed, the involvement of military personnel...
Details:
Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro announced on 4 August 2018 that two explosions during a military parade on Bolivar Avenue in the capital, Caracas, were an attempt to assassinate him. According to Maduro, two Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), each carrying one kilo of C-4 explosives, were shot down by security forces as they approached the presidential s

e. State-owned media carried live foo

e of Maduro being evacuated from the scene and thousands of soldiers breaking ranks and fleeing in panic. Maduro blamed the out-going Colombian government of Juan Manuel Santos and US Florida-based radical groups for the alleged attack. Colombian and US authorities have denied any involvement and commented that the incident might well have been s

ed by Maduro's administration. Minister of Interior Nestor Reverol claimed on 5 August that six people had been arrested and that the masterminds and perpetrators had been identified. A little-known group (which only appeared on social media networks in March 2014) called 'T-Shirt Soldiers' (Soldados de Franela), and believed to be composed of former military personnel and radical civilian groups, claimed responsibility for the event. On 7 August, a Peruvian journalist based in Miami claimed to have attended a meeting at which the assassination attempt was planned; we assess this claim as credible. Maduro is likely to respond to the assassination attempt by purging the military and top government officials perceived as weak or selected as scapegoats. There is also likely to be further repression of opposition political parties and union groups which in the last month have been s

ing protests - over food, medicine and basic goods shor

es, and demanding better public services. On 8 August, the government had ordered the removal of parliamentary immunity and subsequent arrest of two opposition congressmen. The numbers and prominence of military and government officials involved in any purge will be an indicator of the risk of government instability. Second, successful attacks by the 'T-Shirt Soldiers' or another group, probably involving active or retired military and police personnel, would point to increased civil war risk. Headline: Business Backlash over Missing Journalist Saga
Details:
Global pressure on Saudi Arabia continues to mount over the fate of Jamal Khashoggi, a journalist known for his criticism of Riyadh and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) who has not been seen since entering the country s consulate in Istanbul, Turkey, last week. In recent days, a number of foreign businesses, CEOs, and investors have begun re-examining their relationships with MbS and their involvement in infrastructure projects in the kingdom. In particular, the Virgin Group and its founder, Richard Branson, have announced they will give up directorships of two Saudi tourism projects and are suspending talks on a US $1 billion investment with Riyadh. Former energy minister Ernest Moniz, along with officials from an Alphabet subsidiary, the IDEO design company, and Energy Futures Initiative, among others, have also paused their involvement in the Red Sea megacity project known as NEOM. Meanwhile, the New York Times, the Economist, and a number of other notable publications, as well as Uber, Viacom, and AOL have indicated they will not attend the upcoming Future Investment Initiative conference in Riyadh. Slated to begin on October 23, the event has attracted top corporate executives from various sectors and is seen as an opportunity for the Saudi government to fill investment opportunities. Turkish authorities claim that Khashoggi was killed inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul an accusation that Riyadh has repeatedly denied. 
 
	Assessment: Until more information about Khashoggi s fate comes to light, additional foreign companies and officials are likely to suspend their business with Saudi Arabia. If this continues and/or if MbS and the Saudi government are found to be connected to his disappearance, this could threaten the former s Vision 2030 plan to reduce Saudi Arabia s dependence on oil exports. Although a recent rise in oil prices has afforded Riyadh somewhat of a cushion vis- -vis injecting cash into the local economy, investor sentiment is likely to wane. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has indicated that he currently has no plans to limit arms sales to Saudi Arabia over Khashoggi s disappearance.

Headline: Iowa Continuing to Report Significant Damage and Disruptions Following Last Week’s Derecho Event
Details:
Following a severe storm last Monday, communities across Iowa continue to report disruptions and damages. The storm, also known as a derecho, caused winds of almost 100 miles per hour, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane. Cedar Rapids, the second biggest Iowa city by population, was one of the hardest-hit areas, in the central and eastern portions of the state. Eyewitness accounts in Cedar Rapids have described significant destruction with the majority of structures suffering damage and numerous local roads deemed impassable. An estimated 8,200 homes were damaged in the derecho across the state of Iowa. At least four deaths, three in Iowa and one in Indiana, have been blamed on the storm, which also caused widespread damage across the rest of the Midwest after moving east through Iowa. Upwards of two million people across the region lost power, including at least 600,000 in Iowa. 



In response to the storm, President Donald Trump approved a federal disaster declaration for Iowa that allowed for federal disaster aid for the state. In addition, Governor Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for 25 counties. Headline: UPDATE: Truck drivers face delays at border checkpoints amid ongoing strike
Details: Updated sources on September 6 indicate that a number of South African motorists, especially truck drivers carrying goods have faced delays at a border crossing between South Africa and Mozambique due to obstructions caused by people protesting against xenophobia in South Africa. Similar problems have been reported at Botswana and Zambia checkpoints with reports of physical attacks against some truck drivers by the crowds. Earlier reports suggested that South Africa’s president Cyril Ramaphosa convened a security meeting with law enforcement agencies to address the ongoing violent protests across South Africa. Previously, media sources indicated that five people and 189 others have been arrested in anti-foreign riots that broke out in the township of Alexandra that targeted foreign-owned businesses in several parts of the city. Earlier reports also indicated that some transport companies have had their trucks wrongfully impounded in Cape Town during the nationwide truck strike. Previous reports on September 3 stated that numerous trucks have been looted and torched in the areas of the Western Cape, Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal as a means of intimidating foreign truck drivers. Previously, major road traffic disruptions were underway due to an unofficial strike by truck drivers across South Africa protesting against the employment of foreign drivers. According to sources, several roads were blocked; including the N2 at Mew Way, the N7 at Piekenierskloof Pass, M2 near Denver, and the N12 was affected between Johannesburg and Witbank. Two trucks were reportedly burned in Montclair, south Durban, in the morning hours of September 2. Truck drivers were reportedly protesting, blocking roads and burning tires also on Waltloo Road. 11 trucks reportedly blocked the road to Richards Bay Harbour on September 1. Nevertheless, local authorities in Zambia and Namibia have issued travel advisories due to the potential risk of violence targeted at foreign truck drivers on major routes, such as the N2 and N3 highways.

Headline: Southern Virginia - Flooding was reported in the area following Storm Michael. Incident closed.
Details:
Multiple sources report that Post-Tropical Cyclone Michael caused severe flooding conditions across the southern Virginia region. As a result, the National Weather Service issued flood warnings for several counties in the area, and Governor Northam declared a state of emergency. In Blacksburg, Danville, Lynchburg, and Farmville, numerous roads were impassible due to localized street flooding. Across the state, over 1,500 roads were impacted by the storm. Media sources reported several high water rescues were performed in the greater Roanoke area, which included 50 people in Salem. The City of Danville declared a state of emergency and residents were advised to shelter in place. On October 13, a missing person was found deceased in Charlotte County after being swept away by flash flooding. The total death toll due to flooding in Virginia was at six, with five of those deaths coming from southern Virginia.

The Dan River at South Boston and the Meherrin River near Emphoria are now at normal levels. The Nottoway River near Stony Creek is at minor flood stage, but will reach normal levels by noon on Tuesday, October 16.

Resilience360 advises customers to never attempt to drive through areas with high water and to continue to heed the warnings of local authorities. This incident is closed.

Headline: Mineworks Strike Halting Movements from MMG’s Las Bambas Mine
Details:
On Tuesday, the Ministry of Energy and Mines of Peru (Minem) indicated that shipments of copper concentrate and personnel to and from MMG Ltd’s Las Bambas mine in Apurímac, Peru, have been disrupted by a blockade of the Southern Runway (Corredor Vial del Sur) by members of the Velille community. Located about 125 miles from the Las Bambas mine, the blockade was initiated in mid-December to demand about US $360,000 from MMG Ltd for infrastructure development projects in the area, as well as cash payments to families affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. Officials from Minem, the Peruvian National Police, and the Cusco Public Order Prosecutor’s Office reportedly visited the site of the blockade on December 27 in an attempt to mediate a resolution; however, the effort was reportedly spurned by protesters.



Assessment: MMG Ltd has said the disruption of shipments to and from the Las Bambas mine is likely to reduce production at the site, while also delaying shipments of copper concentrate. This in turn stands to negatively affect royalties the Hong Kong-listed company pays to the regional and municipal governments, as well as to local universities. More broadly, the episode highlights how MMG Ltd mining operations at Las Bambas have repeatedly been interrupted by protests of late; the company has suggested that blockades of public roads have disrupted activities 95 days over the past year. This caused the company to cut its output guidance for the mine in 2020 by more than ten percent in October.

Headline: China imposes additional import duties on ethylene-propylene-monomer elastomers (EPDM)
Details:
Industry sources on January 26 indicate that China has imposed additional import duties on ethylene-propylene-monomer elastomers (EPDM), with tariffs for the usual five--year period ranging from 12.5 to 222 percent. This has reportedly affected imports from companies from the European Union, the USA, and South Korea. 

Previously, on June 19, sources reported that China’s Commerce Ministry (MOFCOM) stated that Beijing was launching an anti-dumping investigation imports of a synthetic rubber product from the United States, South Korea and the European Union following a request from major petrochemical producers. The trade measures were launched at the request of Jilin Petrochemical, a unit of China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC), and Shanghai Sinopec Mitsui Elastomers Co. Ltd. The companies are top producers of EPDM, a chemical product that is widely used for electric cables and tyres. According to an application document submitted by the two companies to MOFCOM, export prices of EPDM from the U.S., South Korea and European Union were below the prices of the product in their domestic markets and the dumping into China had caused substantial damage to the applicants. Total shipments from the three countries and region account for almost 80% of China’s overall EPDM imports, according to the document.

Headline: Eastern Honshu   Restoration and reconstruction efforts continued after flooding. Incident closed.
Details:
Japanese officials deemed flooding across eastern Honshu caused by Typhoon Hagabis a major disaster. Approximately 31,000 Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) memebrs were called up to aid in relief efforts. At least 87 people were killed, and around 348 people were injured. Reports indicated that 79,490 homes were damaged or destroyed. Prefectures impacted included Chiba, Fukushima, Gunma, Ibaraki, Iwate, Kanagawa, Mie, Miyagi, Nagano, Saitama, Shizuoka, Tochigi, and Tokyo among others. Levees breached in at least 123 different locations along 67 rivers in the region.  

Following the passage of Hagabis, ten people were killed in Chiba and Fukushima Prefectures due to the offshore passage of Typhoon Bualoi, and at least two people were missing. Approximately 200 buildings were damaged in Sakura as a result. Residual disruptions may persist. This incident is closed.

Headline: Dalian customs authorities announce 12 million tonne coal import cap, ban Australian coal imports
Details: Industry sources indicate that Dalian customs authorities have announced a planned import cap of 12 million metric tonnes of coal for 2019. Additionally, the customs authorities announced a complete ban of coal imports from Australia, who is a top supplier, effective since the beginning of February. The measures will affect all 5 ports under the control of the Dalian customs authorities - Dalian, Bayuquan, Panjin, Dandong and Beiliang. These 5 ports handled 14 million tonnes of coal last year, of which half was reported to be from Australia. Until now, approximately 1.8% of Australia's coal exports were destined for Dalian Port specifically. The ban comes as imports of Australian coal at other ports in China have experienced clearing times of up to 40 days.

Headline: Hyundai Heavy Industries Workers Vote to Strike over Daewoo Acquisition; Date Unspecified
Details:
On Thursday, it was reported that workers at Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) voted to approve a strike against the acquisition of Daewoo Shipbuilding. Workers from Daewoo Shipbuilding and Marine Engineering (DSME) also voted to approve a strike earlier in the week. Nearly 60 percent of HHI workers voted in favor of the strike, along with 90 percent of DSME workers. A date for the strikes have not been set. 
 
	 
		Assessment: HHI signed a conditional agreement last month to acquire DSME from the government, with a formal agreement expected in March. The two shipbuilders cover around 20 percent of the global shipbuilding market share. The unrest among workers in South Korea s shipbuilding sector are tied to mounting financial pressures caused by a decrease in global demand for new vessels and increased competition from Chinese shipbuilders. A coordinated strike between HHI and DSME workers would cause significant disruptions in the shipbuilding industry. Resilience360 customers with interests in the sector are advised to monitor reports regarding a specific date for a strike. Workers may also decide to hold protests or marches, which should be avoided due to the potential for clashes with police. Protests would likely be held in Ulsan or on Geoje Island, where the HHI and DSME are headquartered, respectively.

Headline: Baghdad Extends Curfew; Dubai Shuts Reopened Stores in Set Back to Coronavirus Exit
Details:
On Tuesday, the Iraqi government extended a nationwide curfew adopted as part of efforts to curb the spread of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Under the move, which authorities attributed to a recent rise in COVID-19 infections blamed on public violations of anti-virus restrictions, the nightly curfew has been lengthened by one hour to between 6:00 PM and 6:00 AM local time on weekdays, while a 24-hour curfew remains in effect on the Friday-Saturday weekend. Authorities also announced that individuals who fail to wear face masks outside their homes, carry more than three people in their vehicle, and/or shun social distancing rules in shops and stores will face fines upwards of US $85. As of Thursday, Iraq had recorded 2,085 positive coronavirus infections and 93 deaths attributed to the virus.



On Wednesday, authorities in Dubai shut down 19 shops allowed to reopen last week for failing to comply with social distancing and other precautionary measures against COVID-19. The affected locations were in the areas of Dubai Marina, Satwa, Al Rafaa, Souq Al Kabeer, Karama, Hor Al Anz, Abu Hail, Al Ras, Sabkha, Al Dhagaya, Warqaa, Bani Yas Square, Qusais, Ras Al Khor, Naif, Khaled bin Al waleed, Um Suqeim, Bastakiya, International City, Awir, Al Fahidi, and Port Saeed. Another 165 establishments were issued warnings and fines were levied against two others. Dine-in restaurants, cafes, and shopping malls were allowed to partially resume operations on April 24, and a virtual 24-hour lockdown throughout Dubai was replaced by a 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM local time curfew on April 23. However, mosques, movie theaters, and playgrounds remain closed. As of Thursday, Emirati health officials had registered 12,481 coronavirus infections and 105 associated deaths.



Assessment: The moves by Iraqi and Emirati authorities represent a setback for efforts to ease coronavirus-related restrictions. Non-compliance with such measures could increase the risk of COVID-19 transmission, potentially leading to a resurgence in countries whose outbreaks seem to have stabilized, thereby raising the possibility of new disruptions to economic activities and daily life. Thus, the public is advised to heed all coronavirus instructions and guidance issued by local authorities.

Headline: Electricity stations close due to high levels of water in Lake Victoria causing power cuts
Details: It is being reported that the recent power cuts in the country have been due to the high water levels in Lake Victoria. The lake has been recorded to be at its highest level since 1964. Countries in East Africa have been experiencing rains which are heavier than usual, and they are forecasted to continue this month. The high water levels have caused flooding, with homes and hotels close to the shore affected. It has also dislodged large islands of floating debris and weeds which threatened to block turbines. This caused the electricity suppliers to close down hydro-power dam operations twice in recent days. Authorities in the country are rationing the supply of electricity nationwide until 12 May.

Details: According to reports on Friday, 24 August, police in riot gear have stormed a residential property in Huizhou. Video footage released by the activists during the raid appears to show armed police entering the property with ensuing clashes. It is not clear whether the activists have been detained, with some claiming that they cannot make contact with them. The growing labour movement began gaining momentum in July after workers at a welding machinery company, Jasic International, were fired after attempting to create a union. There are claims that the authorities have flown many of the activists' parents to Guangdong Province for 'training sessions' on how to raise their children. Some related protest action is additionally understood to have spread to Beijing. Travellers are advised to monitor media sources for further information. Though no specific details are known, note the elevated potential for protests related to the rise in labour activism, which should be avoided. Such action is likely to be intervened by the authorities.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - Daily COVID-19 roundup: Novartis’s Ilaris misses endpoint in COVID-19 pneumonia trial as infection numbers surge in Europe
Details: IHS Markit perspectiveImplicationsOn a day when the global cumulative coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caseload approached 49 million, Europe has reported the highest regional number of new cases, at 1,732,918 in the seven days leading up to 1 November, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), compared with 999,652 in the Americas. France and Italy in particular announced new daily record figures, and have ramped up local lockdown procedures, as has the UK. Several countries have been taking a more strategic look at their testing strategies, although concerns have been raised in the UK over the accuracy of a saliva test that may be used in the government’s ambitious Operation Moonshot scheme. In the US, on the other hand, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has raised the importance of developing improved strategies for the tracking of asymptomatic cases in the community.OutlookOn the therapeutics front, the WHO has reportedly drafted priorities (yet to be finalised) on provision of therapeutics to lower-income countries via its ACT Accelerator, favouring neutralising monoclonal antibodies and low-cost steroids such as dexamethasone rather than anti-virals such as Veklury (remdesivir; Gilead Sciences, US), for which evidence recently started to appear more doubtful. The day was also clouded by the latest set of disappointing data from the worldwide effort to repurpose existing drugs for COVID-19, with Novartis (Switzerland)’s anti-IL-1-beta immunotherapy Ilaris (canakinumab) failing to reduce mortality or the need for ventilation in serious COVID-19 patients. Update on COVID-19 infectionsThe number of confirmed coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases globally had reached 48,718,555 at the time of writing on 6 November, according to data compiled by Johns Hopkins University, compared with 48,132,764 a day earlier. The number of confirmed infections in the US – by far the worst-affected country in terms of case numbers – had reached 9,609,569 at the time of writing, compared with 9,487,080 24 hours earlier. The next highest number of confirmed cases was in India, where total confirmed cases had reached 8,411,724, compared with 8,364,086 the previous day; India is followed by Brazil (5,590,025 cases), Russia (1,720,063 cases), France (1,648,989 cases), and Spain (1,306,316 cases). Argentina, Colombia, the United Kingdom, and Mexico all still feature in the top-10 most affected countries in terms of total number of reported cases of the novel coronavirus. The total number of deaths reported to have resulted from COVID-19 globally had reached 1,233,961 at the time of writing, compared with 1,225,881 24 hours earlier. The number of deaths from COVID-19 in the US had reached 234,937, compared with 233,729 the previous day. Brazil remains the next worst-affected country in terms of COVID-19 fatalities, with a total of 161,106 deaths at the time of writing. The number of deaths in Brazil is followed by India (124,985), Mexico (93,772), the United Kingdom (48,210), and Italy (40,929). France, Spain, Iran, and Peru are also in the top-10 countries with the highest numbers of COVID-19 deaths.Europe: COVID-19 infection numbers are surging in Europe, with the region now recording by far the highest number of new cases. Governments in the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and elsewhere in Europe are ramping up measures to contain transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO)’s latest COVID-19 Weekly Epidemiological Update (3 November) shows that as of 1 November, Europe had recorded 1,732,918 new infections in the previous seven days, considerably higher than any other WHO-defined region; this number accounted for 52% of all new confirmed cases reported globally in the aforementioned seven-day period, compared with 46% in the previous week. The Americas reported a total of 999, 652 new cases in the same period, accounting for 30% of the total, compared with 31% in the previous week. Regarding COVID-19 fatalities, Europe accounted for 39% of all deaths recorded globally in the past week, while the Americas accounted for 38% of the weekly total. In the previous week, up to 25 October, Europe had accounted 30% of all newly reported deaths, while the Americas had accounted for 43% of deaths. France: France yesterday (5 November) recorded 58,046 new COVID-19 infections over the previous 24 hours, setting a new daily record for the second time in four days. Health Minister Olivier Véran warned that the second wave that is moving across France would be more severe than the first wave that was experienced in the spring if it continues to spread at the current rate, Reuters reported. Italy: Italy yesterday reported 445 COVID-19 fatalities in 24 hours, the highest daily death toll since 23 April, and 34,505 new COVID-19 infections. According to UK newspaper The Guardian, leaders of Italian regions set to go into partial lockdown today (6 November) have criticised the implementation of the government’s new tiered system, which has reportedly categorised some areas with the lowest infection rates as high-risk “red zones”. Jordan: Jordan is experiencing a sharp increase in COVID-19 infections, just a few months after it appeared to have arrested transmission and after it moved to relax the public health restrictions that it had enforced more rapidly than many other countries. As reported by The Guardian, Jordan had confirmed just 1,100 COVID-19 cases and 11 deaths as of late July, and did not report any new cases for several weeks during the summer. However, the number of new daily cases began to rise steeply in September. According to the WHO’s latest COVID-19 Weekly Epidemiological Update (3 November), Jordan had reported 21, 857 new cases in the previous week as of 1 November; this was the fourth-highest weekly number in the Eastern Mediterranean region after Iran, Morocco, and Iraq. The country this week (3 November) recorded 5,877 new COVID-19 infections in one day, its highest daily number of new cases. According to the Johns Hopkins University data, Jordan had recorded a cumulative total of 95,864 COVID-19 infections and 1,069 fatalities, as of this morning (6 November). Vaccines, treatments, and diagnostics development updateVaccinesChina – United Kingdom: UK firm AstraZeneca has announced plans to initiate early and mid-stage trials of its COVID-19 vaccine AZD1222 in China by the end of 2020. The vaccine is already in Phase III development in several other countries, with a possible release of first data on protective efficacy by the end of this year and potential emergency approvals at that point if appropriate. AstraZeneca has partnered with Chinese vaccine firm Shenzhen Kangtai Biological Products for local manufacturing in China, under an agreement that should ensure a production capacity of at least 100 million doses per year. AstraZeneca has commented in Reuters that AZD1222 may be approved in China by mid-2021, using international data to support the application.France: French biotech OSE Immunotherapeutics has announced the completion of an ex-vivo human study of its second-generation multi-target COVID-19 vaccine CoVepiT, which is based on selected optimised epitopes that induce a lasting sentinel memory-T-cell response against SARS-CoV-2. In the ex-vivo study conducted on cells from 120 convalescent COVID-19 patients versus unexposed patients, T-cell memory immunodominant epitopes were identified, after infection with COVID-19 and incorporation in the vaccine composition. The CoVepiT vaccine aims to address emerging variant forms of the virus during the pandemic by using 11 epitopes from highly-stable conserved regions.United Kingdom – United States: AstraZeneca has indicated in a Reuters report that it plans to base discussions on US emergency approval of its COVID-19 vaccine AZD1222 with the US FDA on a combination of “statistically reliable” efficacy and safety results from over 25,000 Phase III trial participants in the United Kingdom, South Africa, and Brazil, since there has been no signal that the agency would favour US data alone. Data from the ongoing US Phase III trial are likely to be later because of a combination of the later start of the trial and a subsequent prolonged suspension for a safety review, which is now resolved. The company also confirmed that the continuation of the US trial should not be jeopardised by a positive result from another location. TreatmentsSouth Korea: South Korean firm Celltrion has announced promising results from a small trial evaluating its neutralising monoclonal antibody for COVID-19, CT-P59, according to a Reuters report. In a Phase I trial in 18 mild COVID-19 patients, the mean recovery time was 44% shorter in the 15 participants who received CT-P59, versus the three placebo patients. No patients in the study required hospitalisation or other anti-viral therapy. CT-P59 was well tolerated, with no significant safety issues. Celltion is planning international Phase II and III trials for this product, and has already received approval to conduct Phase III development in South Korea, to prevent progression of infection in around 1,000 asymptomatic COVID-19-infected patients or close contacts. The company plans to file for emergency approval for this product in South Korea by the end of this year, and commenced commercial production in September, aiming for around 1 million doses for domestic and foreign markets. While these results are promising, the small size of the study and its placebo group mean that further verification in larger trials will be required to draw more solid conclusions, particularly in light of variable data emerging from other leading COVID-19 antibody projects from US firms Eli Lilly and Regeneron.Switzerland: Novartis (Switzerland)’s repurposed rheumatoid arthritis drug Ilaris (canakinumab) has failed to reduce mortality or the need for ventilation in interim 29-day results from the multinational 454-patient CAN-COVID Phase III trial in COVID-19 patients with pneumonia and cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Ilaris plus standard of care (SoC) did not meet the primary trial endpoint of significantly improved ventilation-free survival versus placebo plus SoC up to day 29, and also missed the key secondary endpoint of reducing the COVID-19-related death rate during the four weeks following treatment. There were no new safety signals. Novartis will submit its interim analysis to a peer-reviewed journal within the next few weeks. The CAN-COVID trial will continue in centres in the United States, Russia, and Europe to day 127, with full results expected in early 2021. These data will come as a setback for Novartis, which had positioned this anti-interleukin (IL)-1-beta immunotherapy as a potentially useful anti-inflammatory to help address COVID-19 complications. DiagnosticsUnited States: US biotech Fluidigm has announced a partnership with US technology firm Healthvana to combine Fluidigm’s saliva-based Advanta Dx SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR assay with a Healthvana-developed mobile platform to deliver test results more rapidly. Healthvana’s system delivers test results directly to patients and supplies user-friendly advice on background and next steps. The platform allows patients to access their health information in under one minute in several languages; negative COVID-19 test data can be printed or downloaded if needed for certification purposes in schools or international travel.Other developmentsHungary: Hungarian Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto yesterday said in a video message on Facebook that his government would start importing small volumes of a Russian-made COVID-19 vaccine in December. The quantities would be imported for final stage testing and for licensing in the country. He added that the government would then ramp up Russian vaccine imports as from late January 2021, and that plans were in place for an unnamed Hungarian manufacturer to switch its production from influenza vaccines to the Russian vaccine against COVID-19. The announcement indicates that discussions between Budapest and Russian officials have progressed on Hungarian participation in clinical trials of a Russian-developed candidate vaccine, and that plans are in place for local production. The Gamaleya Institute’s non-replicating adenoviral vector candidate Sputnik V (Gam-Covid-Vac) has already been granted a temporary conditional authorisation,permitting monitored public access alongside ongoing Phase III clinical trials, from the Russian health ministry. Vektor (Russia)’s peptide subunit vaccine candidate EpiVacCorona has also received an interim approval in Russia for limited “civil circulation” until 1 January 2021, on the basis of Phase I/II data. United Kingdom: Scientists with Greater Manchester’s mass testing expert group (MTEG) have raised concerns about the accuracy of the Optigene (UK) Direct RT-Lamp tests, on which the UK government has spent GBP323 million (USD424 million) for mass-testing hospital and care home staff who have shown no symptoms of COVID-19, UK newspaper The Guardian reported. The rapid test, which is designed to give results in 20 minutes, missed more than 50% of positive cases in an Operation Moonshot pilot in Greater Manchester, identifying only 46.7% of infections during a crucial trial in Manchester and Salford in October, according to the MTEG experts. The MTEG reportedly revealed its concerns to Martyn Pritchard, the chair of the region’s testing strategy group, on 2 November, stating in a letter that “the current available data from the Manchester pilot shows low sensitivity (46.7%) of the Direct RT-Lamp platform”. They added that the group has “significant concerns and do not feel the data supported the investment in the large scale rollout of Direct RT-Lamp saliva testing in any of the proposed clinical settings considered (hospital staff, care staff, community settings) at this time.” The findings cast doubt over the government’s decision to use the test as part of its mass-screening strategy. The Department of Health and Social Care has reportedly said that the test has been validated in three other trials, with their findings differing from those generated in the Manchester trial. However, according to The Guardian, the government “has not made this data public.”United States: Director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Dr Robert Redfield on 4 November called for the development of a US testing strategy to track asymptomatic cases of COVID-19. He said on Twitter, “Now is the time to develop a testing strategy to maximize our ability to identify the silent epidemic of asymptomatic COVID-19 infections.” The CDC estimates that around 40% of people with COVID-19 are asymptomatic, but the agency in August recommended that people who had come into close contact with an infected person did not necessarily need to undergo a test unless they were personally at a higher risk of infection or severe disease. The CDC then changed its position in September, urging any person who had been in close contact with an infected person to seek a test, even if they have not experienced symptoms. According to the CNN, the timing of Redfield’s latest comments was criticised by Dr Thomas Tsai of the Harvard Global Health Institute, who reportedly wrote in an email that the CDC director’s recommendations had come too late. Tsai stated, “The time to develop a national testing strategy to identify asymptomatic COVID-19 infections was a few months ago, but that ship has sailed. Now is the time to implement a testing strategy focused on screening of asymptomatic individuals.” World: A WHO draft document regarding the “therapeutics pillar” of the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator indicates that the scheme will prioritise monoclonal antibodies and the low-cost steroid dexamethasone for lower income countries, according to Reuters. The news agency claims that it has seen an “internal document” that shows the “plan to supply COVID-19 drugs to poor countries” is “betting on experimental monoclonal antibody treatments and steroids”, while “shunning [the US pharmaceutical company] Gilead’s remdesivir therapy.” As previously reported by IHS Markit, the ACT Accelerator’s therapeutics pillar, which is led by Unitaid and the Wellcome Trust, aims to expedite the development and equitable delivery of COVID-19 treatments. This includes plans to ensure equitable distribution of 245 million courses of treatments for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) by 2022. According to Reuters, the WHO draft document shows that nearly 3 million courses of dexamethasone have “already been booked” for “poorer countries.” The paper, which could be subject to change but which is reportedly due for full publication later today, for the first time outlines how the therapeutics pillar may spend donors’ money; according to the source, it states, “Immediate priorities for the (therapeutics) pillar are intensifying efforts on monoclonal antibodies while scaling up dexamethasone use.” It is estimated that USD7.2 billion is needed for the therapeutics pillar over the next 12 months, and the reported document indicates that a considerable chunk of the funding would be used to purchase and distribute monoclonal antibodies, which it describes as “game-changing” but in short supply. This would include investment of USD320 million in the production of antibodies at a Fujifilm Diosynth Biotechnologies (Japan) plant in Denmark, estimating that this would be sufficient to secure 4 million antibody courses, at around USD80 per course. Eli Lilly has reportedly agreed to produce antibodies at the Fujifilm plant as from April. However, no monoclonal antibody has yet been approved as a treatment for COVID-19. Novartis, which is awaiting full results from clinical trials of its anti-inflammatory treatment Ilaris (canakinumab) in COVID-19 and which also manufactures dexamethasone, said yesterday that it had received a request from the WHO scheme “seeking information about medicines to tackle the coronavirus”, according to Reuters. The agency also reports that Roche (Switzerland), which has partnered with Regeneron (US) for the manufacture, development, and commercialisation of the US firm’s COVID-19 antibody cocktail, REGN-COV2, has had preliminary discussions with the ACT Accelerator administrators regarding development, production, and an access plan for the investigational dual neutralising antibody combination. World: The 73rd World Health Assembly (WHA), which is set to reconvene on 9 November for a virtual session, will consider a draft resolution that aims to strengthen member states’ preparedness for health emergencies including pandemics such as COVID-19 through “more robust compliance with the International Health Regulations (2005)”, according to a WHO press release. The draft resolution (here) calls on the international community to ensure that capabilities to detect and respond to COVID-19 and other infectious diseases are strengthened. World: The value of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in the pharmaceutical and life sciences sector fell 87.2% year on year (y/y) for the first half of 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to new data from PriceWaterhouseCoopers (PwC). According to the analysis, 99 deals in the sector were agreed in the sector in the first half of the year, with a total value of USD35 billion, compared with USD272.9 billion in the first half of 2019. In terms of volume, or number of M&A deals, the sector saw a 17% decline from 119 in the first half of 2019. Major players in the sector, which ordinarily drive M&A activities, have instead focused on internal resources and driving COVID-19 research, vaccines, and treatments. As part of this trend, pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies have also focused on collaborations to help accelerate COVID-19 product research and development and manufacturing. More of today’s IHS Markit COVID-19 analysisArgentina: Argentine government fixes maximum prices for several drugs used to treat hospitalised COVID-19 patients (here)Europe: Weekly COVID-19 tendering monitor: UK awards USD26-billion COVID-19 diagnostics tender, European tender opportunities show strongly weekly preference for PPE procurement (here)Outlook and implicationsAt a time of growing concern over the resurgences in infection in Europe, the WHO has reportedly drafted a set of priorities on provision of therapeutics to lower-income countries via its ACT Accelerator, indicating that it may prioritise neutralising monoclonal antibodies and steroids such as dexamethasone, rather than anti-virals such as Veklury, for which evidence has started to look more doubtful lately. Testing strategies have also come under scrutiny lately, with experts raising concerns over the accuracy of a saliva test used in a pilot study and potentially intended for inclusion in the UK’s ambitious Operation Moonshot scheme, and US authorities have given a timely call for strategic tracking of asymptomatic cases in the community.Novartis’s anti-IL-1-beta immunotherapy Ilaris has become the latest repurposed drug to yield disappointing results in controlled trials for COVID-19 complications, showing no significant benefit in survival or progress to artificial ventilation. This follows on from recent setbacks in clinical studies evaluating IL-6 inhibitors such as Actemra (tocilizumab; Roche), with dexamethasone being the only repurposed drug so far to have yielded significantly positive mortality reduction results. However, Novartis has stated its intention to refocus on another repurposed drug, the JAK inhibitor Jakavi (ruxolitinib), and its promising DARPin therapeutic project for COVID-19.© 2020, IHS Markit Inc. Ilaris plus standard of care (SoC) did not meet the primary trial endpoint of significantly improved ventilation-free survival versus placebo plus SoC up to day 29, and also missed the key secondary endpoint of reducing the COVID-19-related death rate during the four weeks following treatment. There were no new safety signals. Novartis will submit its interim analysis to a peer-reviewed journal within the next few weeks. The CAN-COVID trial will continue in centres in the United States, Russia, and Europe to day 127, with full results expected in early 2021. Now is the time to implement a testing strategy focused on screening of asymptomatic individuals.” World: A WHO draft document regarding the “therapeutics pillar” of the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator indicates that the scheme will prioritise monoclonal antibodies and the low-cost steroid dexamethasone for lower income countries, according to Reuters. The news agency claims that it has seen an “internal document” that shows the “plan to supply COVID-19 drugs to poor countries” is “betting on experimental monoclonal antibody treatments and steroids”, while “shunning [the US pharmaceutical company] Gilead’s remdesivir therapy.” As previously reported by IHS Markit, the ACT Accelerator’s therapeutics pillar, which is led by Unitaid and the Wellcome Trust, aims to expedite the development and equitable delivery of COVID-19 treatments. The draft resolution (here) calls on the international community to ensure that capabilities to detect and respond to COVID-19 and other infectious diseases are strengthened. World: The value of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in the pharmaceutical and life sciences sector fell 87.2% year on year (y/y) for the first half of 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to new data from PriceWaterhouseCoopers (PwC).
