Headline: Vietnam bans scrap import to keep its ports congestion-free
Details:
Since May 2018, major ports in Vietnam such as Cat Lai Port and Hai Phong Port have faced severe congestions due to high volume imports of containers filled with paper, plastic and metal scrap materials. The congestion in Vietnamese ports may partially be the result of China’s ban on scrap imports since early 2018, prior to which, it used to allow half of the world’s plastic waste into the country. Due to the new environment policies adopted by China, many waste export businesses were left to find new emerging markets such as Southeast Asia to import their scrap materials. One country in particular is Vietnam, where waste import had increased since China’s ban. Sources indicate that the United States is the largest importer of scrap into Vietnam with around 147 million pounds of plastics imported between January and May 2018. This reflects an increase of about 85 million pounds from 2017 and 56 million pounds from 2016 respectively. 

In May, port operating companies and customs offices experienced capacity constraints with containers being left at ports for more than 30 to 90 days. In Cat Lai Port alone, there were about 8,050 TEUs of long-day stored goods, 5,234 TEUs of plastic and waste-paper materials and a remaining 2,816 TEUs of goods that were being stored for 90 days or longer. As a result, many imported goods were left in queue at Cai Mep and Tan Cang– Hiep Phuoc Ports before they were moved to Cat Lai Port, thus creating a ripple congestion effect at other ports. 

This led the authorities to impose a ban on waste imports on June 15. The ports also stopped accepting plastic scrap shipments effective at all ports from June 25 to October 15. The temporary ban not only buys time for the ports to clean up the abandoned containers but also provides an opportunity for the authorities to formulate short and long-term strategies to assess the ports’ storage capacity constraints and its plastic recycling industry. It is evident that for its short-term plan, legislative actions against unlawful imports of scrap would be taken as the port authorities reportedly started cracking down on illegal shipments of paper, plastic and metal scrap by investigating the owners of the containers and those responsible for the illegal imports. 

Furthermore, the port authorities will take the ownership of inspecting permits of imported scrap containers before allowing vessels to unload. Sources indicate that authorities also found companies that were deliberately importing illegal waste under a false name with fake licenses and incorrect addresses to earn quick profits while they leave their trash at the terminals. Hence, ports are now only allowing vessels to unload scrap containers if they have valid import permits and written date commitments to pick up the cargo.

Moreover, legal documents on the management of waste imports will be revised, taking into account environmental protections, and mechanisms to prevent, control & manage the trade and imports of scraps from other countries will be established. Despite these efforts, as of early October 2018, there were still reportedly 4,000 containers of scrap at Cat Lai Port which includes 3,000 containers that had been left for more than three months.

Although the scrap import ban is temporary and is expected to last only for a few months, it is likely that Vietnam will gradually reduce the import of overseas scraps and simultaneously increase the reuse of recycled materials in its long-term strategic approach. Solid waste ban had impacted local recycling industries, as sources suggested that waste processing is an additional source of raw materials for the country’s paper, plastic and steel industries. 

Despite the environmental and port congestion concerns, there is still a demand for overseas paper and plastic scraps for some domestic productions, due to the inadequate plastic recycling system in the country. Sourcing of scrap locally is reportedly difficult as most plastic wastes are normally mixed with regular trash and are not separated properly. Ho Chi Minh City alone produces about 900 tons of plastic waste daily, of which only 90 tons are recycled. While there are pros and cons in the scrap policy, efforts for local recyclers to switch to domestic waste will progress gradually in years to come as the industry needs time to adjust from handling import waste to domestic waste. 

It is not only Vietnam that needs to find a win-win solution for both ports and the domestic recycling industry; Thailand and Malaysia have also followed Vietnam’s footsteps in banning plastic waste due to an increase in such imports. On July 2, Thailand was the second country after Vietnam to ban the import of certain waste goods, including plastic scrap, electronic waste and hazardous waste at Ports of Laemchabang and Songkhla. However, unlike Vietnam, the duration of the ban remains unclear for Thailand. In the same vein, Malaysia has cancelled the import licenses for 114 of the country’s plastic scrap processors and implemented new operating procedures and regulations for recyclable material import licenses. Sources indicated that authorities will conduct inspections to ensure that only processors with valid permits are allow to continue operations. It is also important to note that Indonesia had begun inspecting 100 percent of scrap imports since early April following an increase in imports of scrap polystyrene from the United Kingdom in the first three months of this year. 

As most Southeast Asian nations take a tougher stance on waste import while they struggle with their own domestic waste problems, waste shippers are left with fewer options to find alternative markets to substitute China. It is no doubt that China’s ban has disrupted the global supply chain which had about 7 million tons of scrap plastic imported annually from the United States and Europe. Although India is likely to be the next location where waste exporters were reportedly shipping to, with volume up 164.4 percent to 70,550 TEU, there is no guarantee that this can remain a viable option in the long run. Perhaps, China’s import ban on scrap is a wake-up call not only for Southeast Asian nations but also for countries with large volumes of scrap to find solutions in its domestic market, particularly in the recycling sector.

Despite the environmental and port congestion concerns, there is still a demand for overseas paper and plastic scraps for some domestic productions, due to the inadequate plastic recycling system in the country. Sourcing of scrap locally is reportedly difficult as most plastic wastes are normally mixed with regular trash and are not separated properly. Ho Chi Minh City alone produces about 900 tons of plastic waste daily, of which only 90 tons are recycled. While there are pros and cons in the scrap policy, efforts for local recyclers to switch to domestic waste will progress gradually in years to come as the industry needs time to adjust from handling import waste to domestic waste. 

It is not only Vietnam that needs to find a win-win solution for both ports and the domestic recycling industry; Thailand and Malaysia have also followed Vietnam’s footsteps in banning plastic waste due to an increase in such imports. On July 2, Thailand was the second country after Vietnam to ban the import of certain waste goods, including plastic scrap, electronic waste and hazardous waste at Ports of Laemchabang and Songkhla. However, unlike Vietnam, the duration of the ban remains unclear for Thailand. In the same vein, Malaysia has cancelled the import licenses for 114 of the country’s plastic scrap processors and implemented new operating procedures and regulations for recyclable material import licenses. Sources indicated that authorities will conduct inspections to ensure that only processors with valid permits are allow to continue operations. It is also important to note that Indonesia had begun inspecting 100 percent of scrap imports since early April following an increase in imports of scrap polystyrene from the United Kingdom in the first three months of this year. 

As most Southeast Asian nations take a tougher stance on waste import while they struggle with their own domestic waste problems, waste shippers are left with fewer options to find alternative markets to substitute China. It is no doubt that China’s ban has disrupted the global supply chain which had about 7 million tons of scrap plastic imported annually from the United States and Europe. Although India is likely to be the next location where waste exporters were reportedly shipping to, with volume up 164.4 percent to 70,550 TEU, there is no guarantee that this can remain a viable option in the long run. Perhaps, China’s import ban on scrap is a wake-up call not only for Southeast Asian nations but also for countries with large volumes of scrap to find solutions in its domestic market, particularly in the recycling sector.

Headline: Dispute around freight rates in Brazil lead to congestion at ports
Details:
The nationwide trucker strikes that swept through Brazil during the last two weeks of May 2018 are continuing to have ripple effects throughout the country. The most recent developments in this regard have been the negotiations between the government and the truckers over minimum freight haulage rates known as the ‘tabela de frete’, or the minimum freight table. The most notable result of this persistent dispute is its effect on sea ports. 
Over the past several weeks, disputes between truckers and shippers have occurred at some of Brazil’s principal ports, such as Santos and Paranagua. This is evident in the backup of cargo at the aforementioned ports, triggered by a dispute between shippers and truckers on what the agreed freight prices are. Shippers claim that the post-strike rates are too high to make shipping affordable. Truckers, on the other hand, claim that the current rates were the best possible concession received during the course of the strike, and any contestation of the rates will lead them back to strike. 
A longer term issue lies with the government setting the definitive price schedule, which it has done so far through a provisional measure. This measure allows ANTT, a national ground transportation entity, to set the freight prices. The Brazilian Supreme Federal Tribunal, the highest court in the country, has heard the arguments posed by both the government and truckers in court on June 28, and is expected to announce its decision on August 27. 
This, however, does not alleviate the immense pressure that the industry will be under pending the decision. The continuing dispute has resulted in freight being stuck at ports, with cargo vessels and containers backed up and unable to move until freight rate disputes are resolved. No similar backlog has been reported in this context at any of the major international cargo airports in the country. The use of air freight as an alternative to circumvent the backlog at the seaports may be considered.
Agribusiness is the most immediately affected industry due to the perishability of the products involved. Until a decision is reached at the Supreme Federal Tribunal in August 2018, customers with cargo at Brazilian seaports are advised to keep abreast of new developments and, where appropriate, explore alternatives.

Headline: Oil workers’ strike causes shortage at Port of Santos
Details: Media sources indicate on February 19 that the ongoing Petrobras oil worker’s strike is causing significant disruptions at the Port of Santos in São Paulo, Brazil. The Port of Santos is the most important industrial cargo port in the country and one of the main ports in Latin America. Cargo ships are receiving half of their usual fuel which is forcing freighters to change routes and reload at another port. Ships that have requested 1,000 to 1,200 tons of fuel are only receiving half of the order and only passenger ships are receiving the requested cargo. There are reports that some ships have waited for 12 hours at the port for supplies, causing an estimated loss of USD 150,000 (BRL 655,965; EUR 139,018).

Headline: COTP for Delaware Bay (including NJ) declares Port Condition WHISKEY
Details:
Industry sources and government announcements indicate the Captain of the Port (COPT) for the Delaware Bay region has declared Port Condition WHISKEY in anticipation of gale force winds, increased seas, surf, coastal flooding, tidal surge and extremely low tides. Such conditions will likely cause delays for all marine cargo and port activity in New Jersey. The declaration applies to all Delaware and New Jersey coastlines and intracoastal waters. Port Condition WHISKEY is usually declared by COPTs in anticipation of such weather within 72 hours; ports remain open to traffic for the time being, but all vessels in the area must report their intentions to remain in port or depart within 12-hours of the arrival of gale-force winds.     

The COPT published the following additional requirements for vessels in the area: Vessels must have effective mooring and anchorage arrangements for anticipated high wind; vessel agents are asked to notify vessel masters of this requirement. Facilities must minimize debris that could become missile hazards. Lightering, bunkering, and cargo operations must cease when sustained winds exceed 40 mph.

Headline: Wind Event to Impact Southern CA This Week; Dangerous Wildfire Conditions and PSPS Events Possible
Details:
Meteorologists are predicting a new round of Santa Ana winds affecting Southern California this week. Winds are expected to gradually increase all week and winds of up to 65 miles per hour are possible by the end of the week in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. The high winds in combination with humidity in the single digits and no expected precipitation may create dangerous fire conditions. Though no warnings have been issued as of this writing, a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) event may be implemented at some point this week by Southern California Edison (SCE) to help mitigate the potential risk of a fire sparking due to SCE equipment. 



Assessment: Santa Ana wind events occur when strong winds blow from mountain ranges inland down towards the Southern California coast. These most often occur during the fall months but can extend into December. These wind events often spark some of the most destructive wildfires in Southern California especially when they occur at the same time as extremely dry conditions or above-average temperatures, as will be the case this week. A similar wind event occurred last week and resulted in a PSPS event that led to over 8,000 SCE customers temporarily losing power on Thanksgiving Day; however, no significant fires spread during that event. 



Though December is past peak wildfire season, California is still susceptible to destructive fires due to the wind events. In December 2017, the Thomas Fire burned over 281,000 acres in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties, making it at the time the largest fire in California history, and the rapid spread of the fire over an initial five-day period was blamed on a Santa Ana wind event. That fire destroyed over 1,000 structures and led to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of residents. Additionally, the cause of the fire was found to be SCE equipment. Due to the potential for quick-spreading and potentially dangerous fires, businesses and residents in Southern California are advised to review and/or create emergency plans and evacuation routes. Cal Fire has created guidance on emergency wildfire plans that can be viewed at the following link: https://www.fire.ca.gov/media/4996/readysetgo_plan.pdf. Moreover, residents and businesses should prepare for potential prolonged power outages in the event of PSPS events implemented by SCE. Details on any potential events can be viewed at the following site: https://www.sce.com/wildfire/psps. Heed all instructions from local authorities.

Headline: Cargo Delays to Continue Through February Following Import Increase at Ports of Long Beach and LA
Details:
Cargo shipping delays are continuing to be reported throughout the United States due to a massive increase in imports of over 20 percent coming to the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach in December of 2018. The increase initially caused the ports to store containers in warehouses but space in warehouses has since been maxed out. As a response to limited warehouse space, retailers are now storing containers on chassis at railroad terminals including significant stockpiles at Union Pacific Railroad terminals in Memphis, TN and Joilet, IL. This has caused a chassis shortage which has led to truckers being unable to return empty containers to ports and causing delays in shipments and turnaround times of cargo. 
 
	Assessment: The massive import increase is directly related to the increase in tariffs on Chinese imports, which were expected to rise from ten percent to 25 percent on January 1, 2019. This caused retailers to front-load spring shipments to avoid the tariff increase. The increase has since been delayed until March 1. The delays and chassis shortages are expected to continue at least through February. Imports from Asia are expected to begin dropping off in February as factories close for several weeks to celebrate the Lunar New Year. This will allow for the backlog of cargo to be moved across the country and help dissipate the chassis and warehouse shortage. There are no reports of the backlog and delays causing disruptions for consumers.

Headline: Telson Mining Corp. reports systematic theft of USD 2-3mil in metal concentrates
Details: Media sources indicate that the Canadian company Telson Mining Corp. has reported that employees of the company systematically stole between USD 2 to 3 million (EUR 1,775,000 - 2,660,000) from the company's Cambo Morado mine in the state of Guerrero while it was in transit to the Port of Manzanillo over approximately 4-5 months. The theft was detected after the company received reports that the quality measurements at receiving destinations were reported lower than those at departure from the mine and the company launched an investigation. The investigation found that 12-15 drivers were stopping unplanned in the state of Jalisco during their journeys to Manzanillo, overcoming tamper-detection systems and replacing stolen cargo with lower quality material. Telson Mining Corp. bought the Campo Morado mine, which produces zinc and lead concentrates, in 2017 and began production in 2018.

Headline: Ecuador   No major protest activity reported after an agreement was reached. Incident closed.
Details:
There have been no indications of major protest activity, and protesters have lifted most road blocks across Ecuador. An agreement was reached between government officials and protest groups on October 13, which included the government withdrawing orders to terminate fuel subsidies and protest groups agreeing to end protests. Celebrations occurred in the streets of Quito overnight following the announcement. Dozens of highways were shut down by roadblocks and/or large groups of protesters across 17 different provinces during the actions; however, most of these have since been lifted. As a result, intercity travel and cargo transportation has resumed, including fuel transport which was disrupted. Furthermore, a curfew in areas of Quito has been lifted. 

There were sporadic reports of looting and vandalism across the country during the unrest. Mobs of protesters broke into multiple government offices throughout Quito, and President Lenin Moreno temporarily relocated the government to the city of Guayaquil. At one point, protesters occupied the House of Culture in Quito and took eight police officers and 27 journalists hostage. Outside of the capital, protesters seized and/or vandalized multiple oil fields, in some cases causing production stoppages. Ecuador s ministry of energy reported that oil production fell by roughly 31 percent; however, production has resumed and is expected to return to normal. Public demonstrations repeatedly degenerated into violent clashes with security forces. Tear gas and water cannons were used to disperse large crowds. Police vehicles and at least one armored personnel carrier were set on fire and destroyed. During the unrest, at least eight people died, 1,340 were injured, and 1,192 were detained. Ecuador's Red Cross suspended paramedic and ambulance services due to security concerns. The recent bout of unrest was sparked when the government passed a bill terminating fuel subsidies. This incident is closed.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - Massachusetts–School regulations have changed due to the change in risk levels. Event closed.
Details:
The following information is a summary of COVID-19 within Massachusetts and its associated impacts.

COVID-19 Numbers: 
- Approximately 172,727 positive or presumptive positive cases have been reported. 
- Up to 10,163 virus-related deaths have been confirmed.
- More than 6,767,987 people have been tested.
 
New Updates:
- Due to 105 of the communities being removed from the high risk list last week, all of those communities are expected to go back to in-person learning in schools as long as they remain in the gray, green or yellow risk levels. 

Reopening Details: 
- According to new state COVID-19 reporting guidelines, only 16 communities in Massachusetts are considered high-risk; a 105 drop from the reporting guidelines of last week. The 16 communities considered in the Red Category are Brockton, Chelsea, Everett, Fall River, Fitchburg, Lawrence, Lowell, Lynn, Methuen, New Bedford, Norfolk, Revere, Seekonk, Somerset, Springfield, and Westport.

- Governor Baker announced a series of new COVID-19 restrictions. A stay-at-home advisory will be implemented from 10:00 PM to 5:00 AM local time, every night, effective Friday, November 6. Indoor recreational facilities, theaters, casinos and entertainment venues are required to close at 9:30 PM local time. Indoor gathering at private residences has been reduced to ten people. Outdoor gatherings have been set at a 25-person capacity. Indoor and outdoor events at homes must end by 9:30 PM local time. Face coverings are required in public spaces. 
- Governor Baker announced that effective October 5, lower risk counties will be permitted to move into Step Two of Phase Three of Massachusetts’s reopening plan. Under Step Two, indoor and outdoor performance venues will be permitted to open at 50 percent capacity with a maximum of 250 people. Gyms, museums, libraries and driving and flight schools will also be permitted to increase their capacity to 50 percent. Fitting rooms will be permitted to open in all types of retail stores. For arcades and indoor/outdoor recreation businesses, additional Step II activities like trampolines, obstacle courses, roller rinks and laser tag will also be permitted to open, and capacity will increase to 50 percent.
	
- Most of the state entered Phase Three on July 6. Under Step One of Phase Three, museums are limited to 40 percent occupancy, tours such as trolleys and harbor cruises are limited to 50 percent occupancy with passengers separated by empty seats, walking tours are limited to ten people, and fitness centers are limited to 40 percent occupancy with equipment spaced 14 feet apart or six feet apart with barriers. Movie theaters and casino gaming floors are also permitted to open with restrictions, frequent cleaning, and limited capacity. Outdoor events of up to 50 people are also allowed with a permit. People participating in these activities must still practice safe social distancing and wear a mask.
- Effective Monday, September 28, restaurants are allowed to expand seating from six to ten people and open bar seating. Tables must be six feet apart, and customers must wear a face covering at all times, unless seated at a table. Bar patrons must remain seated at the bar and must order food. The new guidelines apply to both indoor and outdoor seating. Boston will wait on the seat expansion. Bars and nightclubs are still closed until Phase 4.
- Governor Charlie Baker outlined a four-phase approach for reopening the state. In the “Start” phase, limited industries will be allowed to resume operations with restrictions. In the “Cautious” phase, additional industries can resume operations with restrictions and limited capacity. In the “Vigilant” phase, additional industries may resume operations with guidance. In the “New normal” phase, the development of a vaccine allows for a new normal.
- Anyone traveling into the state will need to quarantine for 14 days or produce a negative COVID-19 test result. Violators can be fined up to US$ 500 per day. Travelers from California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Vermont, Washington and Wyoming are exempt. Travelers from Rhode Island are not exempt and will need to quarantine.

Although case numbers are included, it is important to note that these numbers are constantly changing, and the most up-to-date statistics are published by the CDC or local public health agencies. This risk event is located statewide regardless of where or how many cases are being confirmed. This event is closed.

Headline: UPDATE: Gallina Blanca workers reach an agreement, call off strike
Details: Updated sources reported on February 27, 2019 the end of the indefinite strike of the workers of Gallina Blanca after agreeing on the terms for the transfer of the plant from Sant Joan Despí (Barcelona) to Ballobar (Huesca). The unions have accepted compensation, early retirements and relocations for employees who prefer not to move to the municipality of Huesca. The workers' representatives have agreed compensation of 60 days per year worked, with a maximum of 42 monthly payments, and early retirement for employees between 58 and 61 years that do not want to move.

Headline: United Kingdom: Numerous pro-Brexit demonstrations planned throughout the country over 22-25 March
Details: Numerous demonstrations are reportedly planned throughout the country over 22-25 March, and potentially beyond. The actions are taking place by supporters of a group named ‘Brexit Protest and Direct Action Group UK’, which has formed to demand the government take action to leave the European Union without delay. Many will take the form of ‘go slow’ road protests, with participants expected to cause disruptions along major routes nationwide. A number of blockades at ferry terminals is additionally planned. Known actions will take place on 22 March in Cornwall: Bodmin to Truro (from 15:30); Flintshire: A55 near Deeside Industrial Estate (19:00); Lancashire: circling Morecambe Road, Caton Road and A683 north of Lancaster (18:30); Nottinghamshire: circling M1 between junctions 26-28 (18:00); Shropshire: A5 from Shrewsbury to Telford (17:30); and Suffolk: Copdock Roundabout in Felixstowe (18:00). On 23 March in Anglesey: Holyhead Ferry Terminal blockade (22:00); Cheshire: M62 Junction 9 in Warrington to various locations (12:00); Gloucestershire: Shire Hall in Gloucester (11:00); Greater Manchester/Yorkshire/Merseyside: Manchester to both Leeds and Liverpool (12:00); and Pembrokeshire: Irish Ferries blockade at Pembroke Dock (11:40). And on 25 March in Hampshire: from M3 Junction 6 in Basingstoke in both directions (06:30, all times given are local). Though participations will likely vary, disruptions are anticipated.

Headline: Pedestrian incident prompts rail disruption between Birmingham International and Coventry stations
Details: National Rail is reporting that disruption is occurring to services running between Birmingham International and Coventry stations on Saturday. This is due to a person being hit by a train. As a result, all lines between these two stations are blocked. Avanti West Coast, CrossCountry, London Northwestern Railway and West Midlands Railway services may be delayed by up to 60 minutes or be diverted via an alternative route, not calling at some stations. Rail tickets can be used on some alternative rail and bus routes. The disruption is expected to continue until 15:00 local time.

Headline: Attack at JNU in Delhi Highlights Heightened Threat of Violence in Current Political Climate
Details:
On Sunday, January 5, at around 7:00 PM local time, over 50 masked individuals armed with iron rods, bricks, and stones attacked students and faculty at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), located along Baba Gang Nath Marg and Vedant Desika Mandir Marg, in South Delhi. Prior to the assault, teachers and students had gathered at a central meeting point on campus at JNU to discuss their opposition to the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and tuition fee hikes. The attack lasted for approximately three hours, and involved suspects physically assaulting students and faculty, vandalizing residence halls, and shouting provocative slogans. At least 36 people suffered injuries in the assault, including four with serious injuries. At this time, there have been no reports of arrests made in connection with the attack. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, various left-leaning organizations and students blamed Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), a pro-CAA student group, for carrying out the attack. The Delhi Police were also blamed for not intervening to stop the masked individuals.

Assessment: JNU is a prestigious university in India, where students are known for taking part in political activism and holding protests. Recently, students have led large demonstrations on campus and participated in off-campus demonstrations in opposition to the CAA as well as tuition fee hikes. The CAA, which was approved by the President of India on December 12, 2019, and enacted into law on January 10, 2020, provides a path to citizenship for non-Muslim religious minorities fleeing persecution in India s neighboring countries of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. The act is seen as highly controversial by many left-leaning activists, and has resulted in major nationwide demonstrations, some of which have involved clashes between anti-CAA protesters, pro-CAA protesters, and police. On December 15, clashes between anti-CAA protesters and police in Delhi resulted in over 100 demonstrators being injured. The group blamed for carrying out the attack at JNU, ABVP, has previously been accused of attacking anti-CAA demonstrators, including on December 16, when ABVP members allegedly attacked protesters at Delhi University. Additionally, anti-CAA groups, such as the Students Federation of India (SFI), have been accused of attacking CAA supporters, such as on December 16 when SFI members attacked ABVP members at Kerala College. Recent violent demonstrations and attacks carried out by rival groups highlight the increased threat of violence which characterizes India s current highly divisive political climate. Given that the CAA was recently enacted into law, associated demonstrations and acts of violence are expected to continue. Customers are advised to avoid the vicinity of all protest activity and large gatherings in India due to the potential for violence.

Headline: Potential for Tariffs, Other Measures as China Opens Anti-Dumping Investigation into Australian Wine
Details:
On Tuesday, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced that it had opened an investigation into allegations of dumping of Australian wine in the Chinese market. The investigation is reportedly based on a complaint filed by the Chinese Alcoholic Drinks Association, which represents Chinese winemakers, in July. Authorities are seeking information on whether Australian winemakers are receiving government subsidies allowing them to sell wine in China at artificially reduced prices, which is denied by Australian officials.



Assessment: China is the largest export market for Australian winemakers, accounting for about 39 percent of the country’s wine exports. Wine sales to China from Australia were worth approximately US $795 million in 2019, and China brings in more Australian wine than it does wine from any other country, with the exception of France. In response to questions regarding the anti-dumping investigation, a spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry denied that the inquiry was related to ongoing tensions between the two countries, but stated that a strong bilateral relationship “requires the joint efforts of both sides.” This is similar to previous thinly veiled references that foreign ministry officials have made to the fraught relations between China and Australia in recent months, and likely indicates that the investigation is indeed more about the two countries’ deteriorated ties. In May, China imposed trade restrictions on Australian barley and beef, which was widely viewed as retaliatory following Australia’s push for an independent inquiry into the origins of COVID-19. Since that time, relations have continued to sour over Hong Kong and other issues, and both sides have continued to introduce seemingly tit-for-tat responsive measures. There is the potential for China to place tariffs or other restrictions on imports of Australian wine as the investigation advances, and those with Chinese-Australian trade interests are advised to remain abreast of developments.

Headline: Shell’s Tabangao Refinery to be Refitted as Import Terminal Due to COVID-19 Demand Slowdown
Details:
Pilipinas Shell Petroleum, the Philippines subsidiary of Royal Dutch Shell, announced on Thursday that its Tabangao Refinery will be permanently refitted as a petroleum import terminal. The move comes amid the global economic slowdown and lack of demand for oil caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The facility has been shut down since May 24. According to both Pilipinas Shell and the Philippines Department of Energy (DOE), the conversion of the complex into an import terminal will not affect the oil supply in the Philippines.



Assessment: The Tabangao Refinery, located near the city of Batangas, some 60 miles south of Manila, began operating in 1962 with a production capacity of 110,000 barrels per day (bpd). With its transformation into an import terminal, the Philippines will be left with a single refinery, Petron’s 180,000 bpd facility near Limay in Bataan Province. Petroleum demand in the Philippines has fallen sharply during the COVID-19 outbreak, with the DOE reporting as much as a 60 to 70 percent decline in April. Demand currently remains down and is likely to have dropped again with the recent reimposition of heightened quarantine restrictions in Metro Manila and elsewhere in the country. According to media reports, Pilipinas Shell lost approximately US $137 million in the first half of this year compared to a profitable period during the same time period last year. According to the company, its new import terminal will focus on supplying Luzon and the Northern Visayas regions, while its current North Mindanao Import Facility will continue to deliver supplies to Visayas and Mindanao. Given the fact that oil refined at Tabangao has already been put on the market and all oil coming from Pilipinas Shell since May 24 has been imported, as the company and the DOE stated, there is currently no reason to believe that oil supplies in the Philippines will be negatively impacted by the change. The global slowdown in the oil market is likely to affect other suppliers as well, particularly smaller refiners, with future refinery shutdowns possibly affecting facilities in such countries as Australia, Japan, or New Zealand. It is advised to remain abreast of developments as the refinery’s conversion is carried out.

Headline: Hurricane Michael may disrupt aerospace, auto and industrial engineering supply chains
Details: On October 10, Hurricane Michael is expected to make landfall later today in the Panhandle region or the Florida Big Bend area. The projected path may affect manufacturing and distribution facilities in northwestern Florida and eastern Alabama, potentially impacting aerospace, automotive and industrial engineering supply chains. Aerospace in particular is the most exposed industry, with Airbus and Boeing having large production facilities in the area. Among large aerospace suppliers are Northrop Grumman, Crestview Aerospace and BAE Systems. Numerous auto parts suppliers also own properties in the storm’s path, including Hitachi Cable Automotive Products USA. The hurricane could also greatly affect the industrial engineering industry, with Danfoss Turbocor, Telligentems LLC and Fort Walton Machining having production facilities in the region. Major impacts could arise from strong winds and flooding which may affect facilities and disrupt air, ocean, rail and road transportation.

Headline: UPDATE 7: AP-7 highway between Spain and France reopened after separatist protest
Details: Updated media sources indicate on November 13 that the AP-7 motorway that connects Barcelona with the south of France was reopened after being cut for two days by Catalan separatists protesting against the jailing of nine regional leaders. The highway is mostly used by carriers and was blocked for more than two days at the Franco-Spanish border and then in the city of Girona. The AP-7 motorway connects the entire coastline of eastern Spain with France. According to the confederation of Spanish carriers, 20,000 trucks use the highway to cross the border every day. The confederation estimated the cost of the blockage to be EUR 15 million (USD 16,512,000) per day.

Headline: Tamil Nadu & Puducherry – Clean-up operations underway following flooding. Event closed. - UPDATE 12
Details:
Clean-up operations are underway across Tamil Nadu and Puducherry after two tropical storms passed through the area and caused flooding. Tropical Storm Nivar was the first storm to strike the area, followed by Tropical Storm Burevi. At least five people were killed from flood-related incidents, while thousands of people were evacuated. An unspecified number of homes were damaged in Puducherry.

At least 2,000 homes were damaged by floodwaters across Tamil Nadu. Areas that were impacted include Thoothukudi, Ramasamypuram, Boltonpuram, Pucklepuram, and Mela Thattaparai. In Chennai, Bagyalakshmi Nagar, Ayyanar Colony, and other areas were inundated with floodwater. The heavy rainfall also filled the Gadana, Ramanadhi, Karupppanadhi, and Adavinainar dams to the maximum limit, causing an overflow of the Uppaaru river and subsequently the Korampallam tank which flooded several fields and the Tiruchendur highway. This event is closed.

Headline: Capital Markets: Planned Australian coal terminal facility IPO seeking AUD1 bil. plus, testing appetite for coal-related share sales
Details: Canadian infrastructure firm Brookfield is looking to sell 60–80% of its lease holding in Dalrymple Bay Infrastructure, a major coal terminal facility in Queensland, Australia, reportedly seeking proceeds in excess of AUD1 billion (USD710 million).  This report was prepared with extensive inputs from James Stevenson of IHS Markit’s Coal service and Hannah Cotillon, our Country Risk specialist for Australia, in consultation with other Asian specialists.Dalrymple Bay The terminal is a major coal loading facility. It is owned by the Queensland government and leased to DBCT Management under a 99-year lease arrangement. This consists of a 50-year lease from 2001 and a 49-year extension option. The lease has been owned by Brookfield since 2009. A key feature of the facility is that 80% of its exports – 62 million tonnes in 2019 – are metallurgical coal, used in steel production by mills in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, and China. Sourcing material from the Bowen Basin, DBCT supplies 21% of metallurgical coal exports globally and some 7% of total global seaborne coal traffic. Unlike coal supply for power generation, there is no immediate alternative to the use of coal in steel manufacture. However, its remaining business comes from thermal coal (used in power generation). Queensland held state elections on 31 October, with Premier Annastacia Palaszczuk (Labour Party) re-elected for a third term. She has openly backed the resource industry. In September, the Palaszczuk government approved a new metallurgical coal mine in the Bowen Basin.In March 2020, a planned share sale by the firm worth up to AUD2 billion was postponed given market uncertainties during the global spread of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)-virus pandemic. At the time, the media, notably IPE Real Assets, reported that Korea’s National Pension Service, working with Global Infrastructure, and CK Infrastructure from Hong Kong had been interested in investing in the asset through a trade sale but had been held back by logistical problems with due diligence during the pandemic. Pre-marketing: Deal represents sizeable testPre-marketing for the deal began on 19 October to test initial investor response and seek potential core subscribers. At this stage, the marketing process is to explain the port and discuss its future business and regulatory prospects, with the goal of attracting “cornerstone” strategic investors, potentially for up to half the planned deal, according to media reports. Filing of a prospectus for the issue and its subsequent sale will be subject to the results of this initial phase. Headline: UPDATE 7 - Macao – No new COVID-19 cases reported; Hong Kong, Taiwan, and China residents permitted to enter.
Details:
New Updates:

The total number of confirmed COVID-19 cases in Macao remain at 46, where all cases have recovered and there have been no deaths. No new cases have been reported since the end of June. There are no restrictions on interstate travel or curfews in place. All casinos have resumed normal operations; however, people who enter casinos must show a negative COVID-19 test result.

As of Monday, November 9, only residents from Macao, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and mainland China are permitted to enter Macao; all other travelers will be denied entry. All air travelers from the permitted areas, including Macao residents, are required to show proof of a negative COVID-19 test taken within the last seven days before being authorized to board a flight to Macao. Border and ferry crossings between Hong Kong and Macao have been impacted, where all air and ferry travelers leaving Macao are required to show proof of a negative COVID-19 test taken within seven days of their departure. Air travelers from Macao to Guangdong are required to show a negative COVID-19 test that is only issued from Conde de Sao Januario Hospital or Taipa Maritime Terminal; travelers with tests issued from other hospitals will be denied.

On Wednesday, September 23, the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) and group visas were permitted across China. Initially in August, IVS visas were only authorized for Zhuhau and later in Guangdong province. People applying for a visa are required to show proof of a negative COVID-19 test taken within seven days before arrival in Macau. 

Previous updates:

As of July 13, all passengers travelling from Hong Kong through Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge shuttle busses as well as all arrivals from Hong Kong must present a negative COVID-19 PCR test result issued within the past 7 days. As of July 15, all individuals that enter hotel establishments and guest houses must receive a temperature check.

Headline: Severe Storms Across the South Lead to Widespread Flooding; SOE s in AL, MS, LA, KY, and TN
Details:
Following a week s worth of storms, widespread flooding has occurred across parts of Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, Georgia, Louisiana, and Kentucky. This has led to state of emergencies (SOE) being declared for counties in Alabama, and Mississippi, Morehouse Parish in Louisiana, and for the entire states of Kentucky and Tennessee. At least three deaths related to the severe weather have been reported in Tennessee. The storms also spawned multiple tornadoes, including one in Columbus, MS on Saturday, February 23, that caused damage to hundreds of buildings and killed one person and injured 11 others. 
 
	Counties in Alabama under a state of emergency: Blount, Cherokee, Colbert, Cullman, Dekalb, Etowah, Fayette, Franklin, Jackson, Lamar, Lauderdale, Lawrence, Limestone, Madison, Marion, Marshall, Morgan, Walker, and Winston. 
 
	Counties in Mississippi under a state of emergency: Calhoun, Carroll, Chickasaw, Clarke, Clay, Grenada, Humphreys, Issaquema, Itawamba, Lafayette, Lee, Leflore, Lincoln, Lowndes, Madison, Montgomery, Pontotoc, Prentiss, Quitman, Rankin, Sharkey, Simpson, Smith, Sunflower, Tallahatchie, Tishomingo, Tunica, Warren, Washington, Webster, Yalobusha, and Yazoo. 
 
	Assessment: The state of emergencies allowed states and local entities to open emergency operation centers to help deal with ongoing flooding and recovery efforts from the impact of the flooding and storms. Significant flooding is still being reported in Tuscumbia and Cedar Bluff, AL, and Magoffin and Martin counties in Kentucky, as well as large portions of Tennessee. The flooding in Tennessee has caused a number of evacuations in local communities especially for those residents in Counce, Hamburg, and Columbia. The flooding has also caused multiple landslides in Tennessee and Kentucky. The flooding in Alabama has led to curfews in Cedar Bluff and Leesburg. 
 
	Numerous local road closures have been reported across the region as well as a portion of I-24 in Nashville due to a mudslide. While the majority of forecasted rain has ended for the foreseeable future, river levels may continue to rise exacerbating flooding in some areas. Resilience360 customers are reminded to never attempt to drive through flooded roadways and heed all instructions from local authorities.

Headline: Port of Cape Town issues new instructions over coronavirus outbreak
Details:
Media sources reported that the harbor master at Cape Town has issued instructions due to the coronavirus outbreak:
•	Prior to boarding a vessel, Port Control should be contacted to confirm Free Pratique has been received and enquire about the last three ports of call. Security to also check with ISPS pre-arrival notification.
•	Upon boarding, Health Status of crew to be conformed with the Master.
•	For high risk vessels (those that have been to China, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, United States potts), boarding officers to wear face mask and gloves.
•	For the warning period, all South African citizens should refrain from consuming foods or liquids on board vessels from high risk areas. Gifts of food should not be accepted.
•	All off port limit crew from affected areas to be carefully screened – no crew to be taken off vessel without Port Health clearance.
•	Port Health declaration also required for all Off Port Limit transfers.
•	Medical evacuations from vessels from affected areas to be screened by Port Health before the person is taken off the vessel.
•	Captain to confirm in writing stowaway sweep was conducted before departing last port. Stowaway search may be requested when alongside, at the vessel’s cost, using specialist companies whose staff have undergone Corona Virus Disease training and/or awareness.
•	Security to inform Port Control of any reported stowaways from vessels calling from affected areas. If reported, vessel must remain at anchor until cleared by Port Health for entry or advised otherwise.
•	Masters must report stowaways on board if vessel calling from an affected area. Vessel to remain at anchor until stowaways are examined and cleared by Port Health or otherwise advised.
•	Strict gangway watches to be maintained at all times.
•	All involved in evacuation of infected crew or stowaways must be trained by Port Health on Corona Virus.
•	Separate lists of vessels calling from Corona-affected areas to be maintained for record purposes.
•	All galley waste of vessels from affected areas to be incinerated and should not be accepted ashore.
•	Additional security to be deployed by the agent for contaminated vessels and no-one to be allowed on board a contaminated vessel except Port Health. Only after clearance can anyone be permitted to enter the vessel.
•	If possible, contaminated vessels should be allocated an isolated berth away from other vessels.
Importers are advised to follow the recommended measures to avoid shipment delays as well as to prevent the virus.

On Saturday morning there will be no services between Liverpool Street and Enfield Town, Cheshunt and Chingford until 10:15 local time. On Sunday morning there will be no service between Clapham Junction and Willesden Junction until 11:15. Travellers are advised to use alternative modes of transport if necessary during the affected period and monitor Transport for London sources for any additional information.

Headline: UPDATE: Planned schedule out for strikes at DP World terminals in Australia
Details:
Updated sources on March 20 report about the planned strikes’ schedules (see below) by local stevedores across the DP-World terminals in Australia. The times represent Australian local time and all terminals will suspend operations for one hour accordingly. 

Brisbane Terminal: March 24, 2019
•	07:00 to 08:00
•	15:00 to 16:00
•	23:00 to 00:00

For Brisbane, vessel operations and road operations to the Old Terminal will be affected; however road operations to the automated modules will remain normal. The protected industrial actions are likely to impact shippers such as additional costs, late fees and delays in dropping off or collecting containers during the aforementioned period. Up to 1,800 workers across Australia will participate in the strike as a result of discontent among employees over a new enterprise agreement DP World is proposing. The protected industrial action advised to date includes bans on employees working in tasks above their normal grade, overtime, shift extensions, accepting late call ins and no advanced or delayed start times. Customers should plan shipments accordingly and potentially divert to other terminals

Headline: Tanker Hijacked by Migrants Reached Malta as EU Cuts Patrol Boat Deployments from Operation Sophia
Details:
On Thursday, five men were arrested after a tanker hijacked by migrants off the Libyan coast reached the port of Valletta under the command of Maltese armed forces. The Elhiblu I Palau-flagged tanker had rescued 108 migrants in the Mediterranean Sea Tuesday evening and was heading to Tripoli, Libya, when it changed to a northward course about seven miles from the destination port. The Maltese military said Thursday that the captain of the 170-foot tanker had repeatedly said that he was not controlling the ship, and that several migrants had threatened the captain and crew to make them head toward Malta. A Maltese military patrol vessel blocked the tanker from entering territorial waters and a special operations unit subsequently boarded and regained control of the tanker. The tanker was then piloted to Valletta under navy escort, where the five suspected hijacking leaders were arrested before the others disembarked. There were no initial details of any possible injuries associated with the hijacking. 
 
	Assessment: The incident demonstrates migrants  strong aversion to being taken to Libya rather than a European destination after being rescued attempting to cross the Mediterranean Sea. The hijacking occurred as the European Union agreed in principle on a plan to extend its Mediterranean migrant rescue patrols, called Operation Sophia. The EU announced Wednesday that it plans to extend the operation by six months, but would no longer deploy ships to patrol the sea, instead relying on aircraft for monitoring. The shift was based on strong resistance by the Italian government, which has previously refused to let ships with rescued migrants dock at its ports. Critics have argued that the limitation of the operation s rescue capacity imperils migrants still attempting to cross the sea. A final decision on the operation extension terms is due by March 31. Although attempted crossings have reduced from the peak of the migrant crisis several years prior, it remains to be seen whether commercial and other vessels may face greater pressure or obligation to rescue migrants as the potential nearest vessels, and if the risk of additional incidents such as the tanker hijacking this week could increase. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring associated developments that may impact maritime operations in the Mediterranean and the rates of migrants attempting crossings as summer approaches.

Headline: United States - United Auto Workers members approved contract with GM; strike over. Incident closed.
Details:

The new contract includes raises and an $11,000 signing bonus for workers while allowing GM to close factories in Lordstown, OH; Warren, MI; and outside Baltimore, MD. The strike began on September 16 and lasted for 40 days. 

The strike was initially enacted to demand better wages, fewer temporary workers, caps on health insurance, vacation time, 401k retirement, and the reopening of several recently closed factories.The strike stopped GM s US vehicle and parts production in its 33 manufacturing plants, as well as 22 parts distribution warehouses factories, in Michigan, Ohio, New York, Kentucky, Tennessee, Texas, Missouri, Indiana, and Kansas. Sources indicated the strike costed GM over US $1 billion. Production is expected to resume in the next coming days.

The strike involving UAW Mack Truck members, which began on October 12, has also ended. UAW Mack Truck member went on strike for better pay, benefits, and job protection. Mack Truck has plants in Allentown, PA; Middletown, PA; Hagerstown, MD; Baltimore, MD; and Jacksonville, FL. This incident is closed.

Headline: U.S. Embassy Issues Demonstration Alert on Threats of Nationwide University Shutdown
Details:
On Monday, the U.S. Diplomatic Mission to South Africa issued the following Demonstration Alert for U.S. citizens in the country:

 Location: University campuses in South Africa

Event:  There have been reports that student groups are calling for protests and a national shutdown of all universities in South Africa.  The U.S. Embassy recommends extra caution around university campuses and their surrounding areas over the next week. 

Actions to Take:

-Avoid the areas of the demonstrations.
-Exercise caution if unexpectedly in the vicinity of large gatherings or protests.
-Monitor local media for updates.
-Keep a low profile. 

The Demonstration Alert can be viewed at the following link: https://za.usembassy.gov/demonstration-alert-u-s-embassy-pretoria-4/

Assessment: The South African Union of Students (SAUS) called for a shutdown of all universities across the country last week over fees and other issues. As part of the strike, students at various universities, notably the University of KwaZulu-Natal (UKZN) campuses in Durban have held a series of localized protests, several of which have resulted in vandalism, arson, and other violence. Although the SAUS has since called off its shutdown following a meeting with the minister of higher education and training, protests are continuing at UKZN campuses and the potential for residual demonstrations and unrest at other university campuses cannot be ruled out. As such, customers are advised to exercise caution near universities and are reminded to avoid all protest-related activities due to the potential for unrest.

Headline: King Abdullah II Directs Authorities to Examine Possibility of Resuming Normal Activities
Details:
On Monday, Jordanian media sources reported that King Abdullah II has directed the government to examine the possibility of resuming exports of locally manufactured products and operations in productive sectors. In particular, King Abdullah has called for a solution that is gradual and strikes a balance between complying with public health regulations and restoring economic activities, especially work at small- and medium-sized enterprises. The monarch has also urged lawmakers to begin preparing for the period following the current coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak. As of Monday, Jordan had recorded 349 confirmed COVID-19 cases, along with six deaths attributed to the virus.



Assessment: Despite King Abdullah’s instructions, there are presently no indications that the Jordanian government will lift its social distancing measures and travel restrictions in the near future. Still, the development suggests an assessment that the kingdom’s coronavirus situation could be easing. Indeed, new cases continue to be reported each day; however, the rate of new infections is low and, in recent days, the number of active cases has declined, as the number of patients that have made a full recovery has risen to 126. This is likely due in part to Amman having pursued and enforced one of the most aggressive strategies against COVID-19 in the region, including the deployment of drones on Sunday to monitor for curfew breakers, among other tasks; at least 1,600 people have been arrested for violating travel restrictions to date.

Headline: Floating LNG Terminal Begins Delivering Gas to Chittagong; Hopes to Ease Chronic Shortages
Details:
On Friday, it was reported that Bangladesh s first liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal had started delivering supplies to the Chittagong region. The floating terminal, which is anchored off Moheshkhali Island in the Bay of Bengal, was a result of a US $180 million project developed by Petrobangla, Excelerate Energy, and the International Finance Corporation and is expected to increase LNG supplies to Bangladesh by 20 percent. The terminal will be operated by Excelerate for 15 years and then be transferred to Petrobangla. 
 
	 
		Assessment: The operation of the terminal is important, as Bangladesh suffers chronic shortages of LNG, especially in regards to electricity generation. Gas power plants supply 70 percent of Bangladesh s electricity and a shortage of LNG in October 2017 caused production to be disrupted at more than 350 garment factories in the Gazipur, Ashulia, Savar, and Kashimpur areas. Resilience360 customers with manufacturing interests in Bangladesh are advised to monitor the supply and demand of LNG in the country, as shortages will likely result in power cuts that could impact business operations.

Headline: UPDATE - Spain: Supreme Court sentences Catalan leaders to prison term over failed 2017 independence bid; protests expected
Details: Reports on Monday (14 October) state that Spain's Supreme Court has sentenced nine Catalan leaders to prison terms of between nine and 13 years for sedition for their role in a failed 2017 independence bid. Tensions have been steadily increasing in recent weeks ahead of the decision with police deploying additional officers to the region. In response pro-independence groups in the region have threatened a mass response of civil disobedience, with the region's two biggest grassroots pro-independence groups, the Catalan National Assembly (ANC) and Omnium Cultural, urging supporters to rally this evening. In the coming days, demonstrators will march from five towns towards Barcelona where they will congregate on Friday, 18 October, when a general strike has been called.

Headline: NYC police dismantles counterfeit goods ring
Details: Local sources reported that more than two dozen people have been arrested in connection with one of the largest counterfeit goods busts in New York City history, a scheme that generated nearly half a billion dollars in the sale of fake smuggle Chinese-manufactured luxury items ranging from knockoff Vuitton bags to Chanel perfume, federal officials said Thursday August 16. Officials say the ring used 40-foot shipping containers to smuggle the fake items into the U.S., primarily through the Port of New York/New Jersey.  To get the fakes into the country, prosecutors say the ""importers"" used the names, addresses and other identifying information of legitimate companies and faked the descriptions of the containers' contents on customs paperwork. The counterfeit goods were then taken by trucks to self-storage facilities in Brooklyn, Queens and Long Island, where they were unloaded and stored. Authorities also seized nine properties in Queens, Staten Island and Brooklyn belonging to the suspects.

Headline: PACA Meteorologists Monitoring Tropical Cyclone Weather Pattern in Arabian Sea
Details:
Omani media sources report that meteorologists from the country s Public Authority for Civil Aviation (PACA) are monitoring a weather system that could develop into a tropical cyclone and make landfall in the sultanate next week. According to reports, the weather pattern in question is currently located over southern India and could develop into a low pressure system and eventually a cyclone over the weekend. If these predictions materialize, the storm could strengthen as it moves northwest in the Arabian Sea next week before striking Oman on October 11-12. Parts of Yemen, Iran, and Pakistan also lie in the storm track forecast cone (aka the cone of uncertainty). 
 
	Assessment: Meteorologists have suggested that the storm has the potential to bring heavy rainfall and strong winds. This could result in deaths, injuries, material damage, and economic losses, as the dry environment in Oman and other countries in the Arabian Peninsula makes the region vulnerable to flash flooding and mudslides. One of the strongest tropical cyclones to ever make landfall in Oman did so in May of this year, resulting in power outages, flooding, roadway closures, and disruptions to operations at Salalah International Airport (IATA: SLL) and the Port of Salalah. While the storm s predicted path and strength remain subject to change, and despite local authorities having yet to announce any preparations, Resilience360 customers in Oman should stay informed of weather forecasts in the coming days and consider preparing security and financial contingency plans to mitigate the impact of any potential logistical delays or supply chain disruptions.

Headline: UPDATE 41 - 72 miles SSE of Saguenay – The storm has largely dissipated; US death toll at nine. Event closed.
Details:
Isaias has now moved further north into Quebec and has largely dissipated. Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone while located approximately 72 miles south-southeast of Saguenay. Media sources indicate that the storm caused some flooding in Quebec City and Trois Rivieres. The storm mostly resulted in street flooding; however, some homes were flooded along Rue Lauzon in Trois Rivieres.

Previously, the storm passed through the eastern United States, resulting in widespread power outages. Media sources indicate that at least nine people were killed in storm-related incidents. Two people were killed, and up to 20 were injured when a tornado swept through Windsor, North Carolina. Three people were killed by falling trees in Connecticut, Maryland, and New York respectively. One person was killed in flooding in Upper Saucon Township in Pennsylvania, while at least two people were killed in Delaware; at least one by a falling tree branch. Mandatory and voluntary evacuations were ordered in several locations along North Carolina’s coast, while voluntary evacuations were issued in Volusia County, Florida. 

Prior to making landfall in the United States, the storm passed through parts of the Caribbean. Flooding was reported in Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, where water and power outages were also reported. Two people were killed in the Dominican Republic as a result of flooding, one in Puerto Plata Province and another in El Seibo Province. This event is closed.

Headline: Migrant Workers Clash with Security Following Protest Over Unpaid Salaries in Abu Dhabi
Details:
Dozens of expatriate workers of the Sawaed Holding investment company were arrested in the Mussaffah Industrial area in Abu Dhabi on May 19 following a protest over three months of unpaid salaries; Emirati security reportedly raided the area and dispersed the protest, although exact specifics were not provided. Images posted on social media showed overturned cars and damaged property at the company’s facility, although no injuries were reported. Although it was not immediately clear what led to the company to withhold wages, many Emirati firms have been forced to curtail operations and make layoffs due to the economic downturn caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, especially among expatriate laborers.



Assessment: Migrant workers make up a large population of laborers in the Gulf region, and throughout the Middle East and North Africa in general, and the coronavirus pandemic has had a significant economic effect on the companies that employ them. In Lebanon, migrant workers for the waste treatment company, RAMCO, recently went on strike over pay discrepancies, also caused by the worsening economic situation in the country due to the coronavirus pandemic. And in al Farwaniyah in Kuwait, clashes broke out on May 12 at a shelter housing migrant workers over delayed repatriation due to travel restrictions in place due to COVID-19. Although protests are fairly rare in the United Arab Emirates, and although there have been no public calls for future protests, if the issue of unpaid wages is not resolved, additional demonstrations by expatriate workers may materialize. Any future protests are expected to be met with heavy police presence and may result in casualties especially if security forces use live fire or tear gas to disperse crowds.

Headline: Arrests of Protest Leaders and Banning of Demonstrations Likely to Worsen Hong Kong Situation
Details:
On Friday, police arrested a number of prominent figures in the pro-democracy movement, including members of the Demosisto party Joshua Wong Chi-fung and Agnes Chow Ting, and pro-democracy lawmakers Cheng Chung-tai, Au Nok-hin, and Jeremy Tam Man-ho. In total, at least 28 people were arrested. Their charges were related to protests that have taken place in recent months. Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow have since been released on bail, given evening curfews, and have been prohibited from entering the Admiralty area.

The day before, police also prohibited the main rally called by the Civil Human Rights Front (CHRF) on Saturday, citing the risk of violence due the history of other protests. Police said that they received credible intelligence that some protesters were planning to use petrol bombs, tasers, and drones against police. The protest was scheduled to start at Chater Garden in Central and end at Beijing s Hong Kong Liaison Office in Sai Wan. An appeal filed by the CHRF was denied and as a result, the march was officially canceled. However, a number of protesters have said that they intend to defy the ban and hold the protest march anyway. Police also banned a protest scheduled to take place on Monday at Salisbury Garden in Tsim Sha Tsui in Kowloon that was meant to coincide with a two-day strike called by the Confederation of Trade Unions and other groups.

Reports also emerged that earlier in the summer, the Hong Kong government was prepared to make a key concession to the protesters in officially withdrawing the extradition bill that sparked the recent rounds of protests. However, Beijing rejected the plan and instructed Chief Executive Carrie Lam to not withdraw the bill, open a police inquiry, or make any concessions to the protesters. The plan was reportedly submitted to the Central Co-ordination Group for Hong Kong and Macau Affairs and was reviewed by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Assessment: The arrest of the prominent pro-democracy figures, the banning of protests, and the refusal to make any concessions are likely to worsen the situation in Hong Kong in the immediate future. These actions will likely further radicalize a portion of the more moderate protesters and some of the already more violent protesters now have even less reason to temper their actions if they feel that there are no other options. The mass arrests were also likely timed to take place ahead of the five-year anniversary of the release of the plan for limited democracy for Hong Kong on August 31, 2014. Dissatisfaction over the plan, which required all candidates for chief executive to be approved by a pro-Beijing committee, sparked the Occupy Central protests later that year.

Despite the prohibitions on rallies, it is likely that thousands of people will still be participating in demonstrations in the coming days and weeks, even if overall numbers are down due to the threat of mass arrests. As the protests will be unauthorized, there is a much higher chance for clashes between protesters and police. Absent any central organizing group, the protests are also likely to be more unpredictable in terms of location and march route and could spread to other areas of Hong Kong with little notice.  Resilience360 customers are advised to closely monitor the situation and expect a strong police response to any unauthorized demonstrations. All areas where protests are taking place should also be avoided due to the high risk of violence.

Arrests of Protest Leaders and Banning of Demonstrations Likely to Worsen Hong Kong Situation On Friday, police arrested a number of prominent figures in the pro-democracy movement, including members of the Demosisto party Joshua Wong Chi-fung and Agnes Chow Ting, and pro-democracy lawmakers Cheng Chung-tai, Au Nok-hin, and Jeremy Tam Man-ho. In total, at least 28 people were arrested. Their charges were related to protests that have taken place in recent months. Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow have since been released on bail, given evening curfews, and have been prohibited from entering the Admiralty area.

The day before, police also prohibited the main rally called by the Civil Human Rights Front (CHRF) on Saturday, citing the risk of violence due the history of other protests. Police said that they received credible intelligence that some protesters were planning to use petrol bombs, tasers, and drones against police. The protest was scheduled to start at Chater Garden in Central and end at Beijing s Hong Kong Liaison Office in Sai Wan. An appeal filed by the CHRF was denied and as a result, the march was officially canceled. However, a number of protesters have said that they intend to defy the ban and hold the protest march anyway. Police also banned a protest scheduled to take place on Monday at Salisbury Garden in Tsim Sha Tsui in Kowloon that was meant to coincide with a two-day strike called by the Confederation of Trade Unions and other groups.

Reports also emerged that earlier in the summer, the Hong Kong government was prepared to make a key concession to the protesters in officially withdrawing the extradition bill that sparked the recent rounds of protests. However, Beijing rejected the plan and instructed Chief Executive Carrie Lam to not withdraw the bill, open a police inquiry, or make any concessions to the protesters. The plan was reportedly submitted to the Central Co-ordination Group for Hong Kong and Macau Affairs and was reviewed by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Assessment: The arrest of the prominent pro-democracy figures, the banning of protests, and the refusal to make any concessions are likely to worsen the situation in Hong Kong in the immediate future. These actions will likely further radicalize a portion of the more moderate protesters and some of the already more violent protesters now have even less reason to temper their actions if they feel that there are no other options. The mass arrests were also likely timed to take place ahead of the five-year anniversary of the release of the plan for limited democracy for Hong Kong on August 31, 2014. Dissatisfaction over the plan, which required all candidates for chief executive to be approved by a pro-Beijing committee, sparked the Occupy Central protests later that year.

Despite the prohibitions on rallies, it is likely that thousands of people will still be participating in demonstrations in the coming days and weeks, even if overall numbers are down due to the threat of mass arrests. As the protests will be unauthorized, there is a much higher chance for clashes between protesters and police. Absent any central organizing group, the protests are also likely to be more unpredictable in terms of location and march route and could spread to other areas of Hong Kong with little notice.  Resilience360 customers are advised to closely monitor the situation and expect a strong police response to any unauthorized demonstrations. All areas where protests are taking place should also be avoided due to the high risk of violence.

Headline: 186 miles NE of Tokyo   The storm is forecast to dissipate within the 24 hours. Incident closed.
Details: Former Typhoon Faxai has weakened into a tropical storm and is moving northeast into the Pacific Ocean. The storm is currently forecast to dissipate within the next 24 hours. At least 40 people were injured and two others were killed after the typhoon made landfall as the equivalent of a Category 3 storm. Out of the approximately 40 reported injuries, more than 12 were injured in the area of Tateyama, Chiba Prefecture, and ten were injured in Chiba city. Five people were also injured in Kanagawa Prefecture, and an additional five people were injured in Shizuoka Prefecture. Widespread power outages and public transportation disruptions had been reported, although services are normalizing. More than 220,000 people were also evacuated, but the evacuations have since lifted. This incident is closed.

Headline: Two Arrested for Terror Offenses in London, Showing Ongoing Terror Threat Despite Recent Downgrade
Details:
On Tuesday, two men were arrested at separate addresses in east London on suspicion of terror offenses. One of the men, a 27-year-old, is being held on suspicion of the involvement in the  commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.  The other suspect is 21 years old and suspected of encouraging terrorism and disseminating terrorist publications. In addition to searches of two residences, a third search was conducted at an unspecified commercial premises in east London. Authorities did not indicate whether the arrests were linked in any way, and the latter suspect was subsequently released on bail.

Assessment: While investigations remain ongoing, authorities have not released additional details about the suspected terror plot with which the 27-year-old was purportedly involved. Nonetheless, the arrest highlights authorities  ongoing vigilance of terror threats in the country despite the recent downgrade of the United Kingdom s terror threat level from severe to substantial. Since the March 2017 Westminster attack, UK authorities say 24 attack plots have been foiled, seven of which were tied to far-right motives. No specific, credible threat is known at this time. Nonetheless, there is an ongoing overall threat of terrorism in the country, including the potential for actions motivated by the recent death of Islamic State s leader as well as possible efforts to strike during the election and holiday season to draw additional attention. It is advised to practice heightened vigilance, particularly in crowded and high-profile locations, and to report suspicious items or behavior to local authorities.

Headline: U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa Issues Weather Alert Regarding Hurricane Eta
Details:
On Sunday, the U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa issued the following Weather Alert regarding Tropical Storm Eta, which has since strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson Wind Scale:



“Location: Honduras



Event:  The Government of Honduras has issued a hurricane watch for areas along the Caribbean coast of Honduras. Tropical Storm Eta is currently approximately 600 kilometers off the coast of Gracias a Dios and is expected to strengthen to a hurricane before it reaches the Caribbean coasts of Central American countries early Tuesday, November 3, 2020.



American citizens in the departments of Gracias a Dios, Atlantida, Colon, Yoro, Cortes, Olancho, and the Bay Islands are advised to prepare for possible inclement weather in the form of storm surge, hurricane-force winds, and heavy rainfall. Heavy rainfall predicted through Thursday, November 5, 2020, may lead to flash flooding and river flooding in affected areas.



American citizens in the departments of Santa Barbara, Comayagua, Francisco Morazan, and El Paraiso are advised to remain alert and continue monitoring weather reports.



Actions to Take: 



• Monitor the National Hurricane Center for updates (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/).

• Follow guidelines issued by local authorities (http://www.copeco.gob.hn).

• Seek secure shelter.

• Inform a friend or family member of travel plans over the upcoming holiday.

• Have travel documents up to date and easily accessible.

• Prepare an emergency supply kit (ready.gov).

• Notify friends and family of your safety.



Assistance:



U.S. Embassy Tegucigalpa

https://hn.usembassy.gov/

Tel. (504) 2238-5114

USAHonduras@state.gov



State Department – Consular Affairs

888-407-4747 or 202-501-4444”



The Weather Alert can be viewed in its entirety at the following URL: https://hn.usembassy.gov/weather-alert-u-s-embassy-tegucigalpa-honduras-4/.
