Headline: MIT Militants Kill Police Officer in Central Sulawesi; Reportedly Seven to 14 Militants Remaining
Details:
On Friday, one police officer was killed when East Indonesia Mujahideen (MIT) militants attacked a mosque in the Salubanga village of Parigi Moutong in Central Sulawesi Province. The militants, who were using firearms, also took several civilians hostage before fleeing the scene. Police said that they would intensify efforts to catch the remaining members of the group, who have been operating in the Parigi Moutong, Poso, Sausu, and Torue areas. It is believed that MIT was responsible for the murder of two civilians in the same area in July.

Assessment: The number of MIT militants reached a low of seven last year, although police said that recent recruitment efforts may have grown the group to around 14. At its peak, the group had around 45 militants. The group has pledged its allegiance to the Islamic State, although it is unknown if they have direct links to Islamic State leadership. The main leader of MIT, Santoso, was killed in July 2016 during a clash with security forces. Santoso had previously threatened to strike Jakarta and Bali, but the group has not demonstrated a capability to carry out major attacks in recent years. At the moment, the group, given its small size and ongoing pursuit by security forces, does not represent a significant threat to the security situation in Indonesia. Customers are still advised to avoid areas where clashes have recently occurred, as additional clashes are likely to take place in the future.

Headline: Preparations Ongoing, Emergency Proclamations Issued in Anticipation of Hurricane Florence
Details:
On Monday, Hurricane Florence intensified into a Category 4 storm as it continued to track to the north-northwest across the Atlantic Ocean. The National Weather Service forecasts that Florence will be a major hurricane (meaning a Category 3 storm or above on the Saffir-Simpson Scale) when it makes landfall on the East Coast of the United States later this week. Tropical-storm-force winds may arrive on the East Coast sometime between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. Rainfall totals of between six and ten inches are forecast for much of North Carolina and Virginia, with an area that may expect more than ten inches arcing from eastern North Carolina to the northwest and north into central and northern Virginia. Rainfall totals may exceed current estimates if Florence lingers over the region longer than is currently expected. States of emergency have been declared preemptively by the governors of South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, and Maryland. Evacuation orders have been issued for coastal communities in South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia. Amtrak announced modified services for locations on the East Coast beginning Wednesday, September 13 due to the predicted impacts of Hurricane Florence. 
 
	Assessment: Maritime authorities are monitoring Hurricane Florence s progress and will close port operations as it is deemed necessary. Port condition Whiskey was set Monday for the Ports of South Carolina, as well as for ports in Georgia, North Carolina, Virginia, and the Maryland-National Capital Region. Shipping experts posit that Florence s impacts to shipping will depend on its exact path and intensity when it makes landfall. Disruptions to freight operations may be exacerbated by widespread flooding or damage to roads and railroads throughout the region. Locations inland have been advised to make preparations in the event that additional evacuation orders are issued, especially those areas that are low-lying or are prone to flooding. Resilience360 customers are advised to heed all local weather warnings and evacuation notices. Full coverage of Hurricane Florence s impacts can be viewed by logging onto Resilience360 s Risk Center solution.

The National Weather Service forecasts that Florence will be a major hurricane (meaning a Category 3 storm or above on the Saffir-Simpson Scale) when it makes landfall on the East Coast of the United States later this week. Tropical-storm-force winds may arrive on the East Coast sometime between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. Rainfall totals of between six and ten inches are forecast for much of North Carolina and Virginia, with an area that may expect more than ten inches arcing from eastern North Carolina to the northwest and north into central and northern Virginia. Rainfall totals may exceed current estimates if Florence lingers over the region longer than is currently expected. States of emergency have been declared preemptively by the governors of South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, and Maryland. Evacuation orders have been issued for coastal communities in South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia. Amtrak announced modified services for locations on the East Coast beginning Wednesday, September 13 due to the predicted impacts of Hurricane Florence. 
 
	Assessment: Maritime authorities are monitoring Hurricane Florence s progress and will close port operations as it is deemed necessary. Port condition Whiskey was set Monday for the Ports of South Carolina, as well as for ports in Georgia, North Carolina, Virginia, and the Maryland-National Capital Region. Shipping experts posit that Florence s impacts to shipping will depend on its exact path and intensity when it makes landfall. Disruptions to freight operations may be exacerbated by widespread flooding or damage to roads and railroads throughout the region. Locations inland have been advised to make preparations in the event that additional evacuation orders are issued, especially those areas that are low-lying or are prone to flooding. Resilience360 customers are advised to heed all local weather warnings and evacuation notices. Full coverage of Hurricane Florence s impacts can be viewed by logging onto Resilience360 s Risk Center solution.

Headline: Pipeline Leak in Yvelines Raises Prospect of Grandpuits Refinery Shutdown
Details:
At about 10:35 PM local time Sunday, an alarm was set off indicating a pressure drop along the Ile-de-France pipeline (PLIF) due to a crude oil leak in an area of fields in Autouillet, Yvelines department. Several rivers in Vicq, Boissy-sans-Avoir, and Autouillet (R  le Lieutel, R  de Breuil, and R  de la Coquerie) were also impacted by the underground hydrocarbon spill. The prefecture said up to about 17 acres of fields were affected by the leak, with gendarmerie reporting up to 30 acres impacted overall. The leak has been halted and the pipeline depressurized. The company said that the exact cause of the leak was under investigation, and that the affected stretch of pipeline was being excavated as part of that process. Pumping trucks have been deployed to recover oil and the impacted land is being excavated and removed with the use of construction equipment, with the cleanup process expected to take multiple months. 
 
	Assessment: The approximately 166-mile pipeline connected the port of Le Havre to the Grandpuits refinery, and it is operated by Total to transport primarily crude oil. The Grandpuits refinery is planned to reduce operations gradually this week as reserves decrease, though the exact timing and duration for a prospective shutdown of the refinery was not yet announced. The PLIF had suffered a leak in May 2014 near Le Havre, and there have been calls for increased monitoring and upgrading of underground pipeline, particularly with regard to aging infrastructure. The 2014 spill caused the refinery to shut down for three weeks. However, Total insisted that there is not a shortage risk for fuel supplies in Ile-de-France. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring associated developments that may impact refinery operations, fuel supply, and fuel prices while the pipeline remains out of operation and the Grandpuits refinery has reduced or halted operations.

Headline: Chittagong Port authorities revoked quarantine order for all ships arriving from China
Details: Media sources reported that Chittagong Port authorities have already revoked quarantine orders related to all ships arriving from China. For several months, all ships arriving from China, with an average 11-day long voyage were to undergo quarantine to fit in universal 14-day quarantine demand. The ships had to wait some 3-4 days until cleared for a berth. Effectively from July 12, the restriction has been waived, the ships may proceed to berth immediately on arrival.

Headline: THE Alliance merges FE4 into FE2 service through September 2020
Details:

FE2 (modified): Busan > Shanghai > Ningbo > Yantian > Singapore > Rotterdam > Southampton > Le Havre > Hamburg > Rotterdam > Singapore > Busan. 

FE2 (pre-modification): Busan > Shanghai > Ningbo > Yantian > Singapore > Southampton > Le Havre > Hamburg > Rotterdam > Port Klang > Busan. 

FE4 (blanked until October 2020): Qingdao > Busan > Ningbo > Shanghai > Yantian > Algeciras > Rotterdam > Hamburg > Antwerp > London Gateway > Algeciras > Singapore > Qingdao.

Headline: 134 miles SE of Hong Kong - TD Yutu has dissipated in the South China Sea. Incident closed.
Details:
Tropical Depression Yutu, also referred to as ""Rosita"" in the Philippines, has dissipated in the South China Sea, but may have a lingering impact on southeastern China. There are no current warnings or watches in effect. 

In the Philippines, Yutu reportedly affected approximately 40,000 people and caused significant structural damage in areas of northern Luzon as well as power outages, evacuations, and landslides. In one landslide in Natonin, dozens were feared dead and at least 11 were confirmed killed. In the Northern Mariana Islands, one person was killed and at least 133 others sustained various injuries due to the storm. At least 12 people were killed in total. Over 500 homes were damaged, rendering over 1000 people homeless. This incident is closed.

Headline: Mitsubishi Electric data breach highlights APT threat for manufacturers
Details:
On January 20, Japanese electronics manufacturer Mitsubishi Electric disclosed the occurrence of a data breach that may have compromised information on government agencies and business partners. While the firm confirms that sensitive information on defense, electricity, or other infrastructure operations have not been breached, a total of 120 workstations and 40 servers were affected across all units of the company while personal data on over 8,000 people, including employees, retirees, and job-seekers, may have been endangered. The hacking tools in question were discovered in a company lab based in Japan on June 28, 2019; unauthorized access occurred at the company’s China affiliates before spreading to Japan. 

APT group believed to be responsible

The suspected perpetrator of the hack is reportedly an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group, or a concerted and multifaceted professional hacking organization, called Tick, also known as Bronze Butler or RedBaldKnight. The APT group is believed to be based in China due to the use of Chinese developer constructed tools, documented links with the Network Crack Program Hacker (NCPH) group as well as the start of unauthorized access in the company’s China affiliates.
It is unlikely that the breach will have any operational impact, and information security analysis suggests that the predominant focus of the group is the theft of intellectual property and sensitive communications. A notable impediment to the resolution of this incident is the fact that the APT deleted access logs upon completion of the data theft, thus complicating further investigation, a task already made difficult by the group’s frequent changing of communication IP addresses.

Headline: Authorities Taking Inventory of Hazardous Materials at Port of Chittagong Following Beirut Explosion
Details:
This week, authorities at the Port of Chittagong formed a committee to inventory hazardous materials stored in the port, recommend steps to relocate such materials, and investigate options for upgrading storage facilities for hazardous products. The Chittagong Port Authority acknowledged that some flammable and other hazardous materials are stored in the port. According to media reports, some of these items have been kept at the port facilities for nearly 30 years. Separately, the national government has sought to ascertain whether there are stockpiles of ammonium nitrate at ports or other facilities in Bangladesh. 



Assessment: The focus on ammonium nitrate and ports has arisen following the August 4 explosion of a large stock of the chemical at a port in Beirut, Lebanon, which killed at least hundreds of people, injured thousands, and damaged thousands of buildings. Under Bangladeshi customs requirements, importers must take delivery of their items within 30 days of unloading at the port. If items are not claimed within 30 days, they will be issued a notice by authorities, after which they have 15 final days to claim their items before they are auctioned. According to officials with the Chittagong Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CMCCI), however, these regulations are not enforced, and as much as 25 percent of the port’s storage space is taken up by unclaimed merchandise, which the group says has caused delays to port operations in the past. Officials with both the CMCCI and the Chittagong Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCCI) have warned that unclaimed hazardous items at the port pose a potential danger. A fire that broke out at the port in July took hours to extinguish, although there was no immediate indication that it was caused by hazardous materials being stored. As for the ammonium nitrate inquiry being carried out by the national government, Bangladeshi officials have also stated that such potentially explosive materials are strictly regulated, are not stored in ports once they are imported, and that the investigation is being carried out as a precaution. As much as 90 percent of Bangladesh’s imports and exports move through the Port of Chittagong. While there has been no indication that major delays are expected, it is advised to be aware of the possibility of disruptions should the port’s committee determine that large amounts of materials need to be removed.

Headline: UPDATE 8 - Komari – Fire reignited aboard tanker New Diamond 35 miles off Sangamon Kanda Point. Event closed.
Details: Updated sources report a fire has reignited due to sparks, high temperature, and high wind on Monday, September 7 aboard the Panamanian-flagged crude oil tanker New Diamond in the Bay of Bengal roughly 35 miles off Sangamon Kanda Point in Komari. Sri Lankan and Indian naval and coast guard units had previously extinguished a second fire on Sunday, September 6 and are expected to remain on-scene responding to any additional flare-ups. The first fire began last week in the vessel’s boiler room but did not spread to the oil storage area, and no leak has been reported. At least 21 of the 23 crew aboard were rescued, with one killed, one injured, and one missing. The vessel, carrying an estimated two billion barrels of crude oil from Kuwait to Paradip, India, drifted within approximately 23 miles of the Sri Lankan coast before being towed further out to sea. Reliance Industries diverted one of its nearby tankers to assist the New Diamond crew. Officials are preparing environmental assessments of the event. Event closed.

Headline: Remuneration negotiations increase risk of temporary strikes affecting...
Details: Risks: Labour relationsSectors or assets affected: Oil and gasOn 14 August, the Oil Workers Union (Union Sindical Obrera de la Industria del Petroleo: USO) will begin collective wage negotiations with state oil company Ecopetrol. USO is demanding a 15% salary increase, with an additional 10% increase within six months, a minimum 60% increase in travel expenses and an additional 30% in other economic benefits. Colombian financial journal Portfolio estimates the demands will cost the company around USD680 million. USO represents more than 3,500 workers at Ecopetrol, around 35% of the total of the firm's direct employees. An additional 24,000 sub-contract workers are employed by the firm, according to Colombian newspaper Dinero. Other, non-financial demands include guarantees that the firm will not be privatised and an improvement in the labour rights of sub-contracted workers. In a statement on its official website on 2 August, USO said it was preparing for a general strike to defend its demands if they are not met. USO has approximately 18,000 members in the oil and gas and associated sectors, according to Ecopetrol.Significance: Although USO will support localised strikes several times a year,  it has not held a general strike since 2004, when the union went on strike over plans to partially privatise Ecopetrol, which eventually passed in 2006, allowing up to 20% of private ownership. State ownership is currently 88.49%. The issue resurfaced under the Previous Juan Manuel Santos administration. The appointment of Alberto Carrasquilla, the new Finance Minister in the current Ivan Duque administration â who once supported the full privatisation of Ecopetrol â is unlikely to assuage the union's concerns; swift agreement is very unlikely. The union is likely to deploy localised and general strikes as a negotiating tactic through August and September, to influence both remuneration demands and the government's broader policy towards the state-owned company. A general strike would be likely to last a few days, before a legal injunction forces a suspension or allows police intervention on grounds of preventing commercial disruption. Deployment of additional state security forces to Ecopetrol locations would indicate increased likelihood of impending strike action and temporary commercial disruption. Headline: Data breach suspected at auto manufacturer's Vietnam headquarters
Details: Industry sources indicated on March 29 that hackers perpetrated a data breach at Toyota's Japan offices, its second such attack in 5 weeks since its last one at its Australia head office. Furthermore, the breach is anticipated to have implicated Toyota's Vietnam offices, while this has yet to be confirmed. The breach implicated 3.1 million customers affiliated with the following subsidiaries: Toyota Tokyo Sales Holdings, Tokyo Tokyo Motor, Tokyo Toyopet, Toyota Tokyo Corolla, Nets Toyota Tokyo, Lexus Koishikawa Sales, Jamil Shoji (Lexus Nerima), and Toyota West Tokyo Corolla. While financial data was deemed not to be compromised, Toyota has yet to disclose which type of data was. Based on details relevant to the Australia hack, preliminary attribution points to APT32, or Ocean Lotus, a Vietnamese Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group responsible for targeting multinational auto manufacturers in Vietnam, yet this has yet to be confirmed. Those conducting business with Toyota in Vietnam should consult with supply chain managers and IT professionals to formulate the best possible defense.

Headline: U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa Issues Security Alert: Roadblocks, Theft of Groceries from Vehicles
Details:
On Tuesday night, the U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa issued a Security Alert for American citizens in Honduras. The message reads, in part:



“Location: Honduras



Event: Roadblocks in Tegucigalpa



Protesters have begun to block roads around Tegucigalpa with rocks, trees, burning tires and other debris. The U.S. Embassy has received reports of vehicles being stopped and targeted by the protesters who steal from those cars that appear to have recent purchases from supermarkets. Given the reports of crime at these impromptu roadblocks, the U.S. Embassy recommends the following:



-All U.S. citizens should minimize unnecessary travel. As outlined in a previous health alert, U.S. citizens are expected to abide by the Government of Honduras’ restrictions limiting shopping, banking, and other activities to one day per week, depending on the last number of your identity document.

-U.S. citizens should carry their safe conduct letters (salvoconducto), Honduran ID for residents and U.S. passport for non-residents, when traveling in public.

-Keep any articles of value and recent purchases after any shopping trips out of view, preferably in your car’s trunk or covered up.

-Keep your doors locked and windows up at all times.

-Pre-plan your route and know at least one alternative route; select well-traveled streets whenever possible.

-Maintain sufficient space between you and the car in front of you to allow yourself the ability to maneuver.

-Drive near the center of the road to avoid being forced off.

-Should you see a road block ahead of you, attempt to exit or turn around, if possible and safe to do so.

-If you become a victim of a robbery, DO NOT RESIST.”



The Security Alert can be viewed in its entirety at the following URL: https://hn.usembassy.gov/security-alert-usembassytgu-033120/.



Assessment: In addition to the aforementioned incidents in Tegucigalpa, there have been sporadic reports of similar episodes in other parts of the country in recent days. For instance on Saturday, March 28th, a mob comprised of dozens of people forcibly stopped and ransacked a large van that was transporting groceries in San Pedro Sula. The potential for looting, banditry, and further roadblocks could potentially rise in the coming days and weeks, as COVID-19 movement restrictions remain in effect and the country’s economic woes continue to compound. Moreover, the Honduran healthcare system will likely face the risk of collapse as the country’s caseload continues to grow. Even before COVID-19’s emergence in the country, Honduran healthcare workers regularly staged strikes and protests due to issues such as low pay, excessive hours, inadequate staffing levels, and/or the lack of supplies and equipment. The country’s inability to effectively handle the looming surge in patients could exacerbate the potential for protests and unrest even further. As of this writing, at least 172 cases of COVID-19 have been confirmed in Honduras, ten of which have proven to be fatal. The department of Cortés has recorded the highest number of cases (101), followed by Francisco Morazán (39), Colón (18), and Lempira (4).

Headline: Chinese Military Carries Out Drills in Hong Kong Harbor as Likely Warning to Protesters
Details:
On Friday, the Hong Kong garrison of the People s Liberation Army (PLA) carried out drills around the city s Victoria Harbour. The quarterly exercises involved infantry, special forces, ships, boats, and helicopters. The drills focused on several operations, including search and rescue activities, general emergency responses, joint patrols, escort patrols, and capture operations. In one exercise, troops participated in the simulated takeover of a port facility. Around 1,000 soldiers took part in the drills.

Assessment: Although the exercises are held on a quarterly basis, an officer involved in the Friday drills said that they were larger and lasted for a longer time than usual. They also simulated more actual combat than is typical. Being fairly visible and taking place over and along Victoria Harbour, it is likely that the exercises were also intended, at least in part, as a warning and show of force to protesters who continue to mobilize large numbers of people in the city. There are around 6,000 to 7,000 PLA personnel in the Hong Kong garrison, and military officials reported that the Hong Kong government was notified of the Friday drills ahead of time.

Headline: UPDATE 10 - Vietnam – Recovery efforts are underway after Tropical Storm Sinlaku caused flooding. Event closed.
Details:
Sources indicate that recovery efforts are underway across Vietnam after the passage of Tropical Storm Sinlaku caused flooding and landslides in multiple provinces. Over 2,800 structures were damaged, destroyed, or inundated to some capacity, while seven people were killed, and eight people were injured in storm-related incidents. The major impacts by province were as follows:

- An Giang: At least 19 homes were destroyed and two people were injured.

Headline: WATCH FOR: Large-scale protests and road blockades in Warsaw against tightening of abortion restrictions
Details: Risk analysis: The Women's Strike (Strajk Kobiet) activist group is likely to organise further protests at least until the end of 2020 against the tightening of the abortion law. Protesters are likely to gather in front of government buildings, the Constitutional Court and the house of Law and Justice (PiS) leader Jarosław Kaczynski. Headline: UPDATE 4 - Victoria State extends 'state of disaster' as bushfire threat continues
Details: It has been reported that Victoria State Premier Daniel Andrews has extended the 'state of disaster' across Victoria for another 48 hours. Weather reports say that hot weather and strong winds will heighten the fire threat in the coming days. There are 23 fires burning in Victoria and 13 'watch and act' alerts have been issued. Across the state so far, more than 1.2 million hectares have been burnt and 244 homes destroyed. Clifton Creek residents have been warned that fires burning to the north of the town may threaten their homes tomorrow. This comes after the town suffered significant property loss early last week, including the loss of its local primary school. Earlier on Thursday, the emergency warning that was issued for a fire near Abbeyard, 40 kilometres south-east of Wangaratta, was upgraded to ""Evacuate Now"". However, a second ""Evacuate Now"" warning has been issued, which strongly urges those located in Buffalo River, Dandongadale, Merriang South, Mount Buffalo and Nug Nug to leave. In addition, the town of Mallacoota remains isolated, as a Navy vessel was unable to reach the shore due to a sandbar in the sea. Efforts are underway to clear this so aid can be provided. Emergency text messages have been sent to those residing in East Gippsland and north-east Victoria, urging them to leave as soon as possible.

Headline: Port workers in Valparaiso threaten to resume 35-day strike
Details:
On November 17, 2018 more than 500 casual workers at Chile's flagship port of Valparaiso decided to walk off the job to demand a bonus payment, more formal contracts, and improved working conditions. After a series of small demonstrations, around 50 dockworkers linked to Terminal Cerros de Valparaiso (TCVAL) finally accepted an offer put forward by the port operator and returned to work on November 30. The rest of the protesting workers, however, did not reach an agreement with Terminal Pacífico Sur (TPS), the second and most important concessionaire in Valparaiso, until December 21, 2018, which shut down shipping for over 35 days at one of Chile’s most important ports and a major commercial hub to the capital city Santiago.

The first weeks of the strike were marked by small pickets outside the port facilities and union leaders negotiating with TPS representatives. In recent weeks, however, protests in Valparaiso have turned increasingly violent and spread to other ports along the nation's Pacific coast. The conflict reached a tipping point on Monday, December 19, when strikers set barricades throughout the city and police agents repressed demonstrators with water cannons and tear gas. Protesters also got into the Dockers' Union headquarters, resulting in 20 detainees, two injured, and the destruction of much of the furniture in the building.

One day after the violent protests in Valparaiso, the striking dockworkers received support from their colleagues at the northern ports of Iquique, Antofagasta, Caldera, Ventanas, and San Antonio, the most important one in the country and close to Valparaiso.  In the southern part of the country, dockworkers at the ports of Talcahuano San Vicente and Puerto Montt also stopped their work in support of their colleagues in Valparaiso. The possibility of officially extending the strike to other ports in the country triggered alarms in sectors highly dependent on export activity, such as agriculture, food processing, and chemicals, which send products worth some USD 25 billion to foreign markets each year.

Impacts

According to the Chilean Maritime Port Organization, the strike has caused more than 50,000 containers to be diverted to other ports, with a total revenue loss of over USD 8 million. Chile’s fruit sector was particularly impacted by the strike in Valparaiso, which handles approximately 55% of Chile’s fruit exports. According to the Federation of Fruit Producers of Chile, fruit shipments from the port of Valparaiso fell 95% as a result of the port strike, going from 59,883 tons between November 16 and December 17 in 2017 to only 3,006 tons in 2018.

Meanwhile, there was a large increase in shipments at the port of San Antonio, which had already displaced Valparaiso in cargo handling and efficiency due to past port conflicts. However, not all was positive news for the Port of San Antonio, which suffered from increased congestion due to more than 20,000 additional trucks that arrived during the strike. In a normal day, according to San Antonio’s Port Authority, there are about 100 to 150 trucks that are served in an hour. However, due to the massive arrival of operators from Valparaiso, it was necessary to attend to more than 300 trucks in just one hour.

Outlook

On December 19, the dockworkers union and the port operator TPS reached a pre-agreement, which was later rejected by the dockworkers at a general assembly. The workers argued that the compensations offered by TPS are far below what they demand. Nonetheless, on December 22, workers at port of Valparaiso ended their strike, when union representatives accepted an offer from the operator, TPS, following an agreement signed between the workers and the Ministry of Labor. TPS’s offer includes a bonus of around 760,000 pesos (USD 1,100 or EUR 965), a gift card of 250,000 pesos (USD 365 or EUR 320) and a training course worth over 400,000 pesos (USD 600 or EUR 525).

On January 3, however, a group of port workers resumed demonstrations in Valparaiso, placing barricades near the Dockworkers' Union headquarters. Protesters reportedly claim that port officials have not adhered to an initial payment agreement reached two weeks ago and that as many as 22 dockworkers who participated in the December demonstrations have been denied access to the port facilities. On the same day, TPS issued a public statement confirming that the Port of Valparaiso has continued to operate normally despite the most recent demonstrations.

Lasting 35 days, the 2018 November-December strike at the Port of Valparaiso was the second longest port strike in Chile in the last 20 years and one with important implications for the fruit industry in the country. Supply chain managers should continue to monitor the situation at the Port of Valparaiso because although operations have resumed, further demonstrations are expected in the upcoming days. Moreover, it will take weeks, if not months, to clear the congestion created as a result of the service disruption in Valparaiso.

Headline: First IMF review of Somalia’s Extended Credit Facility suggests progress in debt relief efforts - UPDATE 2
Details: The International Monetary Fund (IMF)’s first review of Somalia’s three-year staff-monitored programme in November suggests debt relief advancements, while natural disasters and the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic contributed to an economic shock in 2020.   The IMF on 30 November announced its approval of an immediate disbursement of USD10 million as part of the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangement with Somalia, following a first review. Following the achievement of the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative decision point, representatives of the Paris Club creditor countries and the government of Somalia agreed to restructure Somalia’s external public debt.The IMF stated that Somalia's performance under the ECF arrangement has been broadly satisfactory despite the significant challenges the economy faced in 2020. The IMF’s official statement highlights that prompt action by the Somalian government and support from the international community has helped mitigate the impact of the latest natural-disaster events and the COVID-19 pandemic. Nevertheless, these shocks have had a significant impact on Somalia’s economic activity, exports, and domestic fiscal revenues, leading to a contraction in real GDP.OutlookIHS Markit projects Somalia’s economy to grow at an average 2.8% annually in the near term (2021–23) given the prevailing headwinds, after contracting 2% in 2020. Drought conditions and security concerns have added to the economic and humanitarian hardships in Somalia in the past year and they are expected to continue to hinder growth prospects in the remainder of 2020 and into 2021. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic is expected to have impacted Somalia’s fiscal revenues negatively, in tandem with a drop in international travel dragging on the transportation sector’s revenues, as well as delays in implementing the new licensing and regulatory framework for the telecommunications sector. We expect that Somalia’s government will strive to align with IMF requirements to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation to create fiscal space for priority spending under the ninth National Development Plan. Fiscal consolidation improved prior to the global outbreak of the COVID-19 virus. Domestic revenue in 2019 reached USD230 million, up from USD183 million in 2018.Somalia’s cabinet approved the 2021 draft budget on 29 October 2020, which has been submitted to parliament for approval and adoption. Striking features of the new budget are the introduction of turnover taxes scheduled at USD2million and an increase of the tax rate on khat scheduled to achieve revenues of USD32.2 million. The potential impact of introducing the single customs tariff from 2021 is expected to be revenue neutral in 2021. To reach the HIPC completion point, Somalia will continue to need extensive capacity development support. In 2020, agreements have been signed with the Paris Club creditors, including Spain and the United States. According to the latest IMF release, agreements are close to being signed with Norway and the United Kingdom. Furthermore, the IMF highlighted that, among other creditors, representatives of the Kuwait Fund for Development, the Saudi Fund for Development, and the Abu Dhabi Fund for Development attended the Paris Club meeting in March as observers, expressing their support.© 2020, IHS Markit Inc. Headline: UPDATE 3 - New Jersey - Governor Phil Murphy lifted the statewide stay-at-home order. Event closed.
Details:
New Updates:

Governor Phil Murphy announced the statewide stay-at-home order was lifted on June 9. The state is set to enter Stage Two of reopening on June 15. This event is closed.

Previous Updates: 

- The limit on outdoor gatherings has been lifted from 10 people to 25 people. Additionally, all recreational campgrounds have reopened across the state. 
- Governor Phil Murphy has created a commission to organize a plan to reopen businesses across the state. However, plan-specific details regarding which businesses can reopen or when they can reopen were not specified. Governor Murphy indicated that before a plan can start, the number of cases and hospitalizations must drop for 14 days and more programs involving widespread testing, contract tracing, and isolation must be implemented.
- State and county parks have reopened across the state, and parking lots must adhere to a 50 percent capacity limit. Public transit will remain in service to transport essential employees, but other people have been advised not to travel unless necessary. The anticipated duration of the restrictions has not been immediately reported.
- Governor Murphy signed an executive order requiring all non-essential businesses across the state of New Jersey to close and residents to stay at home due to the spread of COVID-19. Businesses that do not comply may face fines. Exempted sectors include those related to shipping, media, warehousing, grocery, and food production (including meal deliveries), pharmacies, healthcare, utilities, banking, and law enforcement, among others. Exceptions for exiting the home apply for activities such as obtaining essential goods or services, seeking medical attention, visiting family or close friends, reporting to work, or engaging in outdoor activities.

Headline: Rabat Extends State of Emergency Through August 10, Reopens Borders to Residents
Details:
Morocco announced on July 8 that it would reopen its land and sea borders, which were previously shuttered on March 15 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, to Moroccans and foreign residents living in Morocco, beginning on July 14. The country is only permitting the entry of Moroccan citizens, foreign residents, and family members of citizens and residents. Travelers must take a COVID-19 test less than 48 hours before departing for Morocco. The reopening of maritime crossing points will only be permitted from the ports of Sete, France, and Genoa, Italy. Additionally, on July 9, the Moroccan government extended the state of emergency for one more month, now scheduled to last through 6:00 PM local time, August 10. The move marks the fourth such extension of the state of emergency, which was originally declared on March 20. The state of emergency reportedly allows for local officials to restore lockdowns on a region-by-region basis depending on health situations. As of this writing, Morocco has recorded 15,328 cases of COVID-19, along with 243 virus-related deaths. 



Assessment: Morocco has recorded rising daily incidence of COVID-19 since June 17, though this has not seemed to affect the kingdom’s multi-phase coronavirus exit plan. Significant spikes were recorded on June 19, 24, and July 4. Although the move to reopen air and sea borders connotes that the government is confident that the COVID-19 outbreak is at least under control, local clusters and outbreaks remain a concern. Despite relaxing lockdown restrictions in recent weeks, Prime Minister Saad Eddine El Othmani stated that “confinement remains the only effective solution” to curb the spread of the virus. Indeed, on July 5, the city of Safi was placed on lockdown after an outbreak occurred in a fish canning factory in the area. With authorities wary of a possible resurgence of the virus, local officials may choose to implement new restrictions or delay the country’s coronavirus exit plan in the coming weeks. The public is advised to stay apprised of associated developments in this regard, and heed all official guidance and directives.

Headline: Ten Activists Arrested over Weekend Attempting to Block Dover Port During Week of Climate Actions
Details:
On Saturday, ten climate activists were arrested during a protest attempting to block the Port of Dover. Four activists held a sit-in at the Eastern Docks Roundabout, with some protesters blocking the A20 near the port. Police had cordoned off part of the westbound A20 for protesters to demonstrate legally, but multiple activists also went onto the A2, where police had been diverting traffic. Several demonstrators on the A2 glued themselves to the road before being removed by authorities. The action was conducted under the Extinction Rebellion protest group. The port said it was working with Kent Police to manage  intermittent delays  from the demonstration. No instances of violence were reported during the protest.

Assessment: The demonstration on Saturday followed on the worldwide Global Climate Strike mobilization over climate change, and it is part of a week of demonstration activity around the globe to press governments to take greater action to combat climate change. While police on Saturday sought to protect the right of protesters to demonstrate legally within designated areas of roadway near the port, the protesters efforts to disrupt port and road traffic was effective in causing some disruptions and drawing attention to the demonstration, despite a relatively low number of people involved. Extinction Rebellion activists have advocated nonviolent civil disobedience to advance their causes and have previously held an array of actions effective in causing disruptions and drawing attention while requiring relatively low participation levels. Extinction Rebellion has called for two weeks of protests in central London from Monday, October 7, with the aim of having greater impact than a similar two-week London protest in April. Protests beyond the scope of conventionally authorized rallies or marches that are seeking to cause disruption are frequently not announced in advance. While such climate protests have been largely peaceful, confrontation and incidents of unrest around such events cannot be ruled out. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring associated developments for possible actions throughout this week and in October, to anticipate potential disruptions around any targeted site, and to exercise caution near all protest activity.

Kinder Morgan, Inc. operates as an energy infrastructure company in North America.

Details: Industry media sources report that during the night of March 10, the inland cargo vessel ""Bonito"" (MMSI 244660716) began to take on 300 tons of water in the hold and the engine room after encountering rough and stormy seas on the IJsselmeer. Headline: All transit cargo destined for Uganda, Rwanda and South Sudan to be transported by rail from June 1
Details: Media sources indicated that following a conference held by representatives of Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, and South Sudan amid COVID-19, authorities have considered appropriate cross border transportation modalities to reduce human traffic movement and ensure transportation of cargo across the borders. All transit cargo destined for Uganda, Rwanda, and South Sudan will be transported via standard gauge railway (SGR) for clearance at the Naivasha Inland Container Depot (ICD) starting June 1. This is to reduce interactions along the Northern corridor and thus facilitate the containment of Covid-19. Further, fuel products will be transported by pipeline to Kisumu and thereafter by lake Victoria to Port Bell or Jinja.

Details:
On Thursday, the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP) released a report indicating the number of piracy incidents in Asian waters nearly doubled in the first six months of 2020 compared to the same period last year. According to the ReCAAP report, there were 51 incidents between January and June—compared to 28 in 2019—with 16 reported in the Singapore Strait alone. Of the 51 piracy incidents, 49 were incidents of armed robbery against ships, while two were piracy incidents; ReCAAP defines incidents as piracy if they occur outside the jurisdiction of any state, while those occurring in territorial waters are considered armed robbery. In addition to the Singapore Strait, incidents also occurred off the coast of Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam, as well as in the South China Sea. The report attributed the increase to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on global trade.



Assessment: With the COVID-19 pandemic currently showing no signs of slowing, the associated financial hardship facing individuals impacted by the economic downturn is unlikely to ease in the near term. When coupled with the fact that commercial vessels are expected to be less secured as maritime shipping companies look to cut costs, growing poverty and unemployment could perpetuate the uptick in piracy in Asian waters in the near and medium-term future. Compared to the Horn of Africa, piracy incidents in Asia appear to be more opportunistic, often perpetrated by local fishermen merely looking to supplement their incomes by stealing scrap metal, engine parts, and communication equipment from ships and selling the pilfered items on the black market. Additionally, most piracy remains non-violent, though perpetrators have sometimes abducted crew members and held them for ransom. Therefore, mariners operating in the region should exercise a high level of vigilance at all times and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to deter potential attackers.

Headline: Mexican Navy seizes 80 kg of cocaine on CMA CGM container ship in the Port of Lazaro Cardenas
Details: On September 24, sources report that Mexican Navy and Coast Guard personnel seized over 80 kilograms of cocaine from a container aboard the CMA CGM Mississippi at the Pacific Ocean Port of Lazaro Cardenas. A total of 70 packages containing approximately 82 kilograms of narcotics were reportedly seized in an operation on September 18. An investigation into the matter has been launched. It was not immediately reported whether the vessel was detained for a longer period of time in the port. The containership is operated by French shipping company CMA CGM and was on its way from Guayaquil, Ecuador to Yokohama, Japan.

Details: Industry sources indicate on October 22 that the Maltese-flagged general cargo ship Erna Oldendorff hit the Oshima Bridge in Yanai City at 12:30 AM on October 22 while en route from Qingdao to Kure. The vessel was brought to Kure by 12:20 PM with a damaged mast. While the bridge was not structurally damaged and remains open for traffic, water pipes and telecommunications cables were broken, impeding access to those services for residents of Suo-Oshima island. Those conducting business on Suo-Oshima Island should anticipate difficulties related to water and internet access until repairs are completed and should plan accordingly.

Headline: Madrid Threatens to Send National Police to Catalonia over Protests, Cabinet Meeting in Barcelona
Details:
Earlier this week, Spain s interior minister threatened to send National Police to Catalonia if regional police fail to address  serious disruptions of public order and traffic security.  The comments followed on pro-independence demonstrators in Catalonia blocking the AP-7 coastal toll road for about 15 hours on Saturday as well as lifting toll barriers the next day. Catalonia s Mossos d Esquadra police force has been accused by some in the Spanish government of permitting such disruptive actions by pro-independence activists. Despite the threat of deploying National Police to the region, the government has not indicated any plans at this time to reintroduce Article 155, which suspended Catalonia s autonomy for months following the October 1, 2017, independence referendum. 
 
	Assessment: Catalan government spokeswoman Elsa Artadi responded to the interior minister s threat by saying Tuesday that the planned meeting of the cabinet of the Spanish government scheduled for Friday, December 21 in Barcelona, has to be guaranteed. Weekly cabinet meetings are being held in cities around Spain instead of only Madrid, and concerns of pro-independence protest activity continue over the upcoming meeting of the national government s cabinet. The government plans to deploy National Police and Civil Guard for the meeting, though in the event of more sustained unrest, the deployment of national law enforcement could be increased or extended in Catalonia. While no specific demonstration plans are known at this time, Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring associated developments and to exercise caution near any protest activity due to the risk of clashes and the potential for other disruptive activity.

All magnitude scales should yield approximately the same value for any given earthquake.

Headline: UPDATE - Indonesia: Police commence Operation Lilin after determining countrywide security priorities over holidays
Details: Almost 95,000 police officers have reportedly been deployed across the country over the Christmas and New Year holiday. Though no specific information is known, the risk of terrorism, along with narcotics smuggling operations, remain the highest concerns to the authorities. While travel can continue, clients are advised to exercise additional caution over the holiday period. Where possible, avoid or limit time spent in the vicinity of sensitive sites, such as religious buildings (particularly churches), as well as other areas where Westerners frequent.

Headline: Daily COVID-19 roundup: US’s COVAXX enters USD2.8-bil. deal to supply 140 mil. COVID-19 vaccines to emerging markets as FDA defends Veklury’s efficacy
Details: IHS Markit perspectiveImplicationsThe number of confirmed coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infections globally had reached 60,465,801 at the time of writing on 26 November. The US National Institutes of Health (NIH)’s National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) has launched the ACTT-4 trial that will enrol up to 1,500 patients who will be randomised to receive dexamethasone plus Veklury (remdesivir; Gilead Sciences, US) or Olumiant (baricitinib) plus Veklury to determine which is more effective at preventing patients from progressing to mechanical ventilation or death, among other outcomes. Use of convalescent plasma in COVID-19 patients provided little benefit to patients with severe COVID-19 with no improvement in mortality relative to placebo, according to new research published in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). US drug maker Eli Lilly (US) has entered into an agreement with the Canadian government to supply 26,000 doses of its antibody drug bamlanivimab for the treatment of COVID-19 patients, valued at USD32.5 million. New York-based company COVAXX, which is developing a multitope peptide-based vaccine to fight COVID-19, has announced advanced purchase commitments for more than 140 million doses of its UB-612 vaccine candidate, with a total value of USD2.8 billion, from multiple emerging markets, including Brazil, Ecuador, and Peru.OutlookThe US FDA has published detailed documents of its review of Veklury, and has defended the rigorousness of the NIH trial and its design that was powered to better assess time to recovery compared with the open-label design of the World Health Organization (WHO)’s SOLIDARITY trial. Consequently, the FDA has maintained that the WHO’s trial data does not refute the efficacy evidence for Veklury. Veklury did not demonstrate a favourable efficacy profile in the WHO SOLIDARITY trial including no benefit in 28-day mortality, initiation of ventilation, or duration of hospitalisation, prompting the WHO to issue a recommendation against its use for hosptialised patients. With the NIH continuing to run critical Adaptive trials to quickly identify potential treatments for COVID-19, the research institute will likely continue to use Veklury as the standard of care in hospitalised patients, although this is unlikely to be the case for other regulators. Meanwhile, the FDA’s controversial emergency approval of convalescent plasma based on results from small clinical trials data from the National Expanded Access Treatment Protocol (EAP) sponsored by the Mayo Clinic (US) is likely to further come under scrutiny as new research from a randomised trial published in the NEJM demonstrated no improvement on mortality.Update on COVID-19 infections The number of confirmed coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infections globally had reached 60,465,801 at the time of writing on 26 November, up 1.09% from 59,814,726 the previous day, according to data compiled by Johns Hopkins University. The US has the highest number of cases, reaching 12,777,753, up 1.43% from 12,597,333 cases the previous day. The US is followed by India, which has the next highest number of confirmed infections, with 9,266,705 cases, up from 9,222,216 a day earlier. Countries with the next highest numbers of confirmed cases are Brazil (6,166,606), France (2,221,874), and Russia (2,169,424). Spain has the sixth-highest number of infections globally with 1,605,066 cases, followed by the United Kingdom (1,560,872), Italy (1,480,874), Argentina (1,390,388), and Colombia (1,270,991). The top-10 countries with the highest numbers of infections globally represented a total of 39,910,553 cases, equivalent to about 66% of all confirmed COVID-19 infections recorded internationally. The number of confirmed deaths globally had reached 1,422,247, up 0.84% from 1,410,458 the previous day. The total number of deaths from COVID-19 infection had reached 262,266 in the US at the time of writing, up 0.89% from 259,962 on 25 November. The US accounts for 18.44% of all confirmed COVID-19 deaths globally. The number of fatalities in the US is followed by Brazil with 170,769 deaths, India (135,223), Mexico (103,597), the United Kingdom (56,630), Italy (52,028), France (50,700), Iran (46,207), Spain (44,037), and Argentina (37,714). At the time of writing, these 10 countries accounted for 67.44% of all COVID-19 deaths globally.Americas: As the cumulative number of confirmed COVID-19 infections globally exceeded 60 million, the Americas region recorded its highest weekly number of new infections since the onset of the pandemic. The Americas region has reported 1.5 million cases in the past seven days, and infection numbers have accelerated in countries of North, Central, and South America, according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) branch of the World Health Organization (WHO). PAHO said yesterday (25 November) that new cases continue to surge in the US, and that the daily death toll had reached 2,157, representing the first time since May that daily deaths had exceeded 2,000 in 24 hours. Iran: Iran yesterday recorded its highest single-day number of confirmed infections to date, with 13,843 new cases, according to the country’s health ministry. Sima Sadat Lari, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, told Iranian state television yesterday that the number of confirmed COVID-19 fatalities had increased by 469 in 24 hours. In terms of cumulative case and fatality numbers, Iran is by far the worst-hit country in the Middle East, with a total of 894,385 confirmed cases, followed by Iraq (524,187 cases and 12,086 deaths, although figures are likely to be considerably under-reported). Turkey: Turkey yesterday recorded the third-highest number of new daily COVID-19 cases in the world, after the health ministry resumed publication of all recorded positive infections, including asymptomatic cases. According to the official figures, the country yesterday recorded 28,351 new cases in the previous 24 hours, including 6,814 with symptoms, DuvaR.english reported. The daily infection number was by far the highest reported by Turkey since the start of the pandemic. Since July, the Turkish government had only been reporting symptomatic cases, which critics said hid the true scale of the outbreak in Turkey and hindered effective containment strategies. Health Minister Fahrettin Koca announced during a press conference following a meeting of the government’s Coronavirus Science Committee that “in line with requests from our people, we plan on including positive cases that do not show symptoms in the daily table”, adding that around 80% of people who test positive were asymptomatic or lightly symptomatic.Vaccines, treatments, and diagnostics development updateVaccinesBrazil: Brazil’s National Health Surveillance Agency (Anvisa) said on 25 November that it had received a request from Pfizer (US) to open a rolling review of the company’s COVID-19 vaccine candidate BNT162b2. In a press release, Anvisa said that it had met with Pfizer representatives to discuss the submission process for the review, but had yet to receive the first batch of data pertaining to the vaccine. Pfizer’s BNT162b2 becomes the third COVID-19 vaccine candidate to be submitted to a rolling review by Anvisa, following AstraZeneca (UK) and the University of Oxford (UK)’s AZD1222 and Sinovac (China)’s CoronaVac.China: BioNTech (Germany) and the Shanghai unit of Fosun Pharmaceutical (China) have announced that they are launching a Phase II clinical trial in China for COVID-19 vaccine candidate BNT162b2. The vaccine candidate will be tested on participants in the Jiangsu Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention for safety and immunogenicity in support of future regulatory approval in China. BNT162b2 has demonstrated 94.5% efficacy in late-stage testing conducted by Pfizer and BioNTech, and is currently under review for emergency approval in the US, among others.TreatmentsUnited States: The US National Institutes of Health (NIH)’ National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) has launched the fourth iteration of the Adaptive COVID-19 Treatment Trial (ACTT-4) that will enrol up to 1,500 patients across nearly 100 sites in the US and other countries. The ACCT-4 trial participants will be randomised to receive dexamethasone plus Veklury (remdesivir; Gilead Sciences, US) or Olumiant (baricitinib) plus Velkury, and will be blinded for dexamethasone and Olumiant components. So far, Olumiant and dexamethasone are the only two anti-inflammatory treatments to demonstrate efficacy in large randomised clinical trials. The NIH noted that there are large differences in the study populations, mortality rates, and endpoint data for the ACTT-2 and UK’s RECOVERY trials; therefore, the NIH’s ACTT-4 can help shed light on whether Olumiant or dexamethasone is more effective at preventing patients from progressing to mechanical ventilation or death, among other outcomes. The trial is expected to complete enrolment in around 3–4 months.United States: The US FDA has published its detailed review for Veklury that led to its emergency approval for the treatment of hospitalised patients, and has defended its decision to follow the evidence in the ACTT-1 trial, with its rigorous trial design. According to the FDA statement, the agency is aware of the preprint article describing the WHO’s open-label, randomised SOLIDARITY trial that did not find a statistical significant difference in mortality, but the WHO study had a different design and primary goal than the ACTT-1 study. The ACTT-1 trial was “better suited to rigorously assess a time to recovery endpoint compared to a trial with an open-label design, such as the SOLIDARITY trial”; as such, the findings in SOLIDARITY do no refute the benefit findings in ACTT-1, according to the FDA. The full FDA review document can be found here.Argentina: Use of convalescent plasma in COVID-19 patients provided little benefit to patients with severe COVID-19, according to new research published in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), according to Reuters. Researchers in Argentina randomised 333 hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia, and found that convalescent plasma did not improve the health status of patients or their risk of dying compared with placebo by day 30. Mortality rates were 11% in the convalescent plasma arm and 11.4% in the placebo group. According to the study’s lead investigator, Ventura Simonovich of the Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, convalescent plasma might be more effective in patients with less severe disease, according to the source.Netherlands: Dutch researchers at the Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC) are preparing to launch a “human challenge” trial, according to the 1Day Sooner US advocacy group, although they have not yet decided to conduct the trial. So far, 240 Dutch volunteers have expressed interest in volunteering to be deliberately exposed to SARS-CoV-2 in order to test the efficacy of vaccine candidates. According to LUMC researcher Meta Roestenberg, the trial would provide key information regarding the length of protection after infection or vaccination, the viral load required for infection, and how much antibody is being produced, among other things. The 1Day Sooner group is also involved in human challenge trials that might launch in the UK in January 2021. The challenge trials would likely need regulatory approval from Dutch authorities, according to the advocacy group.Other developmentsBangladesh: The government of Bangladesh has said that it will procure 68 million doses of COVID-19 vaccines from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance via the COVAX Facility, New Age reported. Government officials are cited as saying that the first consignment of vaccine supplies is slated to arrive in February 2021, and that the government will pay between USD1.62 to USD2.00 per dose through a co-financing mechanism. Although not clarified by the source, this most likely refers to the Advance Market Commitment for COVID-19 Vaccines (Covax AMC), the subsidised vaccine supply arm of the COVAX Facility for which Bangladesh is one of 92 low- and lower-middle income countries that are eligible for at cost access to vaccines. The source reported that prior to delivery of the vaccine supplies, the Bangladesh health directorate will submit a National Vaccine Deployment Plan on COVID-19 vaccination, in line with conditions set out by Gavi. Canada: US drug maker Eli Lilly (US) has entered into an agreement with the Canadian government to supply 26,000 doses of its antibody drug bamlanivimab for the treatment of COVID-19 patients. The supply deal is valued at USD32.5 million. The neutralising antibody, which was developed in partnership with Canadian biotech company AbCellera, will be supplied to Canada over a three-month period from December 2020 to February 2021. Additional doses will be supplied on a monthly basis in line with national needs and the availability of supply. The FDA approved emergency use authorisation (EUA) for bamlanivimab on 9 November, while Canadian regulators last week granted the product an interim authorisation for treating COVID-19 in non-hospitalised patients who are at risk of serious illness due to their age or other conditions.Panama: The government of Panama has said that it has signed an agreement to procure 3 million doses of the vaccine candidate BNT162b2 (Pfizer/BioNTech). The vaccine doses will be distributed in 2021 pending local regulatory approval. Details regarding costs have not been reported. The advanced purchase agreement comes after Pfizer and BioNTech filed for US approval of BNT162b2 on 20 November under the FDA’s EUA procedure, following the companies’ release of preliminary Phase III data showing 90% efficacy in preventing COVID-19 infection. A subsequent readout when additional infections occurred indicated that efficacy was even higher, at 95%.Thailand: The Thai government has reportedly committed a THB2.37-billion (USD78.22 million) down payment for an advanced purchase order of AstraZeneca/Oxford University’s AZD1222 COVID-19 vaccine, according to Coconuts Bangkok. Traisulee Traisornranakul, a government spokesperson, emphasised that the vaccine candidate had shown to be at least 70% effective in an early analysis. They said that the vaccine was expected to be available in Thailand by mid-2021. The country’s public health minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, has also said that Thailand aims to reach agreements with other companies – “Pfizer or Moderna” – for the supply of COVID-19 vaccines. Turkey: Fahrettin Koca, Turkey’s health minister, announced yesterday that the government had signed a contract with Chinese vaccine developer Sinovac for the supply of 50 million doses of its inactivated whole-virion COVID-19 vaccine CoronaVac. According to the health minister, who is cited by DuvaR.english, the vaccine doses will be supplied in three batches in December, January, and February. Koca did not disclose the agreed price per dose or the total value of the supply contract. The vaccine candidate is currently in Phase III clinical trials in Turkey, as well as in Brazil, Indonesia, mainland China, Bangladesh, Chile, and the Philippines.United States – World: New York-based company COVAXX, which is developing a multitope peptide-based vaccine to fight COVID-19, has announced advanced purchase commitments for more than 140 million doses of its UB-612 vaccine candidate, with a total value of USD2.8 billion, from multiple emerging markets, including Brazil, Ecuador, and Peru. The commitments from public and private purchasing entities follow the initiation of Phase I human trials in Taiwan and come after an agreement in September with Diagnosticos da America SA (Dasa S.A., Brazil) to conduct Phase II/III clinical trials and distribute vaccines within Brazil. COVAXX, a subsidiary of United Biomedical (US) and not to be confused with the Gavi-led COVAX facility for equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines, is currently completing Phase I clinical trials of UB-612 in Taiwan and has an agreement with the University of Nebraska Medical Center (UNMC, US) to conduct clinical trials in the US. The company has also recently announced a global logistics partnership with major shipping and logistics company Maersk (Denmark) to create a framework for all transportation and supply chain services that will be needed to deliver the candidate vaccine. UB-612 is the only multitope, synthetic peptide-based vaccine candidate in the clinical studies phase, and Phase II/III clinical trials will begin at between the end of 2020 and the first quarter of 2021 in Asia, Latin America, and the United States. A full list of the countries that have entered into advanced purchase agreements has not been published. Nevertheless, the value of the commitments underscores the potential of the vaccine candidate and will enable COVAXX to scale up manufacturing. Co-founder and CEO of COVAXX Mei Mei Hu said, “In parallel with the expedited clinical development of UB-612, we are working to help countries with the greatest unmet needs customize their plans for vaccine studies, supply and distribution.” The commitments ahead of final results from clinical trials also emphasise national efforts to secure access to vaccines that utilise different technologies, particularly in view of the high demand placed on global manufacturing capacities for COVID-19 vaccines. Hu added, “The realistic view of vaccine production is that we will need a wide range of vaccine options utilizing different technologies to meet worldwide demand… To be administered effectively, vaccines need to demonstrate easy and affordable distribution, durability of response with the capability to further extend it with effective boosts, as well as the ability to adapt to a potential mutation in the virus while building on the first vaccines made available.”More of today’s IHS Markit COVID-19 analysisBrazil: Anvisa opens rolling review procedure for Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine candidate BNT162b2 (here)United Kingdom: UK government spending review protects healthcare, life sciences research, and COVID-19 vaccine funding (here)Venezuela: Venezuela blocked from purchasing vaccines through PAHO’s Revolving Fund due to accumulated debt (here)Outlook and implicationsThe NIH Adaptive trials have had a marked impact on the development and approval of COVID-19 treatments to date. So far, the NIH has published data from the ACTT-1 trial for Veklury, which has led to its EUA, and the ACTT-2 trial in Olumiant plus Veklury, which has also recently been granted an EUA. In ACTT-1, Veklury did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in mortality in the total patient population, but did result in a significant reduction in the median time to recovery from 15 to 10 days. ACTT-2 primary results demonstrated that the addition of Olumiant to Veklury further shortened time to recovery by one day. Additional analysis is being conducted to understand the mortality data that will be published in peer-reviewed journal in the coming weeks. Eli Lilly has previously suggested that Olumiant numerically lowers mortality risk by 35% in COVID-19 patients, but this did not reach statistical significance (see United States: 9 October 2020: Lilly’s Olumiant shortens recovery time, numerically lowers mortality risk by 35% in COVID-19 patients). However, much like Veklury, the mortality benefit seems to be more concentrated in certain patients: for Olumiant, its patients receiving oxygen within the grade 5 and grade 6 ordinal scale subgroups, which realised a 60% and 43% lower mortality rate, respectively. Ordinal scale five includes hospitalised patients requiring supplemental oxygen (low flow), whereas level six includes those patients requiring non-invasive ventilation or use of high-flow oxygen devices. Based on subgroup analysis of Veklury in the ACTT-1 trial, patients categorised into ordinal group 5 (requiring low-flow oxygen) did demonstrate statistically improved mortality, but none of the other subgroups did, including patients in ordinal scale 6 (high-flow oxygen), and 7 (requiring invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).Veklury did not demonstrate a favourable efficacy profile in the WHO SOLIDARITY trial in hospitalised COVID-19 patients including no benefit in 28-day mortality, initiation of ventilation, or duration of hospitalisation, prompting the WHO to issue a recommendation against its use for hospitalised patients (see World: 16 October 2020: WHO’s Solidarity trial finds no mortality or hospitalisation duration benefit with repurposed drugs including Veklury and World: 20 November 2020: Daily COVID-19 roundup: Roche’s Actemra shows benefit in severe COVID-19 cases, WHO recommends against use of Veklury in hospitalised patients). The FDA has published detailed documents of its review of Veklury, and has defended the rigorousness of the NIH trial and its design that was powered to better assess time to recovery compared with the open-label design of the SOLIDARITY trial. Consequently, the FDA has maintained that the WHO's trial data does not refute the efficacy evidence for Veklury.With the NIH continuing to run critical Adaptive trials to quickly identify potential treatments for COVID-19, the research institute will likely continue to use Veklury as the standard of care in hospitalised patients, although this is unlikely to be the case for other regulators. Meanwhile, the FDA’s controversial emergency approval of convalescent plasma based on results from small clinical trials data from the National Expanded Access Treatment Protocol (EAP) sponsored by the Mayo Clinic (US) is likely to further come under scrutiny as new research from a randomised trial demonstrated no improvement on mortality (see United States: 24 August 2020: FDA issues EUA for use of convalescent plasma for COVID-19, US administration considering fast-tracking approval of vaccine). Although convalescent plasma is approved in the US as a treatment for COVID-19 and administered to thousands of patients, it is not considered as standard of care in the US, especially without evidence from randomised controlled trials. The NIH has not announced that it will be running an adaptive trial with convalescent plasma.The treatment landscape for COVID-19 is set to change very quickly with the approval of new antibody treatments for patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 and the advancement of a handful of treatments that seem to demonstrate a robust improvement in mortality in patients with severe COVID-19, including dexamethasone, CD24Fc (OncoImmune, US), and RLF-100 (Relief Therapeutics, Switzerland), that could quickly in turn become the new standard of care for hospitalised patients (see United Kingdom: 17 June 2020: UK study reveals “game-changing” mortality reduction with low-dose dexamethasone in hospitalised COVID-19 patients, United States: 24 November 2020: Merck & Co adds promising late-stage COVID-19 therapeutic candidate with OncoImmune acquisition, and World: 25 November 2020: Daily COVID-19 roundup: EU confirms sixth APA contract for Moderna’s mRNA-1273 vaccine candidate, Sinopharm files for marketing approval in China before completion of Phase III testing).© 2020, IHS Markit Inc. Headline: 25 miles SSE of Jackson   Gordon continues to weaken as it moves inland. Incident closed.
Details:
Tropical Depression Gordon continues to weaken as it moves further inland. The storm is currently exhibiting maximum sustained winds of 30 miles per hour. Gordon continues to move northwest at 14 miles per hour and is expected to bring heavy rain and possible flooding through parts of the Midwest as it moves deeper inland. 
   
Media sources reported that one person was killed near West Pensacola, Florida, after a tree fell onto a trailer. 

Voluntary evacuations were lifted for Port Fourchon, LA and Grand Isle, LA, as well as for areas outside levee protection in New Orleans, which includes: Venetian Isles, Lake Catherine, and Irish Bayou. In Mississippi, the cities of Gulfport, Biloxi, and Long Beach issued temporary evacuations for marinas and harbors. States of emergency were issued for Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama in preparation for the storm. 

The threat from Gordon has significantly decreased for the region although heavy rains are still possible in some area. This incident is closed.

Headline: Port of Rotterdam moderately tightens admission rules for vessels
Details:
Sources indicated on April 9 that as a precautionary measure against the spread of the COVID-19 coronavirus pandemic, the Port of Rotterdam issued moderately tightened restrictions on vessel admission for an unknown duration. The measures are as follows: 

Cargo vessels must issue a Maritime Declaration of Health (MDOH) to the Harbour Coordination Center (HCC). If a crew member is declared to be exhibiting mild symptoms, the crew member will be isolated from the rest of the crew. If the crewmember cannot be isolated, the crewmember may be transferred to shore and potentially admitted to a hospital if needed. Shore leave is permitted for crewmembers only for medical reasons, and only medical professionals, maintenance staff, and government employees may board the vessel. Crew changes are still permitted, but must be executed as far as possible via the landward side. Cargo operations can continue, even when a crewmember has tested positive for COVID-19. However, in such cases, no crewmember may come in contact with port personnel. Vessel departure permission for crew with positive COVID-19 cases will be determined on a case-by-case basis.

Headline: Houthi Missile Attack on Aramco Facility in Jeddah Likely to Spur Calls for US Terror Designation
Details:
On Monday, the Yemen-based Houthi rebel movement claimed responsibility for a cruise missile attack that targeted a Saudi Aramco oil facility in the port city of Jeddah hours earlier. There were no initial reports of casualties from the attack on Aramco’s North Jeddah Bulk Plant, and a spokesman from the Kingdom’s energy ministry said that fuel supplies were not affected. However, a satellite photo suggested a fire was burning at the facility around 4:00 AM local time, shortly after the attack reportedly occurred. The United States Consulate General in Jeddah issued a Security Alert advising citizens to “review immediate precautions to take in the event of an attack and stay alert in case of additional future attacks.” The message can be read here: https://sa.usembassy.gov/alert-reports-of-missile-or-drone-attack-on-aramco-facility-in-jeddah-u-s-consulate-general-jeddah/. The November 23 incident occurred hours after Riyadh finished hosting the G20 Leaders’ Summit, and as the US is considering designating the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organization. Such an announcement, which could be made as soon as next month, would freeze all financial assets held by the Houthis in US jurisdiction and also prohibit American citizens and organizations from providing “material support or resources” to the group.



Assessment: It stands to reason that Monday’s attack will increase the probability that Washington will indeed tag the Houthis as a terrorist group. Not only has the US maintained strong ties with Saudi Arabia under President Donald Trump and provided logistical and financial support to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Shi’a rebels, because the latter are seen as Iranian proxies, a designation would align with the White House’s “maximum pressure” campaign on Tehran and allies, especially with the Trump administration seemingly entering its final weeks in office. However, it is unclear if such a would have any meaningful impact on the Houthis or the Yemen conflict in general. Because the Houthis are already regarded as isolated, and given suggestions that the level of cooperation between the group and Iran may be exaggerated, blacklisting the Yemeni rebels could have little more than symbolic value. That said, it could potentially exacerbate humanitarian conditions in Yemen, especially in Houthi-held Sana’a and the country’s northern governorates, by restricting the delivery of aid, along with efforts to broker a peace deal, by potentially subjecting aid agencies and other international organizations to sanctions. More broadly, Monday’s attack highlights the persistent threat of Houthi-fired projectiles in Saudi Arabia. Although most incidents occur along the Kingdom’s southern border and are purportedly intercepted by Saudi air defenses, the rebels have demonstrated a more sophisticated, longer-range arsenal, giving them the ability to strike deep inside the country.  Thus, individuals in Saudi Arabia, especially in the country’s south, should familiarize themselves with what to do in the event of a missile launch and review associated safety procedures.

Headline: UPDATE: Truck drivers at Port of Los Angeles began 3-day strike on October 1
Details: Updated sources continue to report that Los Angeles and Long Beach port truck drivers and warehouse workers commenced a 3-day strike at 07:00 local time on Monday, October 1. Picketing has been reported at XPO and NFI facilities, marine terminals, rail yards, customer warehouses and distribution centers. The strike was called for to protest against the misclassification of workers as independent contractors, instead of as employees, by the trucking companies they work for. Truckers classified as contractors are not eligible for a minimum wage, or forego benefits such as health insurance or holiday pay. This is the 16 th strike staged by Justice for Port Drivers in the past five years. The previous strikes resulted in minimal or no impact on cargo flow at the port complex. Port police have reportedly been positioned at terminals to ensure operations can continue during these strikes. As of late Monday morning, a spokesperson for the Port of Los Angeles stated that there has been no impact on cargo flow. XPO Logistics also indicated that it does not expect any impact on customers or disruptions to its operations.

Coastal flooding, heavy rain and strong winds are expected to continue in central and southern Honshu. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has issued heavy rainfall warnings for several areas in central and southern Honshu, including Kansai, Kanto and Tokai regions. Evacuation orders previously issued for the prefectures of Osaka, Nara, Mie and Aichi have been lifted.
