Headline: Guardia Civil seizes 250 kg of cocaine at the Port of Valencia
Details: Spanish media sources on May 6 report that a Guardia Civil operation has resulted in the seizure of 250kg of cocaine that arrived at the Port of Valencia hidden among the pieces of a helicopter. The aircraft was dismantled in a South American country after being used in a campaign to prevent forest fires, and it arrived at the port of Valencia in containers. Port workers took the helicopter to the APM Terminals Valencia facilities, specifically to a restricted access area controlled by security guards. There were no arrests in the operation. The cocaine stash is valued EUR 8.5 million.

Headline: Individuals: Chinese firm's criminal charges will not trigger arbitrary...
Details: On 29 January, the US Justice Department filed criminal charges against China's Huawei Technologies, its alleged affiliates, and its chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou for alleged bank fraud, wire fraud, and obstruction of justice. Meng will be extradited from Canada if Canadian courts are satisfied that there is sufficient evidence for her to stand trial. Meng and Huawei maintain their innocence. China's foreign ministry spokesman at its US embassy criticised the case as politically motivated but did not threaten ""repercussions"", unlike the Chinese envoy and ambassador to Canada, who have repeatedly issued such threats against Canada. Several Canadian nationals have been detained in China following the arrest of Meng in Vancouver, Canada, in early December 2018. Meanwhile, China's Vice Premier Liu He has arrived in Washington, DC to begin a new round of trade negotiations with US officials led by US Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer. The US and Chinese governments have emphasised that the trade negotiations and the criminal investigation of Huawei are separate issues; the two sides aim to reach a settlement by 1 March that prevents the US's 24 September round of tariffs on USD200 billion-worth of Chinese imports rising from 10% to 25%. China's official news agency, Xinhua, reported on 30 January that the Chinese government intended to pass new legislation relating to foreign investment in its annual National People's Congress in early March. The new rules will prohibit local-level Chinese government officials from 'forcing' the transfer of intellectual property from foreign to local entities engaged in joint ventures; such transfers are a central complaint of the US Trade Representative's office in its Section 301 report.US nationals are not at increased risk of arbitrary detention in China as long as the 24 September tariffs are maintained at 10%. A breakdown in trade negotiations, however, would increase the risk specifically to current or former US federal officials working in either State, Defense, or intelligence services, and to rights activists or those with links to activists; the risk would not be indiscriminate across US nationals in general. US nationals facing ongoing criminal investigations would also see their cases opportunistically prioritised by Chinese courts. Clear threats of 'repercussions' by Chinese officials in the US would be a secondary indicator of increasing risk to US nationals in China. Headline: Three Attempted Acts of Piracy in Singapore Strait Overnight Sunday into Monday Amid Slight Uptick
Details:
Beginning at around 11:00 PM local time on Sunday, there were three attempted acts of piracy in the Singapore Strait in a roughly two-and-a-half-hour period. Each of the situations took place off the Indonesian coast and all three involved ships in the eastbound lane of the Strait’s Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS). The first and third occurred near Nongsa Point, and the second happened off of Pulau Nongsa. Nothing was successfully stolen during any of the attempts, and there were no injuries.



Assessment: According to the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery Against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP), there has been a slight uptick in recent reports of piracy in the Singapore Strait, with October’s six total incidents being the highest monthly number for the year thus far. No injuries have been reported in any of the October incidents, and suspects successfully stole minor items in only one of the attacks. There have been a total of 28 piracy attempts reported in the Strait so far in 2020, compared to 31 for the entirety of 2019. Of this year’s attacks, 24 have taken place against ships traveling in the eastbound lanes of the TSS. Given the short timeframe that the Sunday night attempts occurred in, they were likely carried out by a single group of suspects. Although there were no injuries, the crew of one of the ships was unsure of whether all of the suspects had departed, and the ship was forced to divert to Batam, Indonesia, where it was searched by Indonesian naval personnel. Such diversions could cause significant disruptions for shipping even when there are no injuries and nothing is successfully stolen. As no arrests were made in any of Sunday night’s attempts, ReCAAP has warned that the same suspects may possibly try to attack additional ships. The organization advises ships in the region to take precautions and to report any incidents of piracy to the nearest government.

Headline: UPDATE 4: Thousands continue to protest against Duque and Cali curfew amid nationwide strike
Details: Updated media sources that thousands of protesters marched in Colombia’s main cities in protest against President Ivan Duque following a day that ended in roadblocks and vandalism that forced the decree of a curfew int he city of Cali. The protest has not affected key sectors of the economy such as oil and coal production, although transport routes have been reduced considerably according to the government. Previous media sources indicated on November 21 that the nationwide general strike began in Colombia. The demonstration was initially organized by university students but has grown to several groups to denounce the economic and social policies of President Ivan Duque. Massive demonstrations were reported in Bogota, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellin, and Cali where people are marching towards city centers. In Bogota, marches started in the financial district in the direction of the Plaza de Bolivar. Police clashed with protesters as they blocked Suba Avenue. In Barranquilla, protesters divided into three marches starting in Esthercita Forero Park, Autonomous University, and the Rincon Latino neighborhood all heading towards Paseo Bolivar (the city center). In Cartagena, protesters marched on the Pedro de Heredia Avenue and congregating in the historic city center. Workers and students are protesting against a slew of economic reforms that the president has implemented including eliminating the state pension fund, increasing the retirement age, and hiring young people with salaries below the minimum wage. Social organizations are demanding a greater commitment from the government to implement the peace agreement with the FARC.

Headline: MENA States Continue to Adopt Measures Aimed at Preventing COVID-19 Spread
Details:
Media sources report that countries throughout the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region continue to adopt measures aimed at preventing the spread of the 2019 novel coronavirus (COVID-19). On Tuesday, the Lebanese government banned citizens from traveling to Iran, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia to participate in religious pilgrimages, while also restricting flights to other countries affected by COVID-19. Likewise, Egypt s national flag carrier, Egyptair, has announced it will delay a resumption of flights to and from China, where the coronavirus outbreak began, until at least March 14, while Kazakhstan has indicated it will suspend flights to and from Iran from March 1, and also plans to reduce service to South Korea, another COVID-19 hotspot. Meanwhile, maritime authorities in Jordan have barred entry to crew members from ships carrying Chinese goods arriving at the Port of Aqaba, while Kuwait has barred foreign ships, except those carrying oil, from departing to or arriving from several countries. Elsewhere, the Bahrain Tourism and Exhibitions Authority (BTEA) has reportedly temporarily banned entry to anyone arriving in the kingdom from Iran, warning that violators will be subject to penalties. Iraq has also extended entry bans for travelers coming from China, Iran, Italy, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand.

Assessment: At the time of this writing, approximately 210 COVID-19 cases had been recorded across the MENA region. Iran has emerged as the epicenter of the regional outbreak, as more than half of the confirmed infections have been located there, while cases in at least six other countries have been linked to patients who recently traveled to the Islamic Republic. With a further spread of the virus likely, and the number of cases expected to rise, countries will continue to adopt and tighten travel restrictions and other measures aimed at combatting COVID-19. These efforts could negatively impact travel itineraries and disrupt supply chains and various manufacturing sectors. Therefore, clients should re-confirm their travel itineraries and formulate contingency plans to mitigate the risk of logistical delays, supply shortages, and other complications.

Headline: Undersea Cable Between Chennai, Port Blair Began Partial Service Monday; Will Improve Telecom Links
Details:
On Monday, an undersea fiber optic cable between Chennai and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands capital of Port Blair began partial service after being opened by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Extending from Port Blair, the cable will also provide additional links to the islands of Car Nicobar, Great Nicobar, Kamorta, Little Andaman, Long Island, Middle Andaman, and Swaraj Dweep. The cable is intended to allow broadband internet speeds of up to ten times those currently available in Port Blair and will also allow faster speeds elsewhere in the islands. 



Assessment: The new undersea cable is expected to greatly increase the availability of digital services and telecommunications generally in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Among other things, this will likely help the islands’ tourism industry, which has already been growing steadily in recent years and will probably be greatly boosted by additional connectivity. The cable project began in December 2018 at a cost of around US $160,000, which is being funded by the Ministry of Communications. More than 1,400 miles of cable in total is expected to be laid by government-owned telecom company Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL).

Headline: UPDATE - USA, North Carolina: More than a million people face mandatory evacuations along southern East Coast as Florence nears Category 5 status
Details: US media sources are reporting more than a million people, residents and visitors, face mandatory evacuation orders in coastal areas of North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia as Hurricane Florence approaches. According to the National Hurricane Centre (NHC), the storm is nearing Category 5 status with sustained winds of around 140mph recorded. Officials are warning residents in the path of the storm 'not to underestimate the threat'. Even if the storm does not reach the Category 5 threshold (winds in excess of 157mph), the NHC states 'there remains high confidence that Florence will be a large and extremely dangerous hurricane'. The National Guard has been activated in the states affected and residents have started boarding homes. While there are also reports of long queues at fuel stations and supermarkets/hardware stores being depleted of stock. South Carolina Governor, Henry McMaster, has confirmed that government offices, including schools and medical facilities will be closed. Travellers are advised to 'Know Your Evacuation Zone' by monitoring local emergency management websites and associated media reports. Do not take undue risks and anticipate disruption to travel for several days.

Headline: Hong Kong Human Rights Bill Likely to Further Complicate U.S.-China Relationship if Enacted
Details:
On Tuesday, the U.S. Senate passed the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act with unanimous consent. The bill requires the U.S. Department of State to report to Congress annually if Hong Kong s special status should be continued and if it is sufficiently autonomous from mainland China. The report will address civil liberties and how any erosion of Hong Kong s autonomy would affect relations between the U.S. and Hong Kong. Those who violate human rights, including acts like extrajudicial rendition or torture, would be barred from entering the U.S. and would face sanctions. The U.S. House of Representatives, which passed a similar bill in October, has said that they will attempt to pass the Senate bill, which should make it quicker for the bill to be presented to President Donald Trump for his signature or veto. Beijing criticized the bill as being a violation of international law, while the Hong Kong government also expressed opposition and said that any unilateral changes of U.S. economic and trade policy could impact the 1,300 U.S. companies and 85,000 U.S. residents in Hong Kong. 

The text of the Senate bill can be found here: https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/senate-bill/1838. 

Assessment: Hong Kong s special status is rooted in the United States-Hong Kong Policy Act of 1992, which recognizes the different legal, social, and economic systems that differentiate it from mainland China. This has resulted in benefits like not being subjected to U.S.-China trade tariffs and easier travel to the U.S. for Hong Kong passport holders. Companies enjoy economic benefits as well, which also includes more transparent legal and arbitration mechanisms. Those in the U.S. shipped U.S. $37 billion to Hong Kong last year and Hong Kong exported more than U.S. $33 billion in services, with a significant portion of that originating from Hong Kong branches of U.S. companies providing services to mainland China.

It remains unclear if President Trump will sign the bill, as he has personally refrained from strongly supporting the protesters in Hong Kong. There were also media reports that President Trump had promised Chinese President Xi Jinping in June that he would refrain from commenting on the protests while trade negotiations were taking place. If President Trump decides to sign the bill, it would likely be seen by China as a breaking of that promise and would negatively affect trade talks. While both the House and Senate versions of the bill were passed by unanimous consent, which would theoretically be enough to override a presidential veto, it remains unclear what would happen if President Trump expressed his personal opposition to the bill. Customers are advised to closely monitor the progress of the bill, as its passage could lower chances of a substantive trade agreement and includes the possibility of tariff or non-tariff restrictions being put on U.S. companies or products by China.

Headline: Several Countries Begin Lifting COVID-19 Restrictions, Despite Rising Cases and Warnings
Details:
On Monday, several countries in Sub-Saharan Africa began lifting their lockdowns and other restrictions introduced to contain the spread of COVID-19. Ghana lifted its three-week restriction on movement in the Accra and Kumasi metropolitan areas on Monday, while Madagascar began progressively lifting the confinements in Antananarivo, Fianarantsoa, and Toamasina. In Madagascar, public transportation was expected to resume on Monday and schools will reopen on Wednesday. The restrictions on movement will also be lifted from 6:00 AM to 1:00 PM local time daily; however, the ban on inter-city travel will remain in place and everyone must wear face masks in public. Additionally, Burkina Faso began reopening public markets, which had been closed since March 25. While Zimbabwe and South Africa have extended their lockdowns, both have eased the restrictions slightly. Zimbabwe extended its lockdown until May 3 but will allow mining operations to fully resume. The lockdown in South Africa also remains in effect until April 30, but authorities have stated that port operations will resume to decrease congestion. South Africa also began allowing mining companies to resume partial operations last week.



Assessment: Countries across Sub-Saharan Africa have faced increasing pressure to lift the restrictions from within the local populace, many of whom perceive the measures as affected their livelihoods. While the lifting of the measures is likely to help ease tensions somewhat, health officials have warned that lifting them too soon could lead to a rise in new cases. Much of Sub-Saharan Africa continues to experience exponential increases in cases and testing capabilities remain extremely limited, making the region particularly vulnerable to widespread, under-reported community transmission. Ghana may be one of the few exceptions, as it has ramped up testing significantly, testing over 60,000 people, and has adopted aggressive contact tracing. South Africa has also stepped up testing in recent weeks, and coupled with its lockdown, it appears to have helped stem the number of new cases per day.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - Grenade explosions in Antwerp likely indicative of drug gang rivalry, increasing security risks in Belgian port areas
Details: On 24 August 2020, unidentified perpetrators threw a hand grenade into a vacant building in Deurne, east Antwerp, with the grenade bouncing back and exploding on the street next to the house of a local drug trafficking gang leader, without causing any casualties. The attack followed two other hand grenade explosions over the weekend in east Antwerp’s Ekstelaar and Borgerhout areas, where a shooting targeting the family home of a drug gang member also took place, not leading to any casualties. Prior to the incidents, the police had seized a shipment of 500kg of cocaine at the port and detained two port employees suspected of having facilitated the trafficking of up to 800kg of cocaine, as part of a separate investigation. In 2019, Belgian authorities had seized a record 62 tonnes of cocaine in total, a 23% increase compared to 2018. The Port of Antwerp is the principal entry point for cocaine in Europe, with the substance mostly being trafficked from Brazil, Colombia and Ecuador.Significance: The increase in frequency of violent attacks between criminal gangs with the deployment of hand grenades in residential areas of Antwerp is likely indicative of intensifying rivalry between groups controlling the trafficking of cocaine into Europe through the Port of Antwerp. The escalation is likely to be linked to changes in the dynamics of drug trafficking gangs, particularly of influential drug cartels in Latin America; their revenues from extortion reduced during lockdowns introduced globally from March in response to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak. While violent attacks between gangs have so far been mostly limited to residential areas in east Antwerp, the escalation increases the likelihood of violent confrontations, including shootings and hand grenade deployment, spreading to port facilities where cargo is handled and the trafficking takes place. An increase in the frequency of checks conducted on containers by Antwerp port authorities as a response to the hand grenade attacks would probably mitigate the risk, resulting in more significant drug seizures and detention of suspected traffickers, acting as a deterrent and disrupting the illegal drug route through the port, although probably only temporarily. However, this would also lead to longer security procedures at the port, likely slowing down the handling of cargo containers. Headline: Ecuador   Anti-government protests were reported throughout the country. Incident closed.
Details:
Anti-government demonstrations were reported in multiple locations across Ecuador. The U.S. Embassy reported that in Quito, approximately 2,000 activists planned to gather for a march in the vicinity of Av 10 de Agosto and Rio de Janeiro. The participants reportedly intended to march to Plaza Santo Domingo, located at Guayaquil and Vicente Rocafuerte. 

Ecuadorian media sources indicated that demonstrations were held in Manab , El Oro, Zamora, Riobamba, Puerto Inca, La Crespa, and Babahoyo. Protesters reportedly erected roadblocks at unspecified locations on the Guayaquil - Manab , Manab    Quito, Flavio Alfaro   El Carmen, and Babahoyo   Montalvo Highways. In some cases, such barricades were made with felled trees and other debris. In others, protesters have set fire to piles of tires. 

The demonstrations were reportedly called to raise a wide range of grievances, including rising fuel prices, back payments, low prices for agricultural exports, and healthcare deficiencies. Demonstrators also voiced opposition to plans to privatize roads, hydroelectric power plants, and telecommunications. Some protesters were affiliated with the National Farmers  Movement (FECAOL), which also called for a nationwide general strike. Some teachers reportedly observed the work stoppage as well. This incident is closed.

Headline: Cleanup Underway Following Strong Storm That Killed Three in Melbourne Metro Area
Details:
A strong windstorm that passed through the Melbourne metro area late on Thursday led to three deaths and at least one injury. The deaths were reported in the Blackburn South, Fernshaw, and Tecoma suburbs, while other heavily affected areas included Belgrave, Croydon, Lilydale, Mount Evelyn, and Mount Waverley. Dozens of buildings and vehicles were damaged, and power was temporarily disrupted for up to 80,000 customers. The power outages also led to undisinfected water entering the water system, and around 250,000 Yarra Valley Water customers in up to 88 northern and eastern suburbs were placed under a boil water advisory, which remained in place for at least some areas as of Saturday morning. Power was later restored.



Assessment: Most of the damage was caused by high winds. Gusts of up to 100 miles per hour were reported. All three of the deaths were caused by falling trees, with at least one person killed while driving when a tree struck their vehicle. Due to the boil water advisory, shortages of bottled water were reported in multiple stores in the area as customers bought large amounts. While the advisory remains in effect, authorities urge residents to boil any water used for drinking or cooking. Emergency drinking water is also available from Yarra Valley Water if necessary. No additional strong storms are currently forecast for the Melbourne area over the next several days. Individuals are advised to follow the directions of authorities in any emergency situation and to expect possible residual traffic disruptions in areas with fallen trees.

Headline: Independence Pkwy & Highway 225 - The latest fire at ITC has been extinguished. Incident closed.
Details:
Firefighters extinguished the fire that reignited in two tanks at the ITC chemical plant near Independence Pkwy and Highway 225, after the partial collapse of a dike at the facility earlier in the day. There were no reports of injuries or widespread evacuations, but businesses in the immediate vicinity were advised to shelter in place and several schools in the area cancelled classes for the day. No shelter-in-place orders were issued for residents of the city of Deer Park. A portion of the Houston Ship Channel remains closed from Tucker Bayou to Houston Ship Channel Light 116, due to cleanup efforts related to pollutant runoff. Although the fire has been contained, flare ups and re-ignition remain a possibility. Residents in the area are advised to be vigilant throughout the weekend.

The previous fire at the ITC facility affected at least eight tanks containing naphtha and xylene. This morning s collapse was thought to have caused a possible benzene leak. Naphtha is a reddish-brown or clear colorless liquid, commercially used in solvents, adhesives, varnishes, paints, and automotive products. It has an odor like gasoline. Human exposure to naphtha can cause slight eye, throat, and skin irritation. When ignited the chemical releases carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide into the air. Xylene is a colorless, flammable liquid that is used as a solvent in printing, rubber, and leather industries, and as a cleaner and paint thinner. Contact with xylene as a vapor may cause eye, nose, and throat irritation, and contact with it as a liquid may result in dermatitis. Benzene is a colorless, highly flammable liquid, used to make plastics, resins, dyes, detergents, and pesticides. Direct exposure to benzene can cause damage to the eyes, skin, and lungs. This incident is closed.

Headline: Assault Simulation Planned Wednesday on Thames in London for Visit of Dutch Royals
Details:
On Wednesday, a simulated assault is planned by the Royal Marines on the Thames River in London in conjunction with a visit by King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima of the Netherlands. The assault involving three platoons is planned to occur for ten minutes and will include the firing of blank ammunition rounds. The display will occur on the river in proximity to the HNLMS Zeeland, which will be anchored next to the HMS Belfast. 
 
	Assessment: The demonstration during the state visit is intended to highlight 45 years of cooperation between the amphibious forces of the two countries, including in the UK/NL Amphibious Force that deploys to crises around the world. Royal Marines and their Dutch counterparts are both serving in Norway under the Defense Arctic Strategy, British Defense Secretary Gavin Williamson noted. While specific restrictions along the Thames in conjunction with the demonstration Wednesday were not immediately known, Resilience360 customers are advised to anticipate potential restrictions along the Thames during the demonstration and to heed the guidance of local authorities throughout the duration of the event.

Headline: Robbers continue to target freight trains in Mexico
Details:
Cargo theft, particularly from freight trains, continues to be a significant threat to supply chains in Mexico. The scale of goods moving through Mexico’s freight railway system makes it hard for supply chain security personnel to track everything with precision, with tracks crossing through extremely isolated areas such as the Sonora dessert in the north or densely populated areas such Puebla or Toluca in the center of the country. Train robberies are a thriving business in Mexico and just about any type of cargo, from electric appliances and auto parts to grains, chemicals, and cement, is at risk. It is a phenomenon that not only affects cargo and infrastructure but also the wellbeing of drivers and security personnel. Past studies have estimated that cargo worth hundreds of millions of dollars is lost annually in Mexico in train hijackings and robberies. 
Theft operations have also become more complex in recent years. In the past, thieves usually identified areas where freight trains either stop or slow down to jump on, pop open doors or trailers, and throw products off. In the last few months, however, Mexico has seen an increasing number of choreographed train robberies that often start with robbers damaging tracks or holding up trains with rocks, and involve small armies of people who descend on the derailed cars in waves to carry off the loot.
Train robberies in Mexico have reached alarming levels in 2018. From January to September 2018, Mexico’s Railway Transport Regulatory Agency (ARTF) reported a total of 2,115 train robberies, which represents a 148 percent increase compared to the 850 robberies recorded during the same period in 2017. In other words, the frequency of robberies increased from 22 a week to 54 a week in the space of a year. The regulatory agency also reported that the five states with the most robberies are Puebla (358), Guanajuato (181), Jalisco (178), Coahuila (177), and Sonora (158).
One industry that has been particularly affected by the surge of train robberies in Mexico is the chemicals industry. In Tlaxcala, Puebla and Veracruz, stealing gasoline and diesel from pipelines has not been enough for organized bands of huachicoleros (fuel thieves) who have turned their eyes to cargo theft from trains as an opportunity to expand their tentacles to other underground markets. Products such as pesticides, ethylene, polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene, and other polymers are routinely targeted by these criminal organizations, especially along the Mexico City-Puebla-Veracruz route, the Mexico City-Saltillo route, and the Mexiquense Beltway. 
Polyethylene, a thermoplastic polymer heavily used in the production of consumer products, is by far the most targeted chemical product in Mexico. In 2017, the Etileno XXI Petrochemical Complex in Coatzacoalcos, Veracruz, alone reported losses of USD 2.5 million (EUR 2.2 million) due to polyethylene theft. This year, there have a number of train robberies targeting polyethylene shipments. The most noticeable thefts occurred in February 2 and May 5, with 148 tons of polyethylene, worth approximately USD 195,000 (EUR 170,000), stolen in the town of Apizaco and 236 tons of polyethylene, worth approximately USD 311,000 (EUR 274,000), stolen in Tamariz, respectively. 
This extensive criminal activity is supported by an underground market ready to receive and sell polyethylene to consumers. The towns of Tezuapan and San Antonio la Soledad in the state of Puebla have been identified as two of the main points of sale for stolen chemicals in the country. Reports indicate that in these towns, stolen polyethylene is sold at around USD 0.80 (EUR 0.72) per kilo, well below its market value of USD 1.48 (EUR 1.31) per kilo.
Security concerns in Mexico, especially for rail transportation, are not going away anytime soon. Shippers and carriers likewise are waiting to see if the country’s incoming administration is prepared to take steps to stop the increasing rail cargo thefts. In the meantime, supply chain managers with interests in Mexico must continue collaborating with other members of the value chain, both upstream and downstream, and make use of technology that provide visibility on evolving supply chain security risks. Moreover, railroad carriers must be constantly evaluated and monitored to determine if they are exposed to a higher than normal risk, while companies must continuously assess their shipping routes to find the best way to eliminate or mitigate those risks.

Headline: St Petersburg Military Academy Explosion Being Investigated as Attempted Murder
Details:
Authorities are investigating an explosion at about 1:30 PM local time Tuesday at the Mozhaysky Military Space Academy in St Petersburg as attempted murder. The explosion is now suspected to have been the result of a planned attack rather than an incident that occurred from an unplanned munitions detonation. Updated reports indicate the homemade explosive contained about one pound of TNT and had been placed below a staircase that went to the personnel department for the academy. The explosion, which injured four academy staff, is believed to have been triggered by a mobile phone. No arrests or possible suspects had been announced by authorities in the initial aftermath of the explosion. 
 
	Assessment: The suspected attack on Tuesday is the second time in recent years that the academy has been targeted. Last year, a student at the academy was arrested on suspicion of plotting to set fire to the barracks of the academy before planning to attack a public square using an ice cream cart hiding an explosive, as well as striking a crowd with a suicide belt. The academy has restricted access, and the location of the bomb Tuesday near the personnel department has prompted speculation that the attack could have been motivated by a grievance of a cadet or staff member at the academy. While no specific, credible threat is known at this time, Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring developments related to the investigation and to practice heightened situational awareness in public areas.

Media sources indicate that Sweden is increasing its military presence in the Baltic Sea. Few additional details have been reported, but the move is said to have been prompted by an uptick in military actions in the region by Russia, along with unspecified Western nations, as well as the situation in Belarus, where President Aleksandr Lukashenko’s hold on power is being challenged following a disputed election earlier this month. On Tuesday, local television showed armored vehicles disembarking from a ferry on the island of Gotland, while the military said naval surveillance in the Baltic Sea, both at sea and from the air, will be reinforced.



Assessment: With Sweden’s armed forces assessing the threat of a military attack on the country as low, the move to bolster its military presence in the Baltic Sea appears largely precautionary. That said, a Belarusian military helicopter reportedly entered the airspace of nearby Lithuania last weekend, suggesting the possibility of unintentional incursions or intrusions by foreign actors, while Russian warships taking part in a large naval drill near St. Petersburg in the coming days will first sail near Sweden’s coastline. With Moscow also staging exercises near the border with Belarus, this has led to speculation over a possible Russian military intervention there, akin to eastern Ukraine in 2014, though US intelligence officials have said there are presently no indications of any such plans by the Kremlin. In any event, the heightened tensions in the region, coupled with the presence of foreign militaries operating in close proximity to one another, could lead to contentious encounters and, by extension, inadvertent escalation.

Headline: Authorities Place Industrial Area in Dammam Under Isolation Due to COVID-19 Concerns
Details:
On Saturday, media sources reported that authorities in Saudi Arabia have placed the 2nd Industrial City area of Dammam, the capital of Eastern Province, under a full lockdown and curfew in a bid to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Under the move, all entry and exit from the area has been banned until further notice, and local residents are only allowed to leave their homes for necessary purposes, such as procuring healthcare and food supplies, between the hours of 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM local time. Freight shipments are exempt from the order and factories may continue to operate at one-third capacity, according to Saudi state media. Also Saturday, the government lifted a total lockdown ordered in Dammam’s Al-Atheer district on April 15. As of this writing, Saudi Arabia has recorded 28,656 positive COVID-19 infections and 191 deaths attributed to the virus.



Assessment: Saudi Arabia’s COVID-19 outbreak continues to accelerate, with the kingdom reporting its biggest daily jump in new coronaviruses cases so far on Monday, with 1,645 new infections. This trend could be the result of increased testing, and while authorities have relaxed lockdown measures and curfew times for Ramadan and in light of purported public compliance with the government’s social distancing and other precautionary measures, Saturday’s move nonetheless highlights Riyadh’s strict anti-virus strategy. However, this has taken a toll on the nation’s economy, with the finance minister saying on Saturday that the government will have to take aggressive measures to deal with the financial impact of the coronavirus pandemic, likely including “sharp” reductions in budget expenditures. Because the Kingdom has traditionally relied on its extensive social welfare system and bloated government workforce to help maintain political allegiance and suppress public discontent, such moves have generally been highly sensitive. However, given its ample reserves of wealth and relatively low debt, Saudi Arabi is better positioned to withstand the economic volatility compared to many of its regional counterparts, thereby mitigating the potential for associated social unrest in the near term.

Headline: Cargo surge doubles container dwell times at Port of Vancouver rail facilities
Details: Intelligence obtained by Everstream Analytics incidates that a surge of cargo due to Chinese New Year, upcoming import tariffs in the United States, and weather conditions have brought the utilization capacity of all terminals at the Port of Vancouver to 85% (above the industry standard maximum of 80%), doubling container dwell times at associated terminal rail facilities. As a result, dwell times at Deltaport are reported to be 7+ days; Centerm, 3-5 days; and Vanterm, 5-7 days. Near-normal average dwell times are anticipated to return within weeks. Increased dwell times have also been attributed increasing discharge sizes from mega-ships.

Headline: Truckers stage demonstration against parking cuts in Santos, SP
Details: Local media sources indicate on February 20 that 40 truckers organized by the Sindicato dos Transportadores Rodoviários Autônomos de Bens da Baixada Santista e Vale do Ribeira, or Sindicam, held a demonstration in Santos, SP to protest cuts for cargo transporter trucking in the city, which hosts Brazil's principal seaport. The cuts involve eliminating parking at Morro Ilhéu Alto and the Rio São Jorge to make way for a bridge connecting the Bom Retiro and Sao Manuel neighborhoods in the city, facilitating access to the Anchieta Highway that leads to Sao Paulo proper. The parking lot is able to accommodate 200 trucks at present. At present, the demonstration consists of blocked lanes by the truckers, predominating around City Hall. A meeting is scheduled between Sindicam and the Santos municipal administration on February 21, which may determine the next steps taken by the union in the city. Those shipping by ground in Santos should anticipate mild congestion and should plan accordingly.

Headline: Cambodia – Recovery efforts are underway after flooding killed up to 44 people. - UPDATE 6
Details:
Sources indicate that recovery efforts continue across Cambodia after flooding killed up to 44 people. Flooding has largely subsided and normal operations are resuming. Expect possible residual disruptions. This event is closed.  


At least 26 of the deaths occurred in Banteay Meanchey, seven were reported in Kampong Thom, and six in Pursat. Deaths were also recorded in Sihanoukville, Pailin, Kampong Chhnang, and Stung Treng. Approximately 133,203 homes were damaged or destroyed. In addition, more than 594,388 people have been affected by the flooding, of whom 47,580 were evacuated or displaced, including over 500 from Phnom Penh. Approximately 912,333 acres of crops have been inundated, while at least 951 schools were affected.

Flooding began around Thursday, October 1, following the passage of Tropical Storm Noul, and has affected at least 20 provinces. The provinces impacted include Phnom Penh, Pursat, Pailin, Banteay Meanchey, Battambang, Svay Rieng, Thbong Khmum, Oddar Meanchey, Siem Reap, Takeo, Kampong Speu, Mondulkiri, Sihanoukville, Koh Kong, Preah Vihear, Stung Treng, Kampong Cham, Kandal, Kampong Chhnang, and Kampong Thom. The flooding has also inundated and damaged numerous roads. At least 40 unspecified factories reportedly closed across Kampong Speu Province, Kandal Province, and Phnom Penh.

Headline: Increase in trade circumvention practices to evade U.S. tariffs on Chinese imports
Details:
Over recent weeks, several alleged cases of trade circumvention by foreign companies, mostly believed to be from China, have been reported in Vietnam and Cambodia. These companies are allegedly transshipping and re-routing exported goods through third-party countries in a bid to evade U.S. tariffs during a period of ongoing trade tensions between the United States and China.

On June 9, Vietnamese customs published a notice stating that it would be cracking down on goods of Chinese origin illegally relabeled “Made in Vietnam” by exporters seeking to avoid U.S. tariffs imposed on Chinese imports amid trade tensions. Saigon also announced that it has instructed its provincial and municipal branches to increase inspection and verification of certificates of origin to better identify and impose penalties on businesses that carry out such violations.

Subsequent reports followed on June 19 when the U.S. fined several Chinese companies for exporting goods via Sihanoukville Special Economic Zone (SSEZ) – a Chinese-owned SEZ in Cambodia – in another similar alleged attempt to dodge U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. Given the growing trend of multinational companies contemplating shifting production from China to Southeast Asia, such practices can expose these manufacturers to substantial legal and criminal penalties. Headline: Hapag-Lloyd suspends overseas agricultural container shipments from North America
Details: Shipping sources on October 26 report that the German international shipping and transportation company Hapag-Lloyd indicated to exporters that it will be suspending overseas agricultural container shipments from North America. The decision was reportedly being driven by hard economics during a time of unprecedented demand for higher-value North American consumer imports by containers from Asia at premium prices. Hapag-Lloyd has decided it needs to quickly reposition empty containers back to Asian shipping centers, even if it means forgoing hauling critical food and agriculture products back to manufacturers overseas. This will likely impact exporters in the Minneapolis-St. Paul region. The majority of Hapag-Lloyd delivered agricultural shipments go to food processing customers in Japan, Indonesia, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Malaysia.

The situation involving the crew has further changed the ship’s schedule and Sofia Express is expected to continue its voyage shortly towards Pusan.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - New Belgian government to focus on economic recovery; exclusion of Flemish nationalist parties likely to drive protests
Details: Prime Minister Alexander De Croo delivers a speech at a plenary session of the Belgian federal chamber held at the European Parliament on Friday 2 October in Brussels.Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty ImagesThe new Belgian federal government led by Prime Minister Alexander De Croo was sworn in on 1 October following a seven-party coalition agreement, which ended lengthy government formation talks after inconclusive elections were held in May 2019. Negotiations on policy proposals among the ruling coalition’s seven-member parties are likely to slow down policy implementation. The ruling coalition comprises seven Walloon and Flemish parties: the Socialist Party (Parti Socialiste: PS), Socialist Party Differently (Socialistische Partij Anders SP.A), Ecolo, Green (Groen), Christian Democratic and Flemish (Christen-Democratisch en Vlaams: CD&V), Reformist Movement (Mouvement Réformateur: MR), and Open Flemish Liberals and Democrats (Open Vlaamse Liberalen en Democraten: Open VLD). Significantly, Flemish nationalist parties the New Flemish Alliance (Nieuw-Vlaamse Alliantie: N-VA) and Flemish Interest (Vlaams Belang: VB) secured 16% and nearly 50% of the votes, respectively, in Flanders in the May 2019 federal election. The high number of coalition members will probably slow policy implementation, requiring more dialogue to reach agreements given language community and ideological divisions. Nevertheless, the appointment of former prime minister Sophie Wilmès as foreign minister and De Croo, former development and finance minister, as prime minister indicates continuity of policies of the previous caretaker government, which oversaw the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) virus response. Secretary of State Thomas Dermine was appointed to oversee the response, probably improving co-ordination between the federal and regional governments.Belgium is facing its worst economic downturn since 2008, with consumer-facing services most directly affected. IHS Markit projects Belgium’s real GDP to contract by 8.7% in the current fiscal year, followed by a 3.7% gain in 2021. The negative shock to the economy primarily stems from an 8.5% annual decline in private consumption. Consumer-facing services continue to suffer owing to once again increasing COVID-19 cases. A double-digit fall in fixed investment is another drag on economic activity. The formation of the new government will enable a vote on the budget (which has not occurred since 2017), which is likely to prioritise the COVID-19 virus economic recovery and related healthcare response. IHS Markit projects a sharp widening of the fiscal deficit from 1.9% in 2019 to 11.4% in 2020 and 8.6% in 2021. Prime Minister De Croo’s administration is likely to implement fiscal relief for citizens and businesses, having already announced plans on 30 September to gradually increase the minimum pension to EUR1,500 (USD1,763) per month for workers with 45 years of contributions. The government is planning to increase the healthcare budget by 2.5% annually in response to the country registering the world’s third-highest mortality rate per inhabitant in April. The coalition agreement plans to support investments in the national economy with EUR1 billion, while also allocating EUR1 billion to temporary relief measures. The new government will also now need to submit its recovery plan for the EU rescue fund. However, a key challenge will be introducing structural reforms to the pension system. According to Eurostat, the duration of working life is 33.6 years, notably lower than the average of 35.9 years for the EU27. Previous attempts to lift the pension age to cope with rising costs have not been successful. The N-VA and Socialists have opposing views, therefore tangible progress is unlikely. The economic downturn and the exclusion of Flemish nationalist parties from the coalition government increases the likelihood of anti-government protests and trade union-led strikes affecting the transport and retail sectors. Thousands of nationalist VB party supporters staged a protest near Brussels on 25 September to oppose VB’s exclusion from the government. Further protests staged by the opposition VB and N-VA parties are likely to attract several thousands of people, particularly in Brussels and the Flanders region, likely triggered by the government proposing draft bills on issues that the two parties oppose such as migration and the social security system. The presence of counter-demonstrators would increase the likelihood of violence, with the police probably deploying tear gas. Grievances stemming from the economic downturn also provide a context for anti-government protests and trade union-led strikes, most likely being triggered by large companies announcing job cuts. Strikes are likely to affect the transport and retail sectors, with the potential of halting port operations in Antwerp and Ghent for up to several days in the event of a general strike being called. The risk of looting around large protests remains high in central Brussels, particularly affecting commercial streets in the Louise area.Indicators of changing risk environmentIncreasing riskMPs from one or more coalition parties voting against draft bills sponsored by a coalition partner would indicate internal fractures, increasing the risk of a government collapse.Strong criticisms of government proposals from trade unions would indicate an increasing risk of disruptive labour strikes and associated nationwide protests.Decreasing riskThe effective drawing of funds from the EU’s COVID-19-virus recovery plan would support the government’s fiscal spending objectives and provide relief to key economic sectors. Headline: UPDATE: Fog causing congestion in Houston, affecting ocean shipments
Details: Updated sources report fog has delayed vessel traffic through the Houston Ship Channel every day in the past week, delaying shipments of cargo and container ships. Waiting times for berths have thus increased as the channel has been shut intermittently for a total of 133 hours in the past two weeks. The channel was reportedly open as of 17:30 local time on March 13. The delays this week caused US phenol and acetone producer AdvanSix to declare a force majeure on phenol at its plant in Frankford, Pennsylvania earlier this week. Fog in Houston is particularly bad in the October-March period as warmer, humid Gulf air collides with cooler onshore air.

Headline: Battery Park - Protesters arrived at the park to continue the climate change rally. Incident closed.
Details:
Multiple sources reported that protesters arrived at Battery Park, after marching from Foley Square. Several groups organized the demonstration to demand increased action on climate change by leaders of both the U.S. and the UN, including at the UN Climate Summit occurring on Monday, September 23. The protest is part of a week-long global climate strike action beginning on Friday, September 20. 

After assembling in Foley Square at 12:00 PM local time, the group marched to Battery Park at 1:00 PM. The group marched south on Lafayette St, turned west on Reade St, turned south onto the east side of Broadway, turned east on Ann St, turned south on Nassau St, turned south on Broad St, turned west on Beaver St, and then turned west into Battery Park. Protesters were expected to continue to rally until 5:00 PM. The number of participants was not indicated; however, it is possible that the demonstration saw upward of hundreds of thousands of participants, due in part to New York City schools allowing students to participate in the action. Expect potential residual disruptions in the vicinity. This incident is closed.

More than 400 people were evacuated in central Vietnam and 4,100 people were evacuated in Can Gio District due to the storm, although an unspecified number of people returned home. More than 50 houses were damaged by the flooding. Residual disruptions may persist as cleanup operations continue. This incident is closed.

Headline: Politician Fatally Shot in Karachi
Details:
On Wednesday, media reports indicated that a prominent Pakistani politician was fatally shot in Karachi s Defense Housing Authority (DHA) area late December 25. The victim, 46-year-old Syed Ali Raza Abidi, was alone in his car outside of his home when the attack took place. The assailants fled the scene and reportedly remain at large. Abidi was the former leader of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) and was elected to the National Assembly in the 2013 general election. 
 
	Assessment: No group has claimed credit for Abidi s assassination, and the motivation remains unclear. MQM leaders have assigned blame to Pakistan s security establishment, which has waged a crackdown against the party in recent years. The crackdown has also caused MQM to fragment into several factions that continue to compete for supremacy in Karachi, raising the specter that the incident was the result of internal rivalry. Meanwhile, although it remains unclear if the incidents are connected, two members of the Pak Sarzameen Party, an MQM offshoot that is seen as close to the security establishment, were killed in an attack in Karachi on December 23, elucidating the possibility of sectarian and/or political motives. More broadly, violence of this sort can occur at any time in Karachi and can trigger rioting, protests, and labor strikes.

The victim, 46-year-old Syed Ali Raza Abidi, was alone in his car outside of his home when the attack took place. The assailants fled the scene and reportedly remain at large. Abidi was the former leader of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) and was elected to the National Assembly in the 2013 general election. 
 
	Assessment: No group has claimed credit for Abidi s assassination, and the motivation remains unclear. MQM leaders have assigned blame to Pakistan s security establishment, which has waged a crackdown against the party in recent years. The crackdown has also caused MQM to fragment into several factions that continue to compete for supremacy in Karachi, raising the specter that the incident was the result of internal rivalry. Meanwhile, although it remains unclear if the incidents are connected, two members of the Pak Sarzameen Party, an MQM offshoot that is seen as close to the security establishment, were killed in an attack in Karachi on December 23, elucidating the possibility of sectarian and/or political motives. More broadly, violence of this sort can occur at any time in Karachi and can trigger rioting, protests, and labor strikes.

All magnitude scales should yield approximately the same value for any given earthquake.

Details:

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels from 10pm on 27 December until 10pm on 28 December

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels on day shift from 6am from 29 December for indefinite period

- Ban on the performance of work on all vessels from 2pm on 1 January until 2pm on 2 January

- All terminal operations will be stopped during these hours.

- Work restrictions apply.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - LNG tanker attack indicates increasing piracy and kidnap risks affecting onshore assets in Equatorial Guinea
Details: The Equatoguinean government on 17 October announced that armed pirates attacked the Marshall Islands-flagged LNG tanker Methane Princess in anchorage. The pirates reportedly boarded the vessel at the Punta Europa LNG Terminal off Malabo on Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea’s main LNG marine pier, while it was completing a cargo operation. Reports indicate that the attackers took hostages, including an Equatoguinean and a Filipino, while another Equatoguinean citizen suffered minor injuries. The latest incident follows a growing trend of piracy and kidnap-for-ransom by criminal gangs in Equatoguinean maritime waters and the wider Gulf of Guinea, with similar piracy incidents reported close to Lomé in Togo and Takoradi in Ghana. In May, gunmen boarded the Comoros-flagged general cargo vessel Rio Mitong at anchor near Malabo and foreign and local crew members were abducted. In addition, the Equatorial Guinea-flagged ro-ro vessel Djibloho was attacked off the coast of Luba, Bioko Island, in the same month. Likewise, pirates attacked oil-supply vessel Pacific Warden near Luba in November 2019 and abducted seven out of 15 crew members. In May 2019, pirates boarded heavy-load carrier ship Blue Marlin, but later fled following a gunfight with the Spanish and Equatoguinean navies, with 10 pirates being arrested. Significance: The latest attack at the LNG terminal indicates growing operational reach and capability of these mostly Niger Delta-based assailants, while exposing security shortcomings at a strategic national asset. IHS Markit assesses that such attacks are likely to increase in frequency and would involve crew abductions and robbery of valuables other than fuel cargo. Such attacks are likely to be driven by increased investments in major energy infrastructure projects, such as the proposed development of a Gas Mega Hub. Headline: Disruption occurring on the London Overground and Underground lines
Details: Transport for London (TfL) is reporting that disruption is occurring on the London Underground and Overground lines on Thursday morning. There is no service on the Jubilee Line between Wembley Park and Willesden Green due to a faulty train at Neasden. In addition, severe delays are being reported along the line between Willesden Green and Stratford and lesser delays are occurring between Stanmore and Wembley Park. The Metropolitan Line has been suspended between Wembley Park and Aldgate due to the faulty train at Neasden. The London Overground Line is suspended between South Tottenham and Barking and a reduced service is operating between South Tottenham and Gospel Oak. This is to allow Network Rail to repair damage caused by a derailed freight train.

Headline: Traffic restrictions ahead of the Asian Games to impact in-land freight movement
Details:
From August 18 to September 2, Indonesia will host the 18th Asian Games, a pan-Asian multi-sport event which will be held in Jakarta and Palembang. The opening and closing ceremonies will be held in Jakarta and reports suggest that the sporting event will draw around 17,000 athletes and sports officials as well as more than 100,000 international spectators. The tournament will include a variety of 42 games, out of which 20 will be held inside the Gelora Bung Karno sports complex in Jakarta and the rest will be spread across Jakarta Convention Centre, the International Expo, Ancol Beach and other locations in the North, East, and South of Jakarta. In Palembang, most sporting events will take place at the Jakabaring Sport City and Bumi Sriwijaya Stadium.

To cater to this large sporting event, authorities have increased flights at Soekarno Hatta International Airport (CGK) and Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II International Airport (PLM) which serves Jakarta and Palembang respectively. Furthermore, environmental cleanup programs, as well as traffic restrictions, have been imposed in Jakarta to curb air pollution and reduce congestion. An odd-even license plate policy on vehicles has been on a trial run since July 2 to measure the athletes’ average travel time during the events. The regulation stipulates that vehicles with license plates ending in odd numbers will only be allowed to travel in certain zones on odd-numbered dates. The same applies to plates ending with even numbers on even-numbered dates. The trial period ended on July 31 and the official implementation of the policy came into effect on August 1 again. This will last until September 2 with the hours extended from 06:00 to 21:00 (local time). The notice issued by the transportation authorities indicated that the policy also applies to cargo trucks as they fall under the category of Group III, IV and V vehicles, which includes containers and trailers.

While the games will not have a significant impact on ocean and airfreight as well as on customs clearance processes, in-land freight movement including pickup and delivery services are likely to face localized disruptions due to the scheduled operating hours of a few toll gates in Jakarta during the games. From August 18 to September 2, authorities will reportedly restrict the operating hours of the following toll gates:
  
Toll gates closed between 06:00 to 17:00 (local time):
•	Pintu Tol Angke 2
•	Pintu Tol Tanjung Duren
•	Pintu Tol Slipi 2
•	Pintu Tol Taman Mini 1 

Toll gates closed between 12:00 to 21:00 (local time):
•	Pintu Tol Angke 1
•	Pintu Tol Slipi 1
•	Pintu Tol Taman Mini 2

Trucks carrying goods can use the Kebon Bawang toll gate between 22:00 to 05:00 to access the Tanjung Priok Port to the Inner Circle toll road. Furthermore, reports indicate that trucking will be diverted through the arterial road and will be allowed to enter through the Rorotan Toll Gate and Cakung directly to the Outer Ring Road. 

According to sources, around 60,000 security personnel will be deployed during the Asian Games to ensure public security which may result in vehicle spot checks for trucks that are operating at night due to the change in schedules. Customers with interests in shipments to Indonesia during the Asian Games should keep in mind the traffic policy changes and the potential delays in in-land freight movement. Customers are advised to liaise with local partners to keep abreast of local traffic regulations to ensure timely cargo and pickup delivery services.

Headline: UPDATE - Hong Kong: Polytechnic University operation ends; demonstrations planned for this weekend in Hong Kong
Details: Social media sources indicate that demonstrations are planned for this weekend in Hong Kong. The planned protests follow a week of relative peace following district council elections last Sunday, 24 November, which saw a majority victory by pro-democracy candidates. The call to demonstrate is due in part to Chief Executive Carrie Lam's acknowledgment of public dissatisfaction, but perceived unwillingness to make political concessions following the elections. Additionally, some protesters are believed to be motivated by the events at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, which saw 12 days of violence between demonstrators and riot police before authorities cleared the location. A major rally has been called for Sunday, 1 December, with a subsequent strike on 2 December which will reportedly target morning commutes. Clashes with police cannot be ruled out at these events.

Headline: Customs Commissioner revises 2(iii), 95 ITC(HS) import rules for JNPT toy clearance
Details: Industry sources indicated in Public Notice 113-2019 that the Customs Commissioner has revised Policy Condition 2(iii) to Chapter 95 of teh ITC (HS), 2017 Schedule 1 for Import Policy Procedure regarding toy import clearance at the Jawaharlal Nehru Customs House on December 23. According to the revised policy, samples will be randomly picked from each consignment to be sent to an NABL-accredited lab for testing, and cleared if customs assesses from the tests that the product will be safe for the market. If the sample fails tests, the consignment must be returned or exported at the importer's expense.

Details: Media sources indicate on October 21 that Vietnamese containership Vietsun Integrity capsized on the Long Tau River near Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam on October 19. The incident occurred when the ship was sailing downstream from Ho Chi Minh to Vung Tau with 290 containers onboard. Sources cited that the ship capsized and sank two hours after the crew discovered that the ship was starting to list. All 17 crew members that were onboard the ship made it to the shore safely.

Headline: New security filing requirements may be valid in case of no-deal Brexit
Details: Shipping sources on October 21 indicate that the European Commission (EC) has confirmed that from October 31 and in the event of a no-deal Brexit, the UK will be treated as any third country for security filing purposes. EU export cargo that will be loaded on a vessel service currently not affected by any 24 Hour Rule can become filing-relevant depending on the vessel rotation. For example, cargo loaded at London Gateway or at prior EU ports and remaining on board the vessel while calling at London Gateway, requires to have an Entry Summary Declaration (ENS) filed for it in advance of entry into the EU. This is not limited to cargo discharged in an EU port later on, but also includes FROB cargo (Foreign cargo Remaining On Board) transiting the EU and destined for subsequent non EU ports (e.g. Cartagena).

Headline: Abu Sayyaf Suspected in Two Bombings in Jolo That Killed at Least 15, Injured 75
Details:
At around 11:55 AM local time on Monday an explosion occurred along Serrantes Street near Plaza Rizal in the city of Jolo, capital of Sulu Province. The blast, believed to have been caused by a bomb on a motorcycle, apparently targeted soldiers who were escorting government employees carrying out COVID-19-related relief work. About an hour later, a female suicide bomber detonated her explosives after being stopped by a soldier while attempting to enter the cordoned area near the site of the first explosion. The two explosions killed at least 15 people and injured another 75. Of those killed, at least seven were soldiers and one was a police officer, while the injured include 21 soldiers and six police officers. In the aftermath of the explosions, Jolo was locked down and regional military and coast guard forces have been placed on high alert.



Assessment: There was no immediate claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, but military authorities stated that it was most likely carried out by the Islamic State (IS)-linked Abu Sayyaf terrorist group, or at least a faction of the group. According to some officials, the attack was probably attributable to Abu Sayyaf leader Hajan Sawadjaan. The military is also investigating the possibility that the attack was in retaliation for the arrest earlier this month of another Abu Sayyaf leader, Anduljihad Susukan, who surrendered to authorities in Davao City after previously being wounded in a gun battle with security forces in Sulu. Also on Monday, military officials in a government meeting speculated that the June killing of four military intelligence officers by police in Jolo may have been an effort by police to protect Abu Sayyaf suspects that the soldiers were investigating. The officials stated that the soldiers were following up on reports that two female suicide bombers were operating in Sulu, and theorized that the police officers who killed the soldiers may be related to Abu Sayyaf members. The investigation into the exact nature of the shooting remains ongoing, and, in addition to the possibility of mistaken identity, officials have also previously stated that the soldiers’ killings may have been related to drugs or a local dispute. Regardless of the circumstances surrounding the deaths of the soldiers, if they were investigating reports of the presence of female suicide bombers, it is possible that their investigation was related to suspects involved in Monday’s bombings, and could indicate that additional suspects remain outstanding. Abu Sayyaf is based on Jolo and operates primarily in Sulu and Basilan Provinces. Authorities have urged residents to remain vigilant following the Jolo attack, and to report any suspicious individuals. It is likely that searches and other police operations will take place over the next several days as authorities investigate the bombings, whether in the city of Jolo or elsewhere on the island. A heavy security presence should also be expected to remain in the city, and individuals are urged to comply with all emergency orders issued by authorities. It is also advised to avoid nonessential travel to Sulu Province due to the unstable security situation, including the possibility of terrorism.

Headline: Unpaid Selaras Kausa Busana garment workers strike in Jakarta

SKB is a garment factory based in Bekasi, West Java Province that produces for global brands such as K-Mart, Target and Disney.

Headline: Evaluations Continue Following Severe Winter Storm That Killed 13 in Mediterranean Spain and France
Details:
On Thursday, the death toll in Spain from a storm, locally referred to as Storm Gloria, rose to 13 with an additional four people missing. Mediterranean coastal areas of Spain, including Catalonia, Murcia, and Andalusia, and the Balearic Islands were hardest hit in Spain, with Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez surveying heavily impacted areas on Thursday ahead of a government emergency meeting on Friday as response measures are ongoing. The storm brought wind gusts in excess of 60 miles per hour along with heavy rain and strong waves. The majority of storm-related deaths occurred in Catalonia and Valencia. While the storm had moved from Spain, several rivers in the country s northeast burst their banks on Thursday and rice paddies in the Ebro River delta between Barcelona and Valencia were hard hit from a storm surge that extended about two miles inland. The storm also brought snow to the Pyrenees and flooding to lower-elevation areas of southern France, though no related fatalities in France are known. In France s Pyr n es-Orientales and Aude departments, as much as five months of rain has fallen within three days, prompting more than 1,500 evacuations.

Assessment: Prime Minister Sanchez said that climate change is  accentuating  storms such as Gloria, while forecasters in France noted that Gloria was the worst winter storm to strike the region since 1982. France and Spain experienced heavy flooding in October 2019, however, and both the intensity and frequency of such storms are generally believed to be hallmarks of climate change. Such storms are capable of disrupting regional transportation, damaging coastal infrastructure, and exacerbating erosion that can leave coastal areas more vulnerable to future severe weather events. In more mountainous regions, the heavy snowfall from storm systems typically heightens the risk of avalanches, and data from local officials regarding any restricted areas should be observed. While damage assessments and recovery efforts continue in both France and Spain, it is advised to continue monitoring river levels in affected areas for any further flood risk, to avoid any persisting areas of high water, including while driving, and to heed the guidance of local authorities.

Headline: Transportation strikes over extortion increase supply-chain disruption...
Details: Risks: Death and injury; Criminal violence; ExtortionSectors or assets affected: Individuals; Taxis; Transport; Police and security forces; Cargo; Ground; Ports; ExportsOn 14 February Security Minister Julian Pacheco announced that the anti-gang Operation Morazan II was refocusing its strategy on high crime urban centres linked to Puerto Cortes after confirming that there had been an increase in attacks against transport service operators in Cortes department. Three taxi drivers were shot dead in two simultaneous attacks in Choloma on 11 February by individuals on a motorcycle. To date, seven taxi drivers as well as a cargo vehicle driver for fruit company Chiquita have been killed in 2019. Police stated the incidents are related to extortion payment delays to the Barrio 18 (M-18) and MS-13 gangs. Companies operating along the Puerto Cortes-San Pedro Sula corridor indicate that gangs had been increasing extortion rates since December 2018, making it harder to meet weekly payment demands. 'War tax' rates average HNL70,000 (USD2,853) weekly for taxi companies with an upwards-sliding scale for buses and cargo. Police said that extortion risks are highest for San Pedro Sula, in La Planeta and Miguel Angel Pavon colonies.Significance: The National Anti-Maras and Gang Force (FNAMP) has been running anti-extortion operations involving specialised forces focusing on high-incidence areas like San Pedro Sula since July 2018. Extortion-related arrests of alleged gang members are widely publicised in the national media but have failed to halt the rise of extortion over 2018. Transport strikes responding to the 2019 attacks have taken place in San Pedro Sula, Puerto Cortes, and Choloma. To date, demonstrations have taken the form of public transportation work stoppages but are likely to escalate with go-slow road traffic disruptions along the CA-13 if expanded gang-arrest actions by the authorities prove ineffective. If extortion-related deaths continue to rise in Puerto Cortes, the fourth-largest cargo port in Central America, at the head of the corridor, subsequent transport worker strikes will disrupt traffic at the port and result in processing delays, with knock-on interruptions for supply chains. For the CA-13 corridor, intensification of police operations in municipalities like Choloma and San Antonio de Cortes in the Valle de Sula is likely to disrupt extortion demands but a sustained reduction is unlikely in 2019. Headline: Stevedore strike at Port of Santos to remain unresolved during Carnaval
Details:
Sindestiva (Sindicato dos Estivadores de Santos, Sao Vicente, Guaruja e Cubatao), the largest stevedore union representing dockworkers on the Sao Paulo coast, declared the commencement of a strike at the Port of Santos on March 1 at 7:00 (local time). The strike action is the latest to involve stevedores airing grievances against the port management at Brazil’s largest seaport, and the first of 2019. 
The warning for this strike was issued on February 19, after a Superior Labor Court decision on February 11 permitted the Port of Santos to employ contractors to quantities of up to 100% of its workforce, revoking an earlier agreement from 2015 that permitted only a maximum of 50% contractor employment at the port. The strike also provides the union the opportunity to air grievances over pay and benefits. After a union meeting on February 26, the strike was confirmed on February 28, and is in progress as of this writing. 
What complicates matters is that the strike coincides with the Carnaval holiday in Brazil. Brazilian supply chains and transportation thoroughfares, like many locales which commemorate the holiday, slow down and gradually resume production after Ash Wednesday. Manufacturers traditionally give employees time off for the Carnaval period, with typical holiday duration lasting for about 1 week, starting on the preceding Friday. In extreme cases, the holiday may even extend to 21 days. Sources state that the port management and Sindestiva representatives willing to meet and negotiate during the holiday is unlikely at best.
While past incidents impacting the Port of Santos have been relatively harmless, this open-ended strike over a longer period without any negotiation in sight poses greater uncertainty. Such uncertainty without a resolution is likely to cause cargo delays and subsequent backlogs. As such, those relying on the Port of Santos as a maritime hub are advised to monitor developments. While strikes of this nature typically make provisions for the unimpeded circulation of perishable and element-sensitive goods, no such provisions have been explicitly mentioned at present.

Headline: 2 miles S of Sinawilan- 3 killed, 31 injured, structural damage from earthquake. Incident closed.

Rescue efforts remain ongoing as authorities search for people trapped under rubble. One person was killed in Matanao after a building collapsed. Many structures were damaged throughout Davao del Sur and Mindanao. A total of 13 government buildings have been damaged from the earthquake, including the Magsaysay Municipal Hall. Dozens of minor aftershocks have been reported near the epicenter. There were no tsunami threat associated with this earthquake. This incident is closed.

Headline: UK to Extend Immigration Possibilities if National Security Laws Implemented in Hong Kong
Details:
In an article published on Wednesday, British Prime Minister Boris Johnson reemphasized plans released last week by the Home Office to extend immigration possibilities to British National (Overseas) (BNO) passport holders if national security legislation passed by China’s National People’s Congress (NPC) is implemented in Hong Kong. The Home Office plans include extending United Kingdom visa-free travel for Hong Kong BNO passport holders and their dependents to 12 months with the possibility for renewal, up from the current six months, and to allow BNO passport holders to work in the UK, which could eventually lead to citizenship. The BNO designation was granted to Hong Kong residents who chose to receive it before the 1997 handover of Hong Kong to China, and to those who acquired the status when the handover took effect. According to the Home Office, there are approximately 350,000 BNO passport holders in Hong Kong, with nearly three million other people eligible to apply for BNO passports.



Assessment: The security legislation that was approved by the NPC has been controversial, both for sidestepping Hong Kong’s Legislative Council and for the view that it will be used to end the semi-autonomy that Hong Kong has enjoyed since the handover. Media sources have reported long lines of people attempting to apply for or renew BNO passports at postal offices and shipping businesses in Hong Kong in recent days. UK Foreign Secretary Dominic Raab stated on Tuesday that the UK government had also spoken with the United States, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand over the possibility of mass emigration from Hong Kong if the NPC laws are implemented, and a possible joint response by those countries to such a largescale departure. On Monday, the US Department of State released remarks from Secretary Mike Pompeo in which he said that the US is “taking a look at” increasing the number of arrivals it accepts from Hong Kong, an idea that was also supported by Senate leader Mitch McConnell. The government of Taiwan has also indicated that it is willing to resettle additional people from Hong Kong. Chinese and Hong Kong officials expressed displeasure at the new immigration moves by the UK, and the issue is likely to further exacerbate tensions between China and the UK. Those with interests in UK-Chinese relations are advised to remain abreast of developments.
