Headline: US Embassy Issued a Health Alert Regarding Rising COVID-19 Cases in Japan
Details:
On Friday, the US Embassy in Tokyo issued the following Health Alert:



“COVID-19 in Japan



The U.S. Embassy and consulates continue to monitor COVID-19 conditions in Japan.  Several prefectures, including Tokyo, Osaka, Hokkaido, Aichi, Kanagawa, and Chiba, recorded their highest number of new cases this week, and positive case numbers continue to rise across the country.  The Government of Japan warned that stringent restrictions on social and economic activities are now warranted in some parts of Hokkaido and that the situations in Tokyo, Osaka, and Aichi are growing close to that of Hokkaido.



In Tokyo, on November 19 Governor Koike raised the city’s COVID-19 alert to the highest level short of a state of emergency, indicating rapidly spreading infection.  In Hokkaido, media reports state that hospital capacity is becoming strained .  As infection rates continue to rise in Japan, U.S. citizens are strongly encouraged to monitor changes to prefectural government alert statuses, especially when considering travel across prefectures.



The Government of Japan has renewed calls for residents to wear masks and take other common-sense COVID-19 mitigation precautions.  In particular, both Prime Minister Suga and Governor Koike urge mask wearing while dining out in restaurants.  Diners should only remove their masks for short periods of time to eat or drink, and wear masks while having conversations.



In advance of the holiday season, Governor Koike identified “five keeps” people can follow to minimize COVID-19 exposure risk while dining out or in their homes:



Keep groups small

Keep meals short

Keep voices down

Keep portions separate

Keep rooms ventilated and disinfected

U.S. citizens are strongly urged to continue to take personal health measures to protect themselves, including socially distancing, wearing masks, and avoiding crowded areas with poor ventilation.  The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) strongly recommend that U.S. citizens get flu shots to prevent a major flu outbreak. Finally, U.S. citizens should continue to follow measures introduced by local and central government Japanese officials designed to mitigate COVID-19 outbreaks in their areas.



Travel Restrictions



Japanese government travel restrictions remain in place that prevent most U.S. citizens from entering the country.  Japan continues to modify its policies to facilitate certain kinds of travel.  Recently, the Government of Japan announced new regulations permitting residents of Japan to take short business trips abroad without requiring quarantine upon their return.  The rules governing this program are strict, and business travelers should be sure they understand the program before departing the country.  For complete information on travel restrictions, as well as requirements for reentry, please consult the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (https://www.mofa.go.jp/ca/cp/page22e_000925.html) or the Ministry of Justice (http://www.moj.go.jp/EN/nyuukokukanri/kouhou/m_nyuukokukanri01_00003.html).



Travel for tourism and most other short-term purposes is still not permitted, and there is no indication that this will change in the near term.



The U.S. Embassy strongly urges any U.S. citizens considering travel to Japan to review carefully the information available from the Government of Japan.  Please note these regulations are subject to change with little notice.  The U.S. Embassy’s ability to intervene on behalf of travelers denied boarding at their poing of embarkation or entry into Japan is extremely limited and those travelers denied entry at Japanese ports of entry will likely be immediately reboarded on flights back to the United States.



U.S. military members traveling under the Status of Forces Agreement should consult with their chain of command for the most current requirements pertaining to their entry as United States Forces Japan continues to enforce restrictions associated with a declared Public Health Emergency extended through the end of 2020.



Follow us on Twitter (https://twitter.com/acstokyo) and Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/ACSTokyo/).”



The full text of the alert can be viewed here: https://jp.usembassy.gov/health-alert-nov20-2020/

Keep groups small

Keep meals short

Keep voices down

Keep portions separate

Keep rooms ventilated and disinfected

Headline: Five Suspects Killed during Car Chase and Shootout in Reynosa on Sunday; Three Bystanders Wounded
Details:
On Sunday, a car chase and shootout erupted in Reynosa, located in Mexico s northeastern state of Tamaulipas. The city borders the U.S. state of Texas. Authorities received reports indicating that armed individuals were traveling in a pickup truck in the central neighborhood of La Ca ada. State police were dispatched to the area to investigate. When the criminals observed the police, they attempted to flee, and a high-speed pursuit ensued. The criminals eventually crashed in the central neighborhood of Las Fuentes, and the survivors then exchanged gunfire with police. Five suspects were killed and one was placed under arrest. Three innocent bystanders were wounded throughout the course of the incident. One victim was struck by two stray bullets, and two other people were injured in car accidents that occurred during the police chase. There were no injuries among law enforcement personnel. 
	 
	Assessment: Car chases and firefights continue to occur frequently throughout Reynosa and its environs. Multiple drug trafficking cartels remain entrenched in the city, and continue to vie for control over the lucrative smuggling corridors that pass through the region. Bands of criminals regularly engage in violent clashes with each other and with security forces. Such altercations can involve the use of assault rifles, machine guns, grenades, and other forms of explosives. Militant drug traffickers sometimes travel in large convoys, and occasionally erect barricades on roadways in order to inhibit the movement of security forces. Elements of the military are commonly mobilized to quell large clashes, but response times are often long. 
	 
	Due to the critically high level of cartel activity and violent crime observed in Reynosa, Resilience360 continues to advise customers to avoid all travel to the city. Travelers are advised to always practice strong situational awareness, and to be prepared to shelter in place. Firefights can potentially erupt anywhere and at any time of day, with little or no warning. Sunday s car chase and shootout once again highlight the risk that such confrontations can pose for innocent bystanders. All ongoing military/police activity should be avoided as much as possible due to the risk of stray gunfire. Motorists are advised to give military/police convoys a wide berth, as criminal groups have been known to engage security forces without regard for civilian casualties.

Headline: Increased frequency of strikes and protests by labour unions in South Korea...
Details: Risks: Labour strikes; Protests and riotsSectors or assets affected: Automotive manufacturing; Road and rail transportOn 13 November, South Korean Prime Minister Lee Nak-yeon publicly called for unionised workers to support Hyundai Motor's plan to open a new manufacturing plant in Gwangju Metropolitan City. The project envisions 12,000 new jobs, many at half the current workers' salary because of subsidies from the local authority and the plant manufacturing low-cost vehicles. Also on 13 November, GM Korea's second-largest shareholder, the Korea Development Bank, called for the firm to participate in three-way talks with its labour union about plans to spin-off its research arm, prompting fears that the manufacturing plants would close because of losses since 2014. Disagreements between the government, employers, and labour unions have persisted despite the reinvigoration of a forum for tripartite discussions and mediation: the Economic, Social and Labor Council (ESLC). South Korean President Moon Jae-in's administration remains focused on reducing unemployment (3.8% in 2018) and increasing real GDP growth (2.7%). However, it has failed to co-opt South Korea's influential unions, primarily the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) and the Federation of Korean Trade Unions (FKTU). In particular, in June, the National Assembly passed a bill revising the minimum wage act that the two umbrella unions argued would not meet demands for increased salaries, prompting them to boycott the ESLC.Significance: Strikes are likely to involve walk-outs and protests involving up to tens of thousands of people outside government buildings and firms' offices in the capital Seoul and manufacturing centres in the southeast, including Busan, Gwangju, and Ulsan. Although the risk of violence is low and would most probably take the form of union members fighting with security or harassing substitute workers, firms report KRW billions (USD millions) in annual losses because of strike action. The recent deteriorations in management-union relations indicate that strikes are now likely to last for weeks, rather than days. If the National Labor Relations Commission approves a Korea Railroad union strike scheduled around 20 November, this would indicate an increased risk of disruption to transport and operations, as with railway-workers and truckers' sympathy strikes in 2015. By contrast, if the unions, specifically the KCTU, agree to the official relaunch of the ESLC, this would be a positive indicator for negotiations to resolve pending disputes. Headline: Alleged Houthi Attack on Oil Tanker in Red Sea Highlights Threat to Maritime Security
Details:
Saudi Arabian officials confirmed that a mine exploded off the coast of Shuqaiq, Saudi Arabia, and damaged a Maltese-flagged oil tanker on Wednesday, November 25. Reportedly, the MT Agrari tanker, managed by a Greek private company, was struck approximately three feet above the waterline, which caused an explosion and subsequent fire in the Red Sea, near the Shuqaiq Steam Power Plant. Following the attack, Saudi Arabia claimed to successfully intercept and destroy the explosive-laden boat that perpetrated the attack. There were no immediate reports of any hazardous contents spilling into the water and no reports of any injuries. Although the Houthi rebels have not claimed the attack on November 25, the Saudi semi-official news outlet, al Arabiya, placed blame on the Shia militant group. 



Assessment: This incident highlights the threat posed to maritime security in the Red Sea and the nearby Bab al Mandeb Strait. As the mine explosion was likely purported by the Houthis, it also stands to exacerbate rising tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Shia rebels, amid recent missile and mine attacks in the Red Sea over the past few days. Yemen’s Houthi rebels previously claimed a missile attack on a Saudi Aramco plant in Jeddah on Monday, November 23, though Aramco stated that the attack did not affect oil production. Headline: US Embassy Issues Demonstration Alert
Details:
On Thursday, the United States Embassy in Cairo issued a Demonstration Alert for US citizens in Egypt. The message reads:

 Demonstration Alert: U.S. Embassy Cairo, Egypt (September 26, 2019)   
  
Location: Tahrir Square area, Cairo, Egypt 
 
Event: Noting press and social media calls for demonstrations on Friday, September 27, U.S. citizen visitors and residents are reminded to avoid areas of demonstrations or police activity.  Consult travel.state.gov for more information about safe international travel.     
 
Actions to Take:
-     Avoid the areas of the demonstrations.
-     Exercise caution if unexpectedly in the vicinity of large gatherings or protests.
-     Monitor local media for updates
-     Keep a low profile.
 
For Assistance:
-     U.S. Embassy Cairo, Egypt
      +20-2-2797-3300
      +20-2-2797-3300 (after hours)
      consularcairoacs@state.gov
-     State Department   Consular Affairs
      888-407-4747 or 202-501-4444
      Egypt Country Information  
-     Enroll in Safe Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates
-     Follow us on Facebook and Twitter 

Assessment: At the time of this writing, no further details, including the time and location of any specific demonstrations, had been announced. However, it is reasonable to expect that any gatherings that do materialize will occur in urban centers, including in Cairo, Alexandria, Giza, Damietta, Suez, Port Said, and El-Mahalla El-Kubra, each of which witnessed similar anti-government protests on September 20-21. Resilience360 urges clients in Egypt to avoid any demonstrations that crop up in the coming days to reduce the likelihood of becoming a victim of incidental violence, namely unruly crowd behavior and aggressive crowd control tactics by police. Various media outlets and rights groups have suggested that some 1,200 activists have been arrested in the wake of last week s protests, purportedly including some foreign tourists accused of taking part in and/or filming the demonstrations. Foreigners engaged in any sort of anti-government activities in Egypt may be subject to detention, and there have been reports of police officers stopping individuals in Cairo and checking social media content on their cell phones. There has also been speculation that security forces may exercise less restraint when dealing with future protests compared to last week, potentially including the use of deadly force. Finally, it has been reported that pro-Sisi elements could attempt to organize counter-protests on September 27, raising the specter of clashes between rival demonstrators.

Headline: Individual Motivated by a Personal Dispute Kills at Least Eight in Bus Hijacking in Fujian
Details:
On Tuesday, an individual motivated by a personal dispute hijacked a bus in the area of Denggao Middle Road in Xinluo District in the city of Longyan, Fujian Province. He stabbed a local official and a police officer prior to hijacking the bus, where he stabbed the driver and another officer on board. He drove the bus through 1,300 feet of busy downtown streets, striking pedestrians and vehicles. At least eight people in total were killed, while another 22 people were injured. The suspect was arrested by police shortly after the incident. 
 
	 
		Assessment: The suspect has been identified as a 48-year-old unemployed man who was a resident of Xinluo District. He was involved in a dispute with neighborhood committee officials regarding healthcare for his father and was visited by the committee earlier on Tuesday, which likely sparked the attack. Individuals in China that are involved in disputes with the local government or motivated by personal grudges or other issues have a tendency to carry out mass-casualty attacks using sharp weapons or vehicles. Other recent attacks include a September vehicle ramming attack that killed at least 11 people in Hunan s Hengyang District by a person wanting to take revenge on society, a vehicle ramming and knife attack in Zhejiang s Ningbo that killed three people by a person involved in a familial dispute, and a knife attack at a kindergarten in Chongqing s Banan District that injured 14 children by someone with a grievance against the government. The attack on Tuesday in Longyan does not represent a change in the security situation, and although the risk of being impacted by a mass-casualty attack is extremely low, caution should still be exercised in crowded areas.

Headline: New restrictions for Import of Waste and Scrap into Hong Kong
Details:
Industry sources reported upcoming regulatory changes for waste imports into Hong Kong. Authorities in China announced that:

•16 kinds of solid wastes (including Plastic scrap, compressed scrap automobile, metal and electrical appliance scraps, waste electric motors, waste wires, waste vessels, slag steel and mill scale) are now reclassified as Solid Wastes Forbidden to Import in Hong Kong, and a ban in imports will be imposed from December 31st, 2018. Other waste commodities will be similarly re-classified within a year.
•Import of permitted solid wastes are only allowed to limited customs entries and gateways from January 1st, 2019 onwards. 

Additionally in Hong Kong, new legislation will become effective on December 31st, 2018 to regulate the handling of e-waste, which currently encompasses all abandoned regulated electrical equipment, including air conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, television sets, computers, printers, scanners and monitors. 

The new legislation requires that any person who is engaged in the storage, treatment, reprocessing or recycling of e-waste must first obtain a waste disposal license under the Waste Disposal Ordinance (WDO), while any person who imports or exports e-waste must first obtain a permit. Furthermore, transshipment of e-waste via Hong Kong is prohibited and transit through Hong Kong requires prior consent from Hong Kong Environmental Protection Department.

Headline: Truckers' union announces strike in Sao Paulo state
Details: Local media sources indicate on November 28 that truckers organized by Sindicam Ourinhos have announced their intention to strike on November 29. The truckers, mostly in agricultural commodity shipping, have announced their grievance at lack of adherence by major firms such as Cutrale, Louis Dreyfus, and CitroSuco to the minimum freight table signed into law in August as part of a deal to end the May truckers’ strike. The table is due to expire on December 31, at the end of President Michel Temer’s term and the beginning of that of Jair Bolsonaro, a topic raised by truckers after an October 29 wildcat strike and discussions by the CNT truckers’ union of renewing strike activity nationally. A strike also has the possibility of mobilizing Sindicam Santos, involving blocked highways and impeding shipments to and from Brazil’s principal seaport of entry. Those shipping in Sao Paulo should anticipate a scenario similar to that of May 21 through 31 and should plan accordingly.

Headline: US Embassy Issued a Health Alert Regarding Rising COVID-19 Case Numbers in Japan and Other Measures
Details:
On Tuesday, the US Embassy in Tokyo issued the following Health Alert:



“COVID-19 in Japan



The U.S. Embassy and consulates continue to monitor closely COVID-19 conditions in Japan. Case numbers continue to rise throughout the country. Several areas, including Tokyo, are posting record or near-record numbers daily. Prefectural and local governments indicate that healthcare capacity, including critical care bed space and medical personnel staffing, is becoming strained. On December 17, Tokyo Governor Koike raised Tokyo’s health care alert system to its highest level for the first time since ending the state of emergency in May, indicating that the government task force believes hospitals could soon be overwhelmed. According to press reports, the Tokyo government is concerned that as many as 80 percent of the city’s hospitals and clinics will close during the New Year period, which will further constrain health care capacity.



The national government and many prefectural governments have begun announcing new COVID-19 mitigation measures. The national government announced that the “Go To Travel” campaign will be suspended from December 28 through January 11. Governor Koike continues to urge residents to minimize outings and reconsider traveling during the New Year period.



The U.S. Embassy strongly urges U.S. citizens throughout Japan to monitor changes to prefectural government alerts, especially when considering travel across prefectures. U.S. citizens should continue to follow all measures introduced by Japanese national and local government officials to mitigate COVID-19 outbreaks in their areas.



The Government of Japan has renewed calls for residents to wear masks and take other common-sense COVID-19 mitigation precautions. Residents should continue to avoid the “Three Cs:” closed spaces, crowded spaces, and close-contact settings.



U.S. citizens are strongly urged to continue to take personal health measures to protect themselves, including social distancing, wearing masks, and avoiding crowded areas with poor ventilation. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) strongly recommend that U.S. citizens get flu shots to prevent a major flu outbreak. To reduce the spread of infection, U.S. citizens should consider minimizing their travel over the upcoming New Year holiday period.



U.S. Mission Japan personnel continue to follow practices recommended by the U.S. and Japanese Governments, including social distancing and mask wearing, to prevent the spread of COVID-19. The United States Government does not plan to provide COVID-19 vaccinations to private U.S. citizens overseas. Please follow host country developments and guidelines for COVID-19 vaccination. According to media reporting, the Japanese Government intends to pursue expedited approval of vaccines. U.S. citizens in Japan should consult with their medical providers.



United States Forces Japan bases have instituted a number of restrictions based on local conditions. Many restrictions are specific to individual bases or areas. For more information, please contact base command officials.



The U.S. Congress passed a stimulus bill including an additional series of direct payments. The U.S. Embassy in Tokyo has no insight into the processing of these payments and cannot intervene with banks which decline to process paper checks. For information or assistance with these payments, please contact the Internal Revenue Service (https://www.irs.gov/).



Travel Restrictions



Japanese government travel restrictions remain in place that prevent most U.S. citizens from entering the country. Japan continues to modify its policies to facilitate certain kinds of travel. For complete information on travel restrictions, as well as requirements for reentry, please consult the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (https://www.mofa.go.jp/ca/cp/page22e_000925.html) or the Ministry of Justice (http://www.moj.go.jp/EN/nyuukokukanri/kouhou/m_nyuukokukanri01_00003.html).



Travel for tourism and most other short-term purposes is still not permitted, and there is no indication that this will change in the near term.



The U.S. Embassy strongly urges any U.S. citizens considering travel to Japan to carefully review the information available from the Government of Japan. Please note these regulations are subject to change with little notice. The U.S. Embassy’s ability to intervene on behalf of travelers denied boarding at their point of embarkation or denied entry upon arrival to Japan is extremely limited, and those travelers denied entry at Japanese ports of entry will likely be immediately reboarded on flights back to the United States.



U.S. military members traveling under the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) have different travel regulations governing their entry into Japan. They should check with their command before commencing any travel to ensure they comply with all necessary requirements. The U.S. Embassy and consulates cannot answer questions about SOFA travel.



Follow us on Twitter (https://twitter.com/acstokyo) and Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/ACSTokyo/).”



The full text of the alert can be viewed here: https://jp.usembassy.gov/health-alert-december-22-2020/

Headline: Authorities Threaten Violators of Social Distancing Rules with Caning
Details:
On Friday, media sources reported that authorities in the Philippines have threatened to cane individuals who violate social distancing rules during the Christmas season. According to officials, police officers and soldiers will patrol public areas with roughly three-foot-long sticks to measure distancing, and possibly to strike those who encroach on others. So-called high-traffic areas, including transport hubs and public markets, will reportedly be the focus of the patrols. As of December 4, the Philippines had recorded 436,345 positive COVID-19 infections and 8,509 deaths attributed to the virus.



Assessment: The policy reflects the Philippine government’s aggressive strategy to combat the spread of COVID-19. Between March and June, Manila enforced one of the world’s strictest and longest coronavirus lockdowns, and in the months since, authorities have warned and penalized some 700,000 people for violating social distancing rules and failing to wear masks. The latest order is likely aimed at preventing Christmas from serving as vector for further transmission of COVID-19 in the Philippines. The holiday season is one of the longest in the world, and while the government has prohibited Christmas gatherings due to the pandemic, crowds have reportedly begun flocking to malls and shopping centers.

Headline: Togo bans bulk carrier from unloading its cargo of 18 tons of rice
Details: Industry sources reported on March 20, 2019 that Togo banned the bulk carrier ""Ocean Princess"" from unloading its cargo of 18.000 tons rice. Before this decision of the Togolese authorities, the same measure had been taken by Guinea, which requested the return of the Burmese product to the supplier already on November 30, 2018 to the general manager of the company Huilerie de Guinée. The rice of dubious quality has taken the direction of Dakar for a few days. The vessel was in international waters after failing to land the product in neighboring countries. The ship has been actively monitored in international waters since its departure from the port of Lomé. On March 20 the bulkcarrier reached the Adidjan anchorage.

Headline: UPDATE: Workers in steel industry continue to strike on February 14
Details: Updated media sources on February 14 reported that steel workers with union IG Metall continue to hold warning strikes across northwestern Germany this week after negotiations on pay raises were unsuccessful two weeks ago. On February 14, token strikes occurred at ThyssenKrupp in Finnentrop. Earlier this week, strikes took place at Deutschen Edelstahlwerke in Siegen; Mannesmann in Zeithain and ArcelorMittal in Bremen and Eisenhuttenstadt. Last week, warning strikes were reported at ThyssenKrupp in Dortmund, Eichen und Ferndorf; Salzgitter in Ilsenburg and Peine; Arcelor Mittal in Duisburg; HKM in Hüttenheim; Sona BLW Präzisionsschmiede GmbH in Remscheid; Leistritz Turbinentechnik GmbH in Remscheid; Radio Frequency Systems and Nexans in Hanover; and Bosch in Salzgitter.

There are no casualties reported and all individuals were evacuated from the immediate vicinity. Further details regarding the incident are unavailable at this time.

Headline: Car carrier damaged in collision in Emden
Details: Industry sources reported on January 14, 2019, around 4 p.m that car carrier ""City of St. Petersburg"" allided with pilings of the sea lock in Emden upon its arrival from Grimsby. The ship was assisted by two tugs when it was caught by strong wind gusts and pushed against the pilings off the lock with its starboard side. Both the pilings and the hull of the vessel suffered damage. The ship was detained by the relevant authorities and was to be subject of a port state control on January 15.

Headline: Severe reefer shortage at Port of Xingang prompts carriers to suspend bookings via Port of Busan
Details: Shipping sources on December 4 report that severe reefer plug shortages remain at the Port of Xingang in Tianjin due to COVID-19 inspections before release, resulting in vessel berthing schedules being postponed. All related inbound operations as well as container pickup activities have reportedly been severely impacted. As a result, reefer plugs has been fully utilized. Reefer containers have also been diverted to alternative ports such as Qingdao and Dalian or were kept at the Port of Busan. Some shipping lines including MSC and CMA CGM have reportedly imposed congestion surcharges on reefer only, amounting to up to USD 1,500 per unit from November 18, depending on the carrier. Hapag-Lloyd has now announced that it would suspend the acceptance of fresh import reefers (temperature-controlled) bookings via the Port of Busan, Korea to Tianjin. Bookings with direct discharge in Tianjin remain accepted, however.

Headline: Chinese customs tighten clearance of Australian coal imports over environmental concerns
Details:
In recent weeks, international media sources reported that the Port of Dalian in the Northeast region of China has allegedly blocked Australian coal from clearing customs. The news sparked speculations and prompted most Chinese traders to stop ordering coal from the land down under. While some reports have cited safety and quality as the reasons for the customs delays, others suggested that diplomatic tensions between the two countries are likely to be a factor. As of this writing, there have been no official statement by Beijing or by the port’s authorities pertaining to the bilateral trade situation concerning Australian coal imports into China. Both governments dismissed allegations about a ban, though industry experts have noted that there appeared to be a noticeable prolonged inspection of Australian coal at the port’s customs.  

According to reports, the current clearance time for Australian coal is up to 40-days when it normally takes anywhere between 5 to 20 days. Currently, only coal imports to Dalian have been affected; other ports in China are accepting coal shipments from elsewhere, including Australia. Chinese authorities have confirmed that local customs officials have stepped up efforts to monitor the quality and safety of imported coals in recent years as they reportedly does not meet the environmental standards. While the lengthy inspection implies that Australian coal may have either dropped below the Chinese quality threshold or the standards have become higher, it is important to note that this is not the first time China has put brakes on accepting imported coal. Back in 2017, it restricted Indonesian coal imports for being high in impurities and low in energy efficiency. 

Although it remains unclear why the Port of Dalian is the only port with longer clearance time at the moment, precedents show that Chuanshon anchorage at Ningbo Port and Zhoushan LNG Import Terminal near Shanghai have also restricted coal imports in the past. Beijing’s effort to curb air pollution in the heavy industrial zone of the Northeast region comes as no surprise. China’s smog regulatory measures are evident that it is determined to control coal imports for environmental protection as well as to balance out an oversupply of coal in the local market. In November 2018, coal prices dropped one-third when China banned coal imports from around the world until early 2019 due to an oversupply of coal in the domestic market. 

With this backdrop, Dalian port authorities have set a cap of 12 million tons for the world’s coal imports for 2019 via its terminals, possibly to slow down the intake. This is a reduction from last year when it handled 14 million tons, with half of the amount being from Australia. Dalian customs accounted for 7 percent for China’s total coal imports, handling both thermal and coking coal in 2018.  

Nevertheless, the curb may have limited impact on China’s industrial operations as Chinese steel mills have reportedly built their coal stocks prior to the Lunar New Year. Despite the uncertainties, China continues to be Australia’s biggest trading partner with coal being the topmost exported item to China. Customers with an interest in Chinese industries relying on imported coal are advised to keep abreast of the latest regulatory measures at local ports.

Headline: Security for Sri Lankan President Sirisena Increased; Credibility of Assassination Plot Unclear
Details:
On Thursday, it was reported that security for Sri Lankan President Maithripala Sirisena was increased following reports of an assassination plot. The plot stems from a leaked telephone call from a senior police officer talking about the plot and the arrest of an Indian national in late September who was suspected to be involved. Media reports said that President Sirisena blamed India s Research and Analysis Wing (RAW) intelligence agency, but Sirisena has since denied those reports and said that he was misquoted. 
 
	 
		Assessment: The conflicting reports from both the media and government make it difficult to ascertain the actual threat posed to President Sirisena. The theory is that India was upset with President Sirisena for refusing to allow India to develop a port terminal next to the Chinese-run Colombo International Container Terminal. However, it seems highly unlikely that India would actually attempt to assassinate President Sirisena over the issue. Sirisena s denial of the reports that he attributed responsibility of the plot to India have lowered tensions between the two countries. However, if further evidence is released suggesting greater involvement by the Indian government, it could negatively impact bilateral diplomatic or economic ties.

Headline: India: Bank employees demonstrate in Chennai and New Delhi; potential for protest and strike action elsewhere
Details: A number of bank employees belonging to various associations are reportedly staging a protest in Chennai on 31 August. The action is to denounce a central government decision to merge ten public sector banks into four large entities, with fears of the closure of the six remaining banks. Members of the All India Bank Employees’ Association have additionally demonstrated in New Delhi, with a counter-demonstration also taking place. The ten public sector banks in question are: Allahabad Bank, Andhra Bank, Canara Bank, Corporation Bank, Indian Bank, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab National Bank, Syndicate Bank, Union Bank of India, and United Bank of India. Related protests are possible at their sites throughout the country, with the union additionally planning to meet in New Delhi on 11 September to decide whether to strike over the decision.

Headline: Cosatu and Saftu expected to protest in town and cities across the country
Details: South African sources are reporting that protests and strike action is expected to occur in towns and cities across the country today.  This is due to the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) and the SA Federation of Trade Unions (Saftu) demonstrating against state capture, corruption, and gender-based violence. A large crowd has gathered at Burgers Park in Pretoria, this will be followed by a motorcade leading the demonstrators to the National Treasury’s office on Church Street to hand over a memorandum. The protesters will then march to Francis Baard Street to hand over a memorandum to the Employment and Labour Department. In Johannesburg, the demonstration is expected to start at Cosatu House in Braamfontein and then march to the Chamber of Commerce. A protest has also been planned at the Transnet headquarters in Johannesburg. In Durban a crowd will gather at Curries Fountain Stadium and in Cape Town at the Langa Multi-Purpose Sport Centre, followed by a motorcade along the N2 to the City of Cape Town office in the CBD and then to the parliament buildings. In other regions demonstrators are expected to march to their respective municipal and district council offices. Cosatu and Saftu have stated that they intend to cause as much disruption as possible through these demonstrations.

Headline: Gun-related attacks on foreign exchange bureau staff show violent crime...
Details: Risks: Criminal violence; Death and injury risksSectors or assets affected: All sectors Two workers at the Banco de Credito del Peru (BCP) exchange bureau house were shot and injured on 31 October on Avenida 28 Julio in the Peruvian capital's Lima Miraflores district. The workers were part of staff conducting exchanges of foreign currency outside the BCP to drive-by customers and pedestrians. The workers were shot when they refused to hand over currency to four individuals on two motorcycles. This followed a similar armed robbery by two men on a motorcycle who shot a BBVA Continental Bank bureau exchange worker on 20 October in Lima's Barranco municipality. Separately, a man previously convicted for drug trafficking (but later released) was shot dead at a spa located on Miguel Dasso Street in Lima's San Isidro district. Miraflores, Barranco, and San Isidro are very popular with tourists and are some of Lima's less dangerous areas where expatriates work and live. Public shootouts between rival gangs and/or with police are not especially common in Lima, but do occur at least twice per week in crime hotspots. In the Comas district in March, for example, a gang fight at a public intersection led to three bystanders being shot or run over, two police officers injured, and a suspected gang member killed. Hotspots in Lima include El Callao, Comas, El Agustino, Independencia, La Victoria, Los Olivos, San Juan de Lurigancho, and San Martin de Porres.Significance: This shooting, along with similar incidents that have been monitored by IHS Markit sources, underlines that gun-related violence is likely to more frequently spread to Miraflores, Barranco, San Isidro, and other financial and tourist districts of Lima. This is likely to be driven by greater proliferation of firearms linked to drug trafficking through El Callao port in the one-year outlook and as gangs increase their capabilities and expand operations to more lucrative areas of Lima. Indicators of increasing violent crime are evidence of a large proportion of drugs being exchanged for weapons, as well as incidents involving more strategic targets, including jewellers, banks, and shopping centres, which require co-ordinated operations and the use of surveillance and intelligence-gathering techniques. Headline: Houston Ship Channel - Channel has partially reopened to ship traffic. Incident closed.
Details: Channel traffic has partially reopened from Tucker Bayou to Houston Ship Channel Light 116, as cleanup efforts continue related to pollutant runoff from the ITC facility fire. The runoff has been exacerbated by the partial collapse of a dike wall that took place on Friday, March 22 near the ITC facility. The dike wall has since been repaired. Updated sources indicate that the waterway may be reopened on Monday, March 25. Authorities are conducting cleanup operations and there appears to be no active health hazard. Ships are being able to traverse the channel if they have less than a 34-foot draft. All vessels are required to be inspected for chemical contaminates and are being spaced at approximately one-hour intervals. This incident is closed.

Headline: UPDATE 26 - Northern Laos- Vamco dissipated in Laos; 69 dead in Philippines, 19 injured in Vietnam. Event closed
Details:
Tropical Depression Vamco, known as Ulysses in the Philippines, has dissipated over northern Laos after it made landfall in Vietnam approximately 17 miles north of Dong Hoi on Sunday, November 15. 

In Vietnam, Vamco injured at least 19 people, destroyed six houses, and damaged another 5,755 houses. At least 17 boats sank in harbors along the coast. As Typhoon Vamco approached the coastline, authorities in six Vietnamese provinces (Quang Binh, Quang Tri, Thua Thien Hue, Da Nang, Quang Nam, and Quang Ngai) evacuated approximately 468,000 people.

In the Philippines, at least 69 people have been killed, 52 others injured, and 12 others remain missing following storm-related incidents in the Philippines. The Philippine Coast Guard reported around 2,000 passengers, drivers, and cargo helpers were stranded in ports in the Bicol Region, Eastern Visayas, Southern Tagalog, and the National Capital Region (NCR) due to Typhoon Vamco/Ulysses. Widespread flooding has been reported, as the Philippines remains inundated from a series of typhoons over October and November. The greater Manila area was heavily impacted. This event is closed.

Headline: 362 miles SE of Ho Chi Minh City - Storm Krovanh likely to devolve further. Event closed. - UPDATE 6
Details:
Storm Krovanh, known as Tropical Depression Vicky in the Philippines, was located in the South China Sea, approximately 362 miles southeast of Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, as of 2:00 AM local time on December 21. The storm is moving west-southwest at seven miles per hour with maximum sustained winds of 30 miles per hour and gusts reaching 40 miles per hour. The storm is forecast to devolve into a low-pressure area by Wednesday, December 23. Rough seas and strong winds should be expected in parts of the South China Sea in the next 48 hours, while heavy precipitation is forecast in southern Vietnam starting Tuesday, December 22. The storm previously caused widespread flooding and landslides in the Philippines, killing at least seven people, injuring one, and leaving at least four missing. Several thousand people were evacuated in multiple regions of the Philippines and at least 83 structures were damaged.

Previously, Tropical Storm Risk had issued a Yellow Alert for Vietnam, as well as Phan Rang, Nha Trang, Phan Thiet, and Tuy Hoa. A Yellow Alert indicates there is a 10–30 percent probability that a storm will result in maximum sustained winds of at least Category 1 strength, or greater than 50 percent probability that it will result in maximum sustained winds of at least tropical storm strength. This event is closed.

Headline: Severe Storms Thursday Night Lead to at Least One Death, SOE for 11 Counties in Upstate NY
Details:
On Friday, November 1, Governor Andrew Cuomo declared a state of emergency (SOE) for 11 counties in Upstate New York following widespread severe weather on Thursday night. The storms brought heavy rainfall and high winds which caused flooding and damage across the region. At least one death in Herkimer County was blamed on the flooding. An unknown number of structures across the region suffered damage in the storm, mainly from downed trees and debris caused by the high winds. Areas along the banks of Lake Erie saw significant flooding with Buffalo reporting a seven-foot rise in water levels in just several hours. Widespread power outages and numerous road closures were also reported across the region. There were no reports of widespread evacuations in relation to the storms and subsequent flooding. The state of emergency declaration included the following counties: Cayuga, Chautauqua, Dutchess, Erie, Essex, Hamilton, Herkimer, Montgomery, Oneida, Saratoga, and Warren. 

Assessment: The state of emergency declaration activated the State Emergency Operations Center to help with recovery and rebuilding efforts. In addition, at least 200 members of the state National Guard were activated to assist with cleanup and response operations. The high winds from the storm, upwards of 60 miles per hour for some areas, caused power outages to at least 241,000 utility customers at the storm's peak. As of this writing, the majority of customers have had power restored. At least 60 road closures were reported across the region, though these were mostly local roads and not major highways. An unknown number of roads suffered significant damage and will take multiple days or weeks to be repaired. Flooding has largely receded; however, rain has been forecast beginning Monday night. As of this writing, a Flood Warning remains in effect for Warren County until Wednesday, November 6 at 10:00 AM EST. Customers are advised to use caution in affected due to storm debris and the possibility of damaged roads. Heed all instructions from local authorities.

Headline: San Jacinto River re-opened intermittently after Deer Park petrochemical spill

About 60,000 gallons of oil product have been recovered from the water as of March 24.

Headline: U.S. Embassy Issues a Weather Alert regarding Typhoon Trami s Expected Impact across Japan
Details:
On Thursday, the U.S. Embassy issued the following Weather Alert:   Location:  Okinawa Prefecture (September 28-29, 2018), continuing through Kyushu, Honshu, and Hokkaido (September 29   October 1). 
 
	 Event:  Typhoon Trami (Typhoon No. 24) is expected to affect areas of Okinawa Prefecture and Amami Oshima Island in Kagoshima Prefecture beginning early Friday, September 28 through late Saturday, September 29. The storm is then expected to track northeast, affecting large portions of Kyushu, Honshu, and Hokkaido from September 29 through October 1. According to current tracking, Typhoon Trami will impact major population centers, including Naha, Fukuoka, Osaka, Kyoto, and Tokyo. The typhoon will bring extremely high winds, dangerous storm tides, heavy rainfall, and possible flooding. 
 
	Any closures of Mission Japan facilities will be communicated via Twitter and the Embassy website. 
 
	 Actions to Take:  
 
	 
		Avoid travel to affected areas until the storm has dissipated. 
	 
		All U.S. citizens living in or traveling to the area should monitor local weather reports, follow directions from local officials, and take other appropriate actions as needed. 
	 
		Seek secure shelter as appropriate. 
	 
		The Japan Meteorological Service s Typhoon tracking information may be found in English at this webpage:  http://www.jma.go.jp/en/typh/ . Information about the latest typhoon is also available from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center at  https://metoc.ndbc.noaa.gov/jtwc .  
 
 
	 
		The full message can also be viewed here:  https://jp.usembassy.gov/weather-alert-typhoon24/ . 
	 
		Assessment: The high winds and heavy rains may result in widespread air, sea, and ground transportation disruptions as the storm hits Japan. It is likely that if the storm passes over Japan as a category 1-3 storm as expected, there will be railway suspensions, port closures, and flight delays. Factories may also be closed or shipments delayed, impacting associated supply chains. Local officials are also likely to issue evacuation advisories and instructions, which should be followed by travelers and local residents. The speed of the storm, which is expected to pass over the entirety of Japan in less than 48 hours, will help mitigate its impact, although trailing rain clouds could result in flooding and pose a prolonged threat. Resilience360 customers are advised to closely monitor local weather reports over the next week and expect potential weather-related disruptions.

As the projected path has shifted farther south, there is a potential that coastal areas of Georgia, including Savannah, will be impacted by the storm. Resilience360 advises clients to continue to monitor the hurricane's path closely as new forecasts are released frequently. Comply with official guidance, including evacuation orders.

Headline: Backlash Following Arrest of Opposition Leader Underscores Domestic Tensions
Details:
On Tuesday, October 20, Pakistan’s Army Chief Gen Qamar Javed Bajwa ordered an immediate inquiry into the “Karachi incident”, likely referring to the circumstances surrounding the arrest of Pakistan Muslim League- Nawaz (PML-N) leader, Captain Mohammad Safdar, in Karachi on October 19. Headline: Oil Spill Reported near Karachi Coast
Details:
Pakistani media sources report that an oil spill has occurred off the coast of Karachi. Local fishermen reported a large oil slick near Churna Island on October 24. In the days since, the slick has spread as far as the village of Mubbarak and Sandpit Beach. While the source of the spill remains under investigation, one media outlet has suggested it was from an underground pipeline. According to reports, parts of the slick have become a semi-solid tar, which indicates that the oil was several days old. 
 
	Assessment: Reports indicate that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in Balochistan province has ordered Byco Petroleum Pakistan Limited (BPPL) to suspend its operations due to the spill. However, it was not immediately clear if one of the firm s pipelines was responsible for the leak. Meanwhile, although the impact of the spill on the local ecosystem and marine life has yet to be determined, local wildlife authorities have indicated that several animals have died from the oil, including crabs, fish, eels, and a sea turtle.

Headline: More Than a Ton of Cocaine and Nearly $200,000 Seized in Hamburg
Details:
Police on Thursday intercepted a truck carrying a large quantity of cocaine at an unspecified shipping company in Hamburg. As officers watched, suspects unloaded one ton of cocaine from the truck. Upon the arrival of special forces officers, police moved in and arrested five suspects and seized the drugs. Subsequent searches of other locations in the city led to three further arrests. In addition to the cocaine, police seized roughly US $194,000 and two pounds of marijuana. Authorities were continuing to unload the truck on Friday, and expected to recover additional cocaine from on board. 
 
	Assessment: Of the eight suspects arrested, at least four were Germans, along with one Italian, one Pole, and two of unspecified nationality. One of the Germans, an unidentified 39-year-old male, was reported by police to be a senior member of the Hells Angels motorcycle gang, and is believed to be the suspects  primary contact with drug smugglers. The investigation leading to the searches and arrests had run for several months. Police offered no details on where the cocaine had originated, but the seizure follows on Monday s announcement by customs authorities that they had seized 441 pounds of cocaine in Hamburg on November 1. That shipment, concealed in packages of coffee coming from Brazil, was discovered by the company that received the coffee and reported to customs officials. Hamburg is a popular narcotics trafficking point, with around 4.5 tons of cocaine intercepted in the city throughout 2017. Resilience360 customers are advised of the possibility of additional searches and police operations in the vicinity of shipping facilities.

Headline: UPDATE 5 - United States – Strikes have subsided. Event closed.
Details:
New Updates: 

Strikes have largely subsided, although some residual disruptions may remain. This event is closed.

Previous Updates: 
On Tuesday, May 26, 22 employees of the Telegraph Ave McDonald’s location in Oakland went on strike following at least four workers and their family members tested positive for COVID-19, effectively closing the restaurant. The striking workers are demanding a two-week paid quarantine period, company-paid medical costs, and a deep cleaning of the store, plus proper personal protective equipment. Media sources are reporting that cooks, cashiers, and other workers were told to wear face masks made out of unused dog diapers or use coffee filters to make masks when they ran out of masks handed out by management.

Media sources report that hundreds of McDonald's employees in approximately 20 cities plan to strike on Wednesday, May 20 to protest the inadequate protections for workers during the COVID-19 outbreak. This strike will occur a day prior to McDonald's annual shareholders meeting. The strike has been organized by the 'Fight for $15' minimum-wage labor campaign and it is supported by the Service Employees International Union.

Media sources report strikes at seven fruit processing facilities in the Yakima Valley, Washington State. Hundreds of workers have staged walkouts and protests at the Columbia Reach, Hansen Fruit and Cold Storage Company, Frosty Packing and Roche, Matson Fruit Company, and Monson Fruit Company plants. The workers are demanding hazard pay and improved workplace protections against COVID-19. At least six further strikes are planned for the weekend of May 16. 

Demonstrations involving nurses and hospital staff workers have been reported at Saint Louis University Hospital in St Louis, Missouri, Saint Mary’s Regional Center in Reno, Nevada, as well as in front of the White House in Washington DC. The demonstrations have been called in response to current working conditions amid the COVID-19 pandemic as to demand better personal protective equipment, hazard pay, and paid sick time. The demonstration in Washington DC was organized to also commemorate the hospital workers that have lost their lives during the pandemic. 

Thousands of nursing home workers in Illinois belonging to the Service Employees International Union had planned to walk off the job on May 8 to protest alleged unsafe working conditions during the COVID-19 crisis. Updated sources report that a deal has been made between the union and nursing home owners, therefore averting the strike. Workers had requested more personal protective equipment, hazard pay, more stringent safety measures, and more transparency on confirmed cases of the virus within the workplace. The Service Employees International Union represents more than 10,000 workers at 100 nursing homes, most in the Chicago area.

Approximately 20 workers at Columbia Farms chicken plant in West Columbia, South Carolina walked off the job on May 6 in protest of working conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic including an alleged lack of adequate pay, lack of social distancing requirements, and worker mistreatment.

Demonstrations took place across the country on May 1, also called May Day or International Worker's Day, to protest several issues. Employees of Amazon, Whole Foods, Instacart, Walmart, FedEx, Target, and Shipt embarked on a series of strikes, protests, and sick-outs to bring attention to how the companies have allegedly failed to provide basic protections against COVID-19. Additionally, residents in several states demonstrated against stay-at-home measures and other restrictions in response to COVID-19. While some protests included thousands of participants, no major disruptions were reported.

Hundreds of tech and fulfillment Amazon employees participated in a sickout on Friday, April 24, in the United States to protest alleged unsafe and unethical working conditions and Amazon’s handling of facilities with confirmed positive COVID-19 cases. The action began on Tuesday, April 21, and employees are calling for the protest to last indefinitely until Amazon meets their demands. 

Workers who deliver groceries for the Shipt app company called for a nationwide strike beginning on Tuesday, April 7. They also called for a boycott of the app on Friday, April 10. Workers are asking for additional safety precautions at no cost to workers, such as masks and gloves, hazard pay equaling an additional $5 per order, and changes to pay. It remains unclear how many of the workers are participating in the strike. The strike is intended to remain in place indefinitely until demands are met.

Instacart workers, a grocery delivery service, with the Gig Workers Collective, began a nationwide strike on Monday, March 30. Workers have stated that they will refuse to accept orders unless their demands regarding COVID-19 are met. These include additional safety precautions at no cost to workers such as hand sanitizer and disinfectant wipes, hazard pay equaling an additional $5 per order, and an extension beyond April 8 for qualification and expansion of pay for workers impacted by COVID-19 including those with known risk factors and/or those workers required to self-quarantine.

Workers at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Staten Island, NY walked off the job on Monday, March 30, and Monday, April 6, due to what they say is an inadequate job by Amazon to respond and inform employees about the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak. Employees at the Staten Island facility have alleged that there have been more COVID-19 cases there then reported and are asking the facility to be shut down for two weeks and deep cleaned. There are reports of participation at other Amazon warehouses, including in Chicago, though further plans remain unclear.

Employees at Whole Foods, a subsidiary of Amazon, held a sickout protest and refused to work on Tuesday, March 31. Similar to the Instacart strike, workers are demanding that Whole Foods provide paid leave for all workers who stay home or self-quarantine due to COVID-19, provide free COVID-19 testing for all employees, and give employees who work during the ongoing outbreak hazard pay of double the current hourly wage.

Headline: Growing Opposition Movement Calls for Demonstrations Later This Month
Details:
A meeting has been called for October 2 by the 12-party alliance of opposition parties in Pakistan, known as the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM), with the aim of scheduling rallies and protests against the government of Prime Minister Imran Khan, whose Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party was voted into power in a disputed 2018 election. The meeting will be held virtually and will reportedly also appoint key officials of the PDM. The PDM’s next meeting is expected to be held on October 5. The first rally is expected on October 11 in Quetta as part of the PDM’s strategy to oust the PTI-led government. 



Assessment: The PDM reportedly intends to launch a countrywide protest movement following the Quetta rally focusing on denouncing perceived government corruption, rising inflation, unemployment, and deteriorating living conditions in the country. In addition to these grievances, the opposition movement seems to be fueled by the arrest of several senior members of Pakistan’s political elite. Indeed, on September 28, Shehbaz Sharif, the leader of the opposition Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), was arrested on corruption charges in Lahore. Protests against the arrest of Shehbaz Sharif are expected on October 3 in Lahore and October 9 in the rest of Punjab. Shehbaz Sharif was previously arrested in October 2018 in a separate corruption case while he was chief minister of the Punjab Province. His older brother, Nawaz Sharif, who previously held the position of Prime Minister three times, was forced to resign in July 2017 after the country’s Supreme Court ruled that he had lied on a parliamentary wealth declaration. He was later convicted in two corruption cases. Nawaz left the country for London on medical bail last November but has not returned since. Several other senior members of the PML-N party have been arrested during Khan’s premiership, and this strategy has been criticized by opponents as merely an avenue to strike down political resistance. Protests against Khan’s administration were also reported in November 2019, demanding his resignation, though the movement fizzled out and no major reforms were realized. The current movement has been described as being a “three-phased” plan, including countrywide public meetings, protest demonstrations and rallies in November and December, and a “decisive long march” towards Islamabad in January 2021. Heightened security is likely in Quetta in anticipation of the October 11 demonstrations including increased number of police officers, movement restrictions, and roadblocks.

Headline: Further Protests Possible After Greenpeace Ship Blocked Coal Terminal at Gdansk Port Monday
Details:
On Monday night, a special unit of border guard officers boarded Greenpeace s Rainbow Warrior ship after it had anchored at the Gdansk port s coal terminal, blocking access for a ship delivering coal from Mozambique. Activists had painted  stop coal  on the side of the ship from Mozambique before the raid on the Rainbow Warrior. A group of border officers broke windows to gain entry to the ship cabins and directed a group of activists inside to lie down. The border guard said 22 activists were involved in the obstruction protest Monday, including 18 on the Rainbow Warrior and four on pontoon vessels. No injuries were reported, though activists criticized the level of force used to board and take control of the ship. The Rainbow Warrior captain and another activist were detained while the rest were released. Authorities towed the Rainbow Warrior out of the Gdansk port on Tuesday morning.

Assessment: The environmental protest did not cause long-term disruptions for port operations, though the action underscores the potential for focused protest activity to disrupt targeted operations temporarily. Greenpeace called for climate protection and a shift away from coal as an energy source for both Poland and the European Union more broadly. Activists contend that a quarter of coal burned in Poland is imported, including from countries such as Russia, the United States, Mozambique, Australia, and Colombia. While no specific further actions are known at this time, environmental activists are likely to conduct additional activities in Poland to draw attention to grievances. Resilience360 customers are advised to exercise caution near all protests and to anticipate potential operational and supply chain disruptions from any actions targeting industrial and/or logistical operations.

Furthermore, over 30 people were rescued from floodwaters at HiddenNite Family Campground in Alexander County. There are no waterways in major flood stage and one waterway, the Neue River in Kingston, in moderate flood stage. An unspecified number of structures were also damaged throughout the region. This event is closed.

Headline: Protests over Alleged Police Brutality Continue across Nigeria Despite Bans and Threats from Army
Details:
Over the last few days, protests have continued across Nigeria over alleged police brutality. In Lagos, demonstrators have continued to block roads, notably near the Lekki toll gate, and there were reports that unidentified thugs armed with knives, cutlasses, and guns attacked protesters in the Alausa area on Thursday. In Abuja, demonstrators marched to the gates of parliament on Thursday, defying a ban on protests. In Benin City in Edo State, demonstrators stormed the state house of assembly on Friday and clashed with armed thugs, resulting in two deaths. Additional protests have been reported in around 100 cities, including Port Harcourt, Calabar, Asaba, and Uyo. Amnesty International has reported that at least ten people have been killed in clashes with security forces since the protests began last week.



Assessment: The continuation of the protests, despite the disbandment of the controversial Special Anti Robbery Squad (SARS) police unit and promises by police to refrain from using force, suggest that demonstrators remain unswayed by the government’s concessions and may be broadening their demands. It also suggests that they likely have momentum on their side and that the protests are likely to continue over the coming days. Furthermore, the recent attacks on demonstrators risk further heightening tensions and sparking additional clashes and violence. Although the perpetrators of the attacks remain unidentified, activists claim they were carried out by thugs hired by police, further fueling allegations of repression by government forces. Conversely, the Nigerian Army issued a statement on Wednesday evening following the first attacks claiming it is prepared to “fully support” authorities in maintaining law and order. This could be perceived as a threat and suggests that the military is willing to step in if the protests continue to escalate. The public is advised to exercise an elevated level of vigilance, particularly near government buildings, police stations, and other potential protest locations, and is reminded to avoid all protest-related activities and large crowds due to the risk of violence.

Headline: Unknown Seeds Received by Americans from China Likely Part of an Online Shopping Scam
Details:
On Tuesday, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) reported that it had gotten reports of people across the country receiving unsolicited seeds, mostly from China, although a smaller number have reportedly come from Uzbekistan. Thousands of people have received seeds, including residents in at least Alabama, California, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, and Wyoming. Some of the packages have had exteriors indicating that they contain jewelry, toys, or electronic devices. Some of the recipients had ordered jewelry online, and in at least some cases they received seeds along with the jewelry. Other recipients have reported getting seeds along with other small items. At least some of the envelopes that have been received have contained Chinese characters, although the Chinese foreign ministry has alleged that address labels on the envelopes appear to be fake and has requested to investigate the packages itself. The USDA is investigating the situation with US Customs and Border Patrol and state agencies.



Assessment: According to the USDA, at this time there is no reason to believe that the seeds are related to anything other than a “brushing” scam, in which unscrupulous online sellers send unsolicited items to people before posting positive, fake reviews for the items. This type of scam has reportedly utilized seeds before. It is possible that seeds might be mislabeled during shipping in order to evade the more intense scrutiny applied to imported plants or seeds, but that seems unlikely to be the objective here, given that they have been addressed to people with no knowledge of them. Regardless of the origin of the seeds, there is a potential danger to crops or animals from what could be invasive species. Officials are still examining many of the seeds, but some have been determined to be Chinese water lilies or citrus. Examinations are also focusing on whether they contain pesticides or other chemicals. Authorities have urged recipients not to plant unknown seeds, nor to throw them away, but to contact state plant officials instead.

Industry sources have suggested that the episode could revive maritime threats in the region following a recent lull. At the time of this writing, responsibility for the purported attack remained unclaimed. This incident is closed.

Headline: US Official Alleged That Hezbollah Has Had Caches of Ammonium Nitrate in Several European Countries
Details:
The United States Coordinator for Counterterrorism, Nathan Sales, stated during a conference on Thursday, September 17, that Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah had arranged multiple caches of ammonium nitrate around Europe, and has used European routes to transport this material. The substance was purportedly being transported disguised as cold packs within first aid kits. Sales alleged that transport of ammonium nitrate through Europe was facilitated until at least 2018, with some stores of the material remaining in place at unknown locations, while others have been destroyed by authorities. The countries mentioned reportedly include Belgium, Spain, and Switzerland as transit routes, and France, Greece, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom as storage locations. The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to these claims the next day, stating that such activity has not been confirmed within the country, and that illegal activity committed by foreign organizations on French territory would be dealt with by local authorities with “the greatest firmness”. During the conference, Sales also urged European leaders to impose bans on all Hezbollah organizations, including the political wing, which several European governments, such as Belgium, Italy, Greece, France, Spain, and Switzerland, have not designated as a terrorist organization. Both the militant and political wings of Hezbollah have been designated as terrorist organizations by the US, the UK, and Germany. 



Assessment: In past years, several raids have been conducted in response to reports of ammonium nitrate being stored by Hezbollah across Europe. A warehouse that was raided in Cyprus in 2015 was found to have housed more than eight tons of ammonium nitrate. The same year, an operation involving raids of four safe houses in London uncovered approximately three tons of the substance. Links between the compound and Hezbollah operatives include the fact that the explosive charge used in the 2012 suicide bombing at Burgas Airport in Bulgaria, which killed six and injured 32, contained ammonium nitrate. Aside from the alleged storage of compounds with applications as explosives, Hezbollah’s presence in Europe also includes human operatives, as well as a financial network. While designating the political wing of the organization as a terrorist organization could create restrictions to its operations in Europe, there have been allegations that some European governments, such as France, have not given such a designation in order to protect nationals and key business connections based in Lebanon. However, countries that have banned the entirety of Hezbollah continue to see organizational activity within their borders. The number of Hezbollah recruits in Germany has reportedly been increasing in recent years. Following the August 4 explosion at the Port of Beirut, caused by a large amount of ammonium nitrate, there may be enhanced focus by security authorities on the identification of caches of this specific compound. While no specific, credible threat is known at this time, it is advised to continue to monitor developments, including any possible future raids on facilities suspected of storing potentially dangerous substances and any developments related to Hezbollah’s classification by European governments.

The substance was purportedly being transported disguised as cold packs within first aid kits. Sales alleged that transport of ammonium nitrate through Europe was facilitated until at least 2018, with some stores of the material remaining in place at unknown locations, while others have been destroyed by authorities. The countries mentioned reportedly include Belgium, Spain, and Switzerland as transit routes, and France, Greece, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom as storage locations. The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded to these claims the next day, stating that such activity has not been confirmed within the country, and that illegal activity committed by foreign organizations on French territory would be dealt with by local authorities with “the greatest firmness”. During the conference, Sales also urged European leaders to impose bans on all Hezbollah organizations, including the political wing, which several European governments, such as Belgium, Italy, Greece, France, Spain, and Switzerland, have not designated as a terrorist organization. Both the militant and political wings of Hezbollah have been designated as terrorist organizations by the US, the UK, and Germany. 



Assessment: In past years, several raids have been conducted in response to reports of ammonium nitrate being stored by Hezbollah across Europe. A warehouse that was raided in Cyprus in 2015 was found to have housed more than eight tons of ammonium nitrate. The same year, an operation involving raids of four safe houses in London uncovered approximately three tons of the substance. Links between the compound and Hezbollah operatives include the fact that the explosive charge used in the 2012 suicide bombing at Burgas Airport in Bulgaria, which killed six and injured 32, contained ammonium nitrate. Aside from the alleged storage of compounds with applications as explosives, Hezbollah’s presence in Europe also includes human operatives, as well as a financial network. While designating the political wing of the organization as a terrorist organization could create restrictions to its operations in Europe, there have been allegations that some European governments, such as France, have not given such a designation in order to protect nationals and key business connections based in Lebanon. However, countries that have banned the entirety of Hezbollah continue to see organizational activity within their borders. The number of Hezbollah recruits in Germany has reportedly been increasing in recent years. Following the August 4 explosion at the Port of Beirut, caused by a large amount of ammonium nitrate, there may be enhanced focus by security authorities on the identification of caches of this specific compound. While no specific, credible threat is known at this time, it is advised to continue to monitor developments, including any possible future raids on facilities suspected of storing potentially dangerous substances and any developments related to Hezbollah’s classification by European governments.

Headline: Nationwide Juneteenth Actions Planned in Relation to Ongoing Use of Force Protests
Details:
Widespread protest activity is expected across the United States in relation to the upcoming Juneteenth holiday on Friday, June 19. Juneteenth commemorates the full emancipation of slaves in 1865. Generally, the holiday is celebrated with parades and celebrations; however, with ongoing use-of-force protests across the United States, many activists are using the holiday for additional protests both about police use of force, as well as racial inequality. Major actions are planned in a number of cities including Tulsa, OK; Washington, DC: Los Angeles, CA; New York, NY; Seattle, WA; and Chicago, IL, among others. In addition to the expected protest activity, dockworkers with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) have planned a solidarity strike for Friday at 29 ports along the West Coast. 



Assessment: While widespread protests are likely in relation to Juneteenth, these protests are expected to have a more celebratory tone than what has occurred during use-of-force protests over the last three weeks. Many of the planned actions on Friday have been described as “block party” type events with performances like singing and dancing, rather than just protest marches. However, marches are likely to still occur and several localities, including Washington DC, have called for Juneteenth protests with intentions to block major roads and interstates. The protest action planned in Tulsa also presents a chance for escalation due to a planned rally by President Trump in the city on Saturday. The rally had been initially scheduled to be held on Friday but was pushed back following widespread public outcry. As such, the tensions at the Tulsa action are likely to be heightened and could potentially lead to clashes. Road closures are likely to be the main disruption from the Juneteenth actions; however, escalation of protest activity cannot be ruled out. The public is advised to anticipate associated disruptions and avoid protest activity due to the potential for incidental violence, such as unruly crowd behavior and/or the use of crowd control measures by law enforcement.

Headline: Malaysia Detained Crew After Greek Ship Collided with Malaysian Vessel near Johor Baru Port
Details:
On Saturday, a Greece-registered ship collided with the Malaysia-registered Polaris, a vessel that lays buoys, near Johor Baru Port in waters claimed by Singapore. The collision occurred while the Greek ship was headed to Tanjung Pelepas in Malaysia. There were no reports of any oil leaks or injuries associated with the collision, or any impacts to maritime shipping. The crew of the Greek ship was detained by the Malaysian Marine Department (Mardep) after the collision. Following the incident, Singapore called on Malaysia to withdraw its ships from Singapore s waters. 
 
	Assessment: Saturday s incident highlights the disputes over airspace and sea territory between Malaysia and Singapore that began last year. In 2018, the Malaysian government extended its port limits into Johor, and Malaysian vessels started entering waters that are claimed by Singapore. Singapore disputed the port limit extension, and its foreign minister has called on Malaysia to comply with international law. Bilateral talks held last month between the nations proved unsuccessful. The ongoing territorial dispute can cause confusion for vessels entering the Johor area, and increase the risk of safety hazards such as collisions. Although the likelihood of direct conflict between Singapore and Malaysia is low, Resilience360 customers are advised to exercise caution if travelling in the Johor area.

Headline: Increasing Chinese investment likely to help diversify Bruneian economy and...
Details: Risks: Policy instability; Interstate warSectors or assets affected: Oil and gas; InfrastructureOn 19 November, Chinese President Xi Jinping made his first official visit to Brunei. Xi and Bruneian Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah issued a joint statement following the meeting saying that Brunei would encourage more Chinese investment, particularly via the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Chinese investment in Brunei is focused on infrastructure and energy projects, including a petrochemical complex on Muara Besar island and a bridge connecting the island to the capital. Importantly, the two countries also agreed to jointly explore oil and gas resources along Borneo island in the South China Sea (SCS), which both countries claim to have sovereignty over.Significance: Brunei is highly likely seeking increased Chinese investment to diversify its economy: the country relies heavily on oil and gas, which reportedly contributes about 90% of its export revenue. However, lower oil prices have restricted the government's ability to fund public spending. According to Brunei's Ministry of Finance, the country's national budget for fiscal year (FY) 2017â18 was about USD3.3 billion, down from about USD3.9 billion for FY 2015â16. Although Brunei and China have rarely engaged in naval confrontations over sovereignty claims around the Borneo island (in the SCS), a joint exploration programme most probably ensures that Brunei is unlikely to stake claim strongly even in the future. Furthermore, China is likely to deter Brunei from participating in third-party military and/or naval exercises in the SCS, importantly with the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (led by Australia, India, Japan, and the United States). In August 2018, Brunei and the United States held their first joint military exercise; IHS Markit assesses that China is likely to discourage such participation by Brunei going forward. A failure to hire local workers while developing projects is likely to trigger small-scale protests, involving less than 100 people, against BRI projects in Brunei. If Brunei and China (and other members of ASEAN) agree upon an SCS Code of Conduct, it will probably establish norms around settling disputes in the SCS further reducing the likelihood of confrontations. Headline: UPDATE 2 - Police and military operation ends with seven stowaways in custody near Shanklin, Isle of Wight
Details: It is being reported that seven stowaways have been arrested following a police and military operation on an oil tanker near Shanklin on the Isle of Wight today (25 October). The Special Boat Service were deployed to the scene after the stowaways became violent to the ship's crew. The ship was travelling from Lagos in Nigeria to Southampton in England, when the Liberian-flagged oil tanker dropped its anchor and the crew retreated to the citadel, which is a secure area in which they can lock themselves into, making it nearly impossible for others to get in. From the citadel, the crew were able to communicate with the Maritime Coastguard Agency. A three nautical mile exclusion zone is still in place around the vessel and it is unknown when it when be lifted.
