Headline: Hong Kong Police Detail Plot by Arrested Protesters, Highlighting Threat despite Lower Activity
Details:
On Wednesday, six protesters were charged in Hong Kong with conspiring to injure police officers in a plot using explosives. The protesters were allegedly planning to carry out the attack during a protest that took place on Sunday to memorialize Alex Chow Tsz-lok, a protester who died during a protest in November 2019. The suspects were allegedly planning to put a bomb inside of a shrine and then detonate it when police approached. The suspects were also accused of other bomb plots, including one that targeted the Caritas Medical Centre on January 27, the Shenzhen Bay port on January 28, and an MTR train on February 2.

Assessment: Protest activity across Hong Kong has decreased significantly compared to last year, although demonstrations are still taking place, such as a protest on Thursday, March 12, that resulted in scuffles between protesters and police in the Mong Kok District of Kowloon. The outbreak of novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has also provided another reason for the protesters to criticize the Hong Kong government and Beijing more broadly. Since the start of the year, police have carried out multiple raids against radical protesters that were in possession of firearms and/or explosive materials. This highlights the continued threat posed by such actors and all areas where protests are taking place should be avoided due to the potential for violent incidents taking place.

Headline: Port of Montreal strike continues for tenth consecutive day
Details: Employers at the Port of Montreal have stated that they are at an impasse with striking dockworkers, as the port shutdown reaches the 10-day mark. The negotiations between them and the striking workers is reportedly moving slowly, despite a comment from Labour Minister Filomena Tassi stating that there had been “encouraging progress made between the two parties.” The union have been asked to clear essential goods such as pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, as well as perishable foods and hazardous materials from the waterfront; however, the union has agreed only to move COVID-19-related cargo. The strike, which is being carried out by 1,125 dockworkers, revolves largely around wages and scheduling disputes.

Headline: Restrictions on heavy truck traffic throughout Colombia during Holy Week
Details: Local media sources reported that according to the the Official Press Release by the General Directorate of Traffic and Transport (DGTT), heavy cargo will be restricted at different points throughout Colombia during the Holy Week (April 12 - April 21). The DGTT has established restrictions on the circulation of vehicles of more than 3.4 tons at certain times of the year, specifically, in the so-called ""Exit Operations"" and ""Return Operations"" during vacation, as the number of vehicles tend to increase considerably during these periods. The roadways with heavy cargo traffic restrictions include:  Barranquilla - Cartagena, Bogotá - Choachi, Bogotá - Villavicencio - Acacías, Bucaramanga - Pamplona - Cúcuta, Ibagué - Honda, Medellín - Santa Fe De Antioquia. Headline: Magnitude 5.1 earthquake reported 12 kilometers north of Hachijo, Tokyo Prefecture
Details:
The United States Geological Survey has confirmed that a magnitude 5.1 earthquake has been recorded 12 kilometers north of Hachijo, Tokyo Prefecture. The quake occurred at a depth of 118 kilometers and no tsunami warning has been issued. 
USGS (United States Geological Survey) is a scientific agency of the U.S. government which monitors earthquake activity worldwide. USGS earthquake alerts are assessed primarily using the moment magnitude (Mw) scale. However, local magnitude (ML), surface-wave magnitude (Ms) or body-wave magnitude (Mb) may be used in lieu of the Mw scale. All magnitude scales should yield approximately the same value for any given earthquake.

Headline: Migrant Workers, Others Being Transported Home as India Extends Lockdown
Details:
On Friday, India extended its COVID-19 lockdown to at least May 18. It was originally set to be lifted after May 3. While business and travel restrictions will remain in place throughout much of the country, areas classified as lower risk will see some regulations lifted. Friday also saw the beginning of a government push to relocate migrant workers, students, pilgrims, tourists, and others who were caught away from their homes when the lockdown first went into effect. A train left the Hyderabad area Friday morning transporting around 1,200 migrant workers to Hatia in the state of Jharkhand. Another train was scheduled to depart Kerala for Odisha later on Friday. Some buses have also been put into service transporting people who had been stranded away from home, and ferries are operating between Chennai and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to facilitate returns. Such trips must be organized by the central or state-level governments, as private interstate travel remains mostly blocked during the lockdown.



Assessment: Workers or other returning passengers are receiving temperature checks and being screened for other COVID-19 symptoms before being allowed to board their trains or other forms of transportation, and police have been deployed at stations to ensure there are no unauthorized passengers. Social distancing measures are also being taken on trains, with train cars carrying fewer people than normal and returnees being separated into smaller groups to make the journeys. Many states have been making preparations for the expected return of large numbers of migrant workers, and most of them will be quarantined for 14 days upon their arrivals back home. The government has faced pressure from migrant workers in particular, who have sought to return to their hometowns from the cities they work in since the start of the lockdown. The workers transported out of Hyderabad Friday morning were themselves involved in a violent protest earlier this week demanding to return to their homes. Providing transportation for migrant workers and others who have been stranded away from their homes during the lockdown could help to reduce tensions in some areas where large numbers of workers have been stuck; however, there is also the potential for additional unrest or altercations with police if large numbers of travelers attempt to gather at transit hubs, or if some groups are not given transportation as soon as they would like. 



Transportation for these groups also raises the prospect of further spread of COVID-19, especially in the case of migrant workers, most of whom will be departing from cities, which have been the epicenters of the outbreak in India, to smaller towns and more rural locations, which have been relatively less affected. Although travelers will receive health screenings before their departures, there is the potential for asymptomatic cases to slip through. In addition, although many returning travelers will face quarantines when returning home, there have been reports of returning migrant workers in rural areas leaving quarantines early or coming and going at will. On the other hand, officially registering and transporting workers across state borders using government transportation may help to cut the number of unsanctioned interstate crossings that some state officials have expressed concern about. Individuals are advised to expect possible traffic increases around transit centers and to continue to follow all guidelines and restrictions issued by local authorities.

Headline: Protests Reported Over Illegal Housing Demolitions; Further Demonstrations Possible in Coming Weeks
Details:
In recent days, protests have broken out in numerous Egyptian cities over the government demolition of “illegal” housing. In Alexandria, demonstrations reportedly took place in the Mansheya neighborhood. Protests were also reported in Port Said on September 15, and some reports indicate that other governorates, including Qalyubia and Giza witnessed similar demonstrations last month. No further specifics were provided. Additionally, on September 12, the government reduces the fines for building code violations in over 20 governorates. 



Assessment: In order to minimize illegal building on agricultural sites, state-owned land, and unlicensed multi-story buildings, Egypt enacted the Law on Reconciliation and Building Violations in 2019, which allows citizens to pay fees to the government in order to legalize their building’s status and avoid demolition. However, recent protests highlight the opposition to the law as they claim it is discriminatory towards those with limited incomes who cannot pay the fines. The reconciliation period for building violations is set to end on September 30. Following this date, an uptick in government demolitions of housing is likely. As such, sporadic demonstrations are likely to continue in the short term, though large-scale protests are less likely to manifest due to harsh crackdown on opposition in Egypt and a 2013 law severely restricting protest activity.

Headline: UPDATE: Congestion issues ameliorate slightly at Los Angeles and Long Beach
Details: Shipping sources indicate on January 30 that congestion conditions are showing signs of improvement at the Port of Los Angeles and Long Beach. While congestion times average 3.31 days, higher than the 2.5-3 day 2018 average, it is an improvement over the 7.5-day peak in late 2018. The extent of the congestion has been described as reaching inland ports in Southern California as well. The congestion is due to increased volumes passing through the port as well as reduced productivity during the holiday season. Some shipping lines have diverted calls to the Port of Long Beach instead or may even omit the port call and discharge containers at the Port of Oakland. The cause has been attributed to the import surge of December 2018 that left a glut of containers with few chassis's available to meet the demand. Landside congestion with long lines of trucks at the terminal gates has also been reported, likely resulting in higher costs for end customers. Customers should expect the situation to continue until at least the beginning of February 2019.

Details: Industry sources indicate that customs authorities at both the Port of Wai Gao Qiao and the Yangshan deep-water port have implemented restrictions on meat transshipments, effective immediately. For the Yangshan deep-water port, all animal meat food products including hog casing (except seafood) that have been disinfected will be allowed to transship. The period of these special restrictions is not clear. The effort is likely in response to rising concerns about a swine flu outbreak in China.

Headline: UPDATE 1 - Opposition parties’ losses in Jordanian election to encourage ongoing mostly peaceful protests, highly unlikely to destabilise monarchy
Details: The Islamic Action Front (IAF), the Jordanian Muslim Brotherhood’s political arm, lost five seats (down from 15) in the parliamentary elections held on 10 November 2020. Voter turnout of 30% was down from 36% in 2016, and 57% in 2013, likely due to reduced public trust in the government and in its ability to enact change due to overruling royal prerogatives. Recurring anti-austerity protests have increasingly demanded that the system of governance change to increase the power of parliament at the expense of the monarchy. Parliament’s decisions are non-binding and King Abdullah II holds executive constitutional control, and appoints the prime minister. Independent, royalist candidates from rural areas continue to be overrepresented as a result of the electoral law.Significance: The results indicate that parliament will be more supportive of government policies (see Jordan: 19 October 2020: Election unlikely to affect Jordan’s COVID-19 recovery plan, focus on reducing state spending and growing agribusiness, pharmaceuticals). This is expected to reduce delays in decision-making on contentious issues, such as likely austerity measures in the 2021 budget. Prior to the election, the government had taken several steps to curtail the opposition, including dissolving the Muslim Brotherhood and closing the Muslim Brotherhood-controlled teachers’ syndicate for two years, as well as suppressing anti-government protests through wide-scale arrests (see Jordan: 31 July 2020: Jordanian actions against dissent, including application of COVID-19 state of emergency, increase protest risk around November election). The IAF is now likely to take a less conciliatory stance toward the government, by co-operating with other opposition parties on formulating alternative fiscal and foreign policy and suggesting frameworks for political reform, notably to increase the power of the Lower House and to change the electoral law. The opposition is likely to exploit protests by unemployed people and trade unions on any austerity measures to further their goals, resulting in more frequent and protracted rallies, likely attended by several thousand people at Amman’s Fourth Circle roundabout. Any effort to increase sales or income tax or reduce subsidies or public-sector salaries would be likely to trigger protests and strikes by public sector workers. Headline: Brief Seizure of Tanker near Strait of Hormuz Reflects Persistent Risk of Maritime Incidents
Details:
On Wednesday, media sources indicated that the brief seizure of a Hong Kong-flagged oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, near the Strait of Hormuz, on April 14 may have been a botched operation by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). According to reports, armed men boarded and commandeered the Hong Kong-flagged SC Taipei, bound for Saudi Arabia, near Iran’s Ras al-Kuh coast. The ship was detained for a short time before it and its 22-member crew of Chinese nationals were released and underway under the captain’s control. A United Nations database reportedly listed the mail-forwarding address for the ship’s owners as associated with the Shanghai-based Aoxing Ship Management, which was sanctioned by the US State Department last month for “knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.” This has led to speculation that the armed men were unaware of the vessel’s affiliation, and once this was discovered, released it to avoid an entanglement with ally Beijing.



Assessment: Indeed, it is also possible that the SC Taipei had been in distress and was merely being assisted by Iran; however, it has been reported that, prior to its release, the ship was heading toward Bandar Jask, the same location where a Norwegian-owned oil tanker was taken last year after it was hit by an explosion the US blamed on an Iranian mine. Additionally, Tuesday’s episode was reportedly one of several maritime incidents near the Strait of Hormuz recently, as, according to a private shipping firm, a US-flagged container ship was approached by two boats with a raised ladder on March 27, while another tanker said it was approached by IRGC vessels on April 2. While the frequency of harassment and other provocative activities around the Strait of Hormuz has generally tapered off following a spate of such incidents last year, the tensions between the US and Iran that are widely believed to have precipitated those interactions remain escalated, leaving open the possibility that oil tankers, container ships, and other commercial vessels could be targeted as part of Tehran’s efforts to push back against Washington and its Western allies over sanctions burdening its economy. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations organization has advised vessels operating in the region to exercise vigilance and caution, and to report all suspicious incidents.

Headline: U.S. Embassy in Panama City Issues Health Alert Regarding Changes to Movement Restrictions
Details:
On Monday, the U.S. Embassy in Panama City issued a Health Alert for American citizens in Panama. The message reads, in part:



“Event: Changes to Movement Restrictions Beginning September 14



On August 25, the Government of Panama announced plans to reduce movement restrictions and open up additional economic sectors, starting on September 7. The plan is conditional upon meeting certain criteria regarding the control of the COVID-19 pandemic in Panama.



On September 7 the Government of Panama opened the following economic sectors: Construction and related activities (engineers, architects, project managers, contractors, moving services), Panama Pacifico, Colon Free Zone and other free trade zones, private ship docks and sports fishing, tailor shops, shoe shops, and carwashes will resume operations.



On September 14, the following changes in movement restrictions will be implemented: Gender-based movement restrictions are lifted and ‘salvoconductos’ become null and void, except for those occupations that require movement during curfew hours. Curfew will be from 11pm to 5am, Monday through Saturday, with Sunday as a day of total quarantine in all provinces except for Bocas del Toro, Colon, and Chiriqui, where curfew will be from 7pm to 5am Monday through Friday, with a total quarantine on Saturday and Sunday.



For additional details about the plan, visit the website of the Ministry of the Presidency (https://www.presidencia.gob.pa/).”



The Health Alert can be viewed in its entirety at the following URL: https://pa.usembassy.gov/health-alert-u-s-embassy-panama-city-panama-september-14-2020/.

Headline: Search Continues for Two Missing Sailors from Cargo Ship that Sank Off of Vietnam
Details:
The Xin Hong, a Panama-flagged cargo ship, sank near Phu Quy Island off the coast of southern Vietnam’s Binh Thuan Province on Thursday afternoon. The ship’s captain had contacted Phu Quy authorities shortly before the incident to request emergency docking permission, but the ship capsized before being able to arrive at the island. There were 11 Chinese and four Vietnamese sailors on board, of whom 11 had been rescued by Friday morning, while two others were found dead. A search for the remaining two crew members was continuing.



Assessment: The Xin Hong was transporting clay from Malaysia to Hong Kong. The accident occurred in rough seas during inclement weather that is believed to have shifted cargo, which caused the ship to list to the side before capsizing. Disruptions to shipping activities are possible in the area while search and rescue operations are carried out for the two outstanding sailors, and there is also the potential for transportation problems arising from loose shipping containers fallen from the ship.

Headline: Traffic restrictions severely disrupt container movements in Mumbai
Details: On August 21, local sources reported that traffic restrictions imposed by the police department in Thane city, a suburb of Mumbai, have severely disrupted export-import container movement at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) since August 9. The restrictions have been imposed to allow repair works of the Mumbra-Kausa bypass road and a flyover along the road. Container movement to the following terminals are impacted: Gateway Terminals India, Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal (NSICT) and Nhava Sheva (India) Gateway Terminal (NSIGT). The traffic restriction for a few hours on an arterial road linking India’s busiest container port has roiled evacuation of import containers from the port to the container freight stations (CFS) and movement of export boxes to the port, resulting in congestion. As a result, police has stopped traffic movements from and to all terminals from 05:00 to 11:00 and from 17:00 to 23:00 on a daily basis from August 16 for one month, further exacerbating the situation. Trucks will reportedly be stopped at the PUB - Y junction. This week, tractor trailers carrying containers have been stuck on the road for 8-10 hours and inventory has piled up at the terminals.
